It automatically becomes a permanent member
It always stays for another four years
40090.e: Under Article 23 of the Charter, a retiring non-permanent member cannot be re-elected immediately. That way more states get a turn.
40090.m: A non-permanent member cannot be elected twice in a row.

40091.q: What majority does a state need in the General Assembly to be elected to the Security Council?
40091.e: Election to the Security Council counts as an important question. It needs two thirds of the states present and voting.
40091.m: A seat on the Security Council needs two thirds of the votes in the General Assembly.

40092.q: When was Switzerland a member of the UN Security Council for the first time?
40092.e: Switzerland was elected for 2023 and 2024. In May 2023 it held the presidency for the first time.
40092.m: Switzerland was on the Security Council for the first time in 2023 and 2024.

40093.q: In which city does the UN Security Council normally meet today?
40093.e: The Security Council meets at the UN headquarters in New York. Its very first meeting took place in London in 1946.
40093.m: The Security Council meets in New York.

40094.q: Who is Secretary-General of the UN (as of 2026)?
40094.e: António Guterres from Portugal has led the UN since 2017. He is supported by his deputy, Amina Mohammed.

a: A travel document for UN staff
40095.e: The laissez-passer is the UN's own travel document. Many states recognise it like a passport when staff travel on UN business.
40095.m: UN staff travel on official business with a laissez-passer.

40096.q: What title does the person who heads the United Nations Office in Geneva hold?
40096.e: The United Nations Office in Geneva is led by a Director-General, who reports directly to the Secretary-General.
40096.m: The UN Office in Geneva is headed by a Director-General.

40097.q: What is the Vienna International Centre, the UN seat in Vienna, popularly called?
40097.e: The building on the Danube opened in 1979. In Vienna it is usually just called UNO City.
40097.m: The UN seat in Vienna is popularly called UNO City.

40098.q: U Thant from Burma led the UN from 1961 to 1971. What was special about him?
a: He was the first Secretary-General from Asia
He was the first Secretary-General from Europe
He was the first Secretary-General from Switzerland
He led the UN for over 30 years
40098.e: Burma is now called Myanmar and is in Asia. U Thant was the first Secretary-General from this continent.
40098.m: U Thant was the first UN Secretary-General from Asia.

40099.q: Which office has António Guterres held since 2017?
40099.e: António Guterres has been Secretary-General of the United Nations since 1 January 2017. He succeeded Ban Ki-moon.

40100.q: Until when does António Guterres's second term as UN Secretary-General last?
40100.e: In 2021, the Security Council and the General Assembly confirmed Guterres for a second five-year term, which ends on 31 December 2026.
40100.m: António Guterres's second term ends at the end of 2026.

40101.q: What does the first name Kofi mean in the Akan language of West Africa?
40101.e: In Akan culture, children are often named after the day of the week they were born. Kofi is the name for a boy born on a Friday.
40101.m: The name Kofi stands for a boy born on a Friday.

40102.q: For which divided island did Kofi Annan present a reunification plan in 2004?
40102.e: The so-called Annan Plan was put to a vote in both parts of Cyprus in 2004. The Greek Cypriots rejected it, so it did not come into force.
40102.m: The Annan Plan for Cyprus failed in a referendum in 2004.

40103.q: What does a country have to be in order to become a member of the UN?
40103.e: Only independent states can join the UN. Montenegro, for example, became independent in 2006 and a member shortly afterwards.
40103.m: Only independent states can become UN members.

40105.q: Which state is not a member of the UN but only an observer?
40105.e: Vatican City and Palestine have the status of observer states at the UN. They may take part in discussions but not vote.
40105.m: Observer states may speak at the UN but not vote.

40106.q: Which small country in the Pacific is a member of the UN?
40106.e: Tuvalu is an independent island state and has been in the UN since 2000. Greenland belongs to Denmark, Hawaii to the USA and Tahiti to France.
40106.m: Even tiny island states like Tuvalu are in the UN.

40107.q: Which is the smallest UN member by area?
40107.e: Monaco is only about 2 square kilometres in size. Vatican City is even smaller, but it is not a UN member.
40107.m: Monaco is the smallest member of the UN.

40108.q: In which country on the border with Israel have Blue Helmets been deployed since 1978?
40108.e: The UN mission UNIFIL was set up in southern Lebanon in 1978 to calm the situation on the border with Israel. It is one of the largest Blue Helmet missions.
40108.m: Blue Helmets have been deployed in Lebanon since 1978.

40109.q: What does SWISSINT, a Swiss Army centre, do?
a: It prepares army members for peace missions abroad
40109.e: SWISSINT in Stans-Oberdorf in the canton of Nidwalden trains army members for missions abroad, for example UN missions or in Kosovo.
40109.m: SWISSINT prepares Swiss army members for peace missions.

40110.q: Which prize did the Canadian Lester Pearson receive in 1957 for his idea of a UN peacekeeping force?
40110.e: In 1956, Lester Pearson proposed placing a neutral UN force between the warring parties. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for it in 1957.
40110.m: Lester Pearson is considered one of the inventors of the Blue Helmets.

40111.q: What is typical of UN military observers, compared with armed Blue Helmet troops?
a: They fight on the front line
40111.e: Military observers monitor ceasefires and report on them. They carry no weapons and rely on the protection their UN role gives them.
40111.m: UN military observers carry no weapons.

40112.q: How are UN peace missions funded?
a: Through their own budget with compulsory contributions from states
Only with donations from private individuals
With entrance fees from the headquarters
With taxes the UN collects itself
40112.e: There is a separate budget for peacekeeping. All member states pay compulsory contributions to it according to a fixed formula.
40112.m: Member states pay for peace missions with compulsory contributions.

40113.q: What is special about Switzerland joining UNESCO?
a: It joined long before joining the UN
It joined only after joining the UN
It is still not a member today
It joined together with the EU
40113.e: Switzerland became a member of UNESCO as early as 1949. It only joined the UN itself in 2002, more than 50 years later.
40113.m: Switzerland was a member of UNESCO long before joining the UN.

40114.q: Which festival in Vevey did UNESCO add to the intangible cultural heritage list in 2016?
40114.e: The Fête des Vignerons is a winegrowers' festival that takes place in Vevey only about every 20 to 25 years. UNESCO added it to the intangible cultural heritage list in 2016.
40114.m: The rare winegrowers' festival of Vevey is UNESCO intangible cultural heritage.

40115.q: What is the UNESCO programme that protects important manuscripts, books and archives called?
40115.e: The “Memory of the World” programme lists valuable documents as documentary heritage.
40115.m: UNESCO protects valuable documents with the “Memory of the World” programme.

40116.q: What does the World Food Programme (WFP) mainly fight against?
40116.e: The WFP is the largest humanitarian organisation fighting hunger. It delivers food in emergencies and helps communities to feed themselves.

40117.q: How is the World Food Programme (WFP) funded?
40117.e: The WFP has no fixed budget from compulsory contributions. It relies on voluntary donations from states, companies and private individuals.
40117.m: The WFP depends on voluntary donations.

40118.q: What does the abbreviation WFP stand for?
40118.m: WFP is the abbreviation for the World Food Programme.

40119.q: With which two UN organisations does the WFP share its location in Rome?
40119.e: Three UN organisations dealing with food work in Rome: the FAO, the agricultural development fund IFAD and the WFP.
40119.m: Rome is the UN's centre for food and agriculture.

40120.q: What does the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) fight against?
40120.e: The FAO is a UN organisation. It helps countries produce enough food so that nobody has to go hungry.

40121.q: What does the FAO's Latin motto “Fiat panis” mean?
40121.e: “Fiat panis” means “Let there be bread”. The motto is in the FAO logo and shows its aim of defeating hunger.
40121.m: The FAO's motto means “Let there be bread”.

40123.q: On which day is World Environment Day, which UNEP organises?
40123.e: World Environment Day takes place every year on 5 June. It marks the start of the Stockholm environmental conference on 5 June 1972.

40124.q: In which African city does the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) have its headquarters?
40124.e: UNEP is based in Nairobi, the capital of Kenya. It was the first UN organisation with its headquarters in Africa.
40124.m: The UN Environment Programme is based in Nairobi in Kenya.

40125.q: Which toxic metal does a UN agreement from 2013 protect against?
40125.e: The Minamata Convention is meant to protect people and the environment from toxic mercury. Mercury used to be found, for example, in thermometers.
40125.m: A UN agreement protects against toxic mercury.

40126.q: What does the abbreviation UNDP stand for?
40126.e: UNDP stands for “United Nations Development Programme”. It helps countries reduce poverty and develop.
40126.m: The UNDP is the UN's development programme.

40127.q: In which city does the UNDP have its headquarters?
40127.e: The UNDP is based in New York, near the UN headquarters. But it works in around 170 countries and territories.
40127.m: The development programme UNDP is based in New York.

40128.q: Which well-known index has the UNDP published every year since 1990?
40128.e: The Human Development Index (HDI) measures life expectancy, education and income. It appears in the Human Development Report.
40128.m: The HDI shows how well people can live in a country.

40129.q: Which three areas go into the Human Development Index?
40129.e: The HDI measures life expectancy, years of schooling and income per person. That way it shows more than just a country's wealth.
40129.m: The HDI measures health, education and income.

40130.q: What does a high score on the Human Development Index (HDI) show?
a: People live long, are well educated and have enough income
The country has a large army
The country has a particularly large population
40130.e: The HDI measures life expectancy, education and income. A high score means people there have good living conditions.
40130.m: A high HDI means good living conditions.

40131.q: What does the development programme UNDP mainly work against?
40131.e: The UNDP helps countries reduce poverty and develop. It works in around 170 countries and territories.

40132.q: Which goals from the 2030 Agenda does the UNDP support in many countries?
40132.e: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in 2015. The UNDP helps countries reach them by 2030.
40132.m: The UNDP helps with the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

40133.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals does the 2030 Agenda, which the UNDP supports, include?
40133.e: In 2015 the UN adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals, for example zero hunger and quality education. They are to be reached by 2030.

40134.q: Which disease is the work of UNAIDS aimed at?
40134.e: UNAIDS is the joint UN programme against HIV and AIDS. It coordinates the work of many UN organisations in this area.
40134.m: UNAIDS fights HIV and AIDS worldwide.

40135.q: In which city does UNAIDS have its headquarters?
40135.e: UNAIDS is based in Geneva. The World Health Organization (WHO) is also there.

40136.q: What does “UN” stand for in the name UNAIDS?
40136.e: UN is the abbreviation for United Nations. UNAIDS has been working since 1996.
40136.m: UNAIDS is a programme of the United Nations.

40137.q: On which day is World AIDS Day?
40137.e: World AIDS Day has taken place every year on 1 December since 1988. It remembers the victims and calls for solidarity.

40138.q: Which symbol stands worldwide for solidarity with people living with HIV?
40138.e: The red ribbon became well known in 1991. It shows solidarity with people living with HIV.
40138.m: The red ribbon is the symbol of solidarity with people living with HIV.

40139.q: What does the “I” in the abbreviation HIV stand for?
40139.e: HIV stands for “human immunodeficiency virus”. It weakens the body's defences.
40139.m: HIV is a virus that weakens the body's defences.

40140.q: What is special about UNAIDS compared with other UN organisations?
a: It is a joint programme of several UN organisations
It is paid for only by Switzerland
40140.e: UNAIDS brings together several UN organisations such as the WHO, UNICEF and the UNDP. These co-sponsors work together against HIV and AIDS.
40140.m: Several UN organisations work together in UNAIDS.

40141.q: By which year does UNAIDS want to end AIDS as a threat to public health?
40141.e: The aim of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 is part of the 2030 Agenda. UNAIDS bases its strategy on it.
40141.m: UNAIDS wants to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

40142.q: In which city is the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) based?
40142.e: The IAEA is based at the Vienna International Centre in Vienna. This complex of buildings is also called “UNO City”.
40142.m: The IAEA is based in Vienna.

40143.q: What does the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) work for?
a: The peaceful use of nuclear energy
40143.e: The IAEA was founded in 1957. It promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy and wants to prevent nuclear weapons from being made.
40143.m: The IAEA works for the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

40144.q: Which famous speech by US President Eisenhower led to the founding of the IAEA?
40144.e: Dwight D. Eisenhower gave the “Atoms for Peace” speech at the UN in 1953. He proposed an agency for the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
40144.m: The IAEA goes back to the idea of “Atoms for Peace”.

40145.q: Which prize did the IAEA receive in 2005 for its work against nuclear weapons?
40145.e: The IAEA and its then head Mohamed ElBaradei received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2005. It honoured their work against the spread of nuclear weapons.
40145.m: The IAEA was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2005.

40146.q: What does the INES scale, which the IAEA helped develop, rate?
a: How serious a nuclear accident is
How hot a summer's day is
40146.e: The INES scale ranges from level 1 (anomaly) to level 7 (major accident). This allows nuclear accidents to be compared worldwide.
40146.m: The INES scale rates nuclear accidents.

40147.q: Which two accidents were rated at the highest level, 7, on the INES scale?
40147.e: The disasters at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 are the only level 7 accidents. The 1969 accident at the Swiss experimental reactor in Lucens is rated lower.
40147.m: Chernobyl and Fukushima are the worst nuclear accidents in history.

40148.q: What do IAEA experts check in many countries?
a: Whether nuclear facilities are used only peacefully
40148.e: IAEA inspectors visit nuclear facilities. They check that no material is diverted for nuclear weapons.
40148.m: The IAEA checks that nuclear facilities are used peacefully.

40149.q: What is the World Meteorological Organization (WMO)?
a: A UN organisation for weather and climate
40149.e: The WMO is a specialised agency of the UN. Through it, the weather services of almost every country work together.
40149.m: The WMO is the UN's weather organisation.

40150.q: In which city does the World Meteorological Organization have its headquarters?
40150.e: The WMO is based in Geneva. Many international organisations work there.
40150.m: The WMO is based in Geneva.

40151.q: Which early warning goal is the UN pursuing with the WMO by 2027?
a: Everyone should be protected by early warning systems
Every country should own a weather plane
All weather forecasts should be printed for free
Every school should have a weather station
40151.e: With the “Early Warnings for All” initiative, everyone should be protected from dangerous weather by early warning systems by the end of 2027. The WMO plays a leading role in this.
40151.m: Early warnings of severe weather should soon reach everyone.

40152.q: In which city is the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) based?
40152.e: WIPO has its headquarters in Geneva. It is responsible for protecting inventions, trademarks and works.

40153.q: What is meant by intellectual property?
a: Rights to inventions, trademarks and works
40153.e: Intellectual property protects ideas and creative achievements, for example through patents, trademarks and copyright. WIPO promotes this protection worldwide.
40153.m: Intellectual property protects ideas and creative works.

40154.q: In which Swiss city was an important copyright agreement, now administered by WIPO, signed in 1886?
40154.e: The Berne Convention of 1886 protects works of literature and art. Today it is administered by WIPO.
40154.m: The Berne Convention has protected books, music and art since 1886.

40155.q: What does a patent protect against?
40155.e: A patent gives the inventor the sole right to use the invention for a certain time. Others may not copy and sell it without permission.
40155.m: A patent protects an invention from being copied.

a: Books, music and pictures from being copied
40156.e: Anyone who writes a book, composes a song or paints a picture is its creator. Others may not simply copy and sell the work without permission.

40157.q: Which country topped WIPO's Global Innovation Index in 2025?
40157.e: In the Global Innovation Index 2025, Switzerland came first, as it has done in many years before. The index compares how innovative countries are.
40157.m: According to WIPO, Switzerland is the most innovative country in the world (as of 2025).

40158.q: In intellectual property, what is meant by a “trademark”?
a: A company's protected name or logo
40158.e: A trademark identifies a company's products, for example with a name or logo. If it is protected, nobody else may use it.
40158.m: A trademark is a protected company name or logo.

40159.q: In which city was the office BIRPI, the forerunner of WIPO, until 1960?
40159.e: The BIRPI office administered the intellectual property agreements from Bern. In 1960 it moved to Geneva and later became WIPO.
40159.m: WIPO's forerunner was based in Bern.

40160.q: What does UN Women work for?
40160.e: UN Women was founded by the UN in 2010. It works worldwide for the rights of women and girls.

40161.q: Where does UN Women have its headquarters?
40161.e: UN Women has its headquarters in New York. It also has offices in many countries.
40161.m: UN Women works from its headquarters in New York.

40162.q: Which well-known actress presented UN Women's HeForShe campaign at the UN in 2014?
40162.e: Emma Watson, known as Hermione from Harry Potter, gave a speech at the UN in 2014. The first head of UN Women was Michelle Bachelet from Chile.
40162.m: Emma Watson made the HeForShe campaign well known.

40163.q: What is the name of the UN Women campaign in which men and boys stand up for equality?
40163.e: The HeForShe campaign started in 2014. The actress Emma Watson presented it with a speech at the UN.
40163.m: In HeForShe, men stand up for equality.

40164.q: Which colour is at the centre of the UN campaign against violence against women?
40164.e: With the “Orange the World” campaign, buildings are lit up in orange every year from 25 November. This draws attention to violence against women.
40164.m: Orange is the colour against violence against women.

40165.q: Which of the Sustainable Development Goals directly concerns the work of UN Women?
40165.e: The fifth goal of the 2030 Agenda is gender equality. UN Women helps countries achieve this goal.
40165.m: The fifth sustainability goal calls for equality between women and men.

40166.q: Which people is the UN agency UNRWA responsible for?
40166.e: UNRWA is the United Nations agency for Palestine refugees in the Middle East. It looks after the refugees and their descendants.
40166.m: UNRWA helps Palestine refugees in the Middle East.

a: To help Palestine refugees after a war
To organise football tournaments in the Middle East
40167.e: After the war of 1948, many Palestinians had to leave their homes. The UN founded UNRWA for them in 1949.
40167.m: UNRWA was founded for Palestine refugees.

40168.q: In which region of the world does UNRWA work?
40168.e: UNRWA helps in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. All these areas are in the Middle East.
40168.m: UNRWA helps refugees in the Middle East.

40169.q: Which country does Philippe Lazzarini, who led UNRWA from 2020, come from?
40169.e: Philippe Lazzarini comes from Neuchâtel. He worked for many years for the ICRC and the UN before becoming Commissioner-General of UNRWA in 2020.
40169.m: A Swiss man led UNRWA from 2020.

40170.q: What do people receive at UNRWA's health centres?
40170.e: As well as schools, UNRWA runs health centres. There the sick are treated and children are vaccinated.
40170.m: UNRWA also looks after the refugees' health.

40171.q: Which service does UNRWA mainly offer refugee children?
40171.e: UNRWA runs hundreds of schools for refugee children. There are also health centres and social support.
40171.m: UNRWA enables many refugee children to go to school.

40172.q: How does UNRWA differ from the UN Refugee Agency UNHCR?
a: It is responsible only for Palestine refugees
It is responsible only for climate refugees
40172.e: The UNHCR looks after refugees all over the world. For Palestine refugees in its five areas of operation, however, only UNRWA is responsible.
40172.m: UNRWA is a separate agency just for Palestine refugees.

40173.q: Where does most of UNRWA's money come from?
40173.e: UNRWA receives only a small part from the regular UN budget. Most comes from voluntary contributions from states and organisations.
40173.m: UNRWA lives mainly on voluntary contributions.

40174.q: In which city is the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) based?
40174.e: The ICAO is based in Montreal in Canada. The airlines' trade association IATA is also based there.
40174.m: The ICAO is based in Montreal.

40175.q: What does “civil aviation” in the ICAO's name mean?
40175.e: Civil aviation includes, for example, passenger and cargo flights. The ICAO is based on the Chicago Convention of 1944.
40175.m: Civil aviation means all flights that are not military.

40176.q: What are four-letter ICAO codes like LSZH for Zurich used for?
40176.e: Every airport has its own ICAO code, Zurich for example LSZH. Pilots and air traffic controllers use it. Luggage tags, on the other hand, show the three-letter IATA code ZRH.

40177.q: Which language must pilots and air traffic controllers master for international radio communication?
40177.e: The ICAO requires pilots and air traffic controllers in international traffic to speak good English. That way everyone understands each other.
40177.m: English is spoken in international aviation radio.

40178.q: Which spelling alphabet with words like “Alfa, Bravo, Charlie” comes from the ICAO?
40178.e: The international spelling alphabet was set by the ICAO. Pilots and air traffic controllers use it to spell clearly, for example “Zulu” for Z.
40178.m: With “Alfa, Bravo, Charlie” you spell clearly over the radio.

40179.q: Thanks to ICAO standards, which document has a machine-readable zone worldwide?
40179.e: The ICAO sets out what machine-readable passports must look like. That way passports can be read in the same way at borders worldwide.
40179.m: Thanks to the ICAO, passports can be read by machine worldwide.

40180.q: What is the ICAO's main task?
40180.e: The ICAO draws up standards and recommendations for safety, navigation and environmental protection in aviation. Member states put them into their laws.
40180.m: The ICAO ensures safe flying with worldwide rules.

40181.q: What kind of organisation is the ICAO?
40181.e: The ICAO has been working since 1947 and soon became a UN specialised agency. It sets rules for aviation.
40181.m: The ICAO is a UN specialised agency.

40182.q: What does the ICAO want to achieve with the CORSIA programme?
a: To offset the CO2 emissions of flights
40182.e: CORSIA is a system for offsetting CO2 emissions in international air transport. The ICAO adopted it in 2016.
40182.m: With CORSIA, aviation wants to offset its CO2 emissions.

40183.q: Which mountain sports tradition did UNESCO add to the intangible cultural heritage list in 2019 at the request of Switzerland, France and Italy?
40183.e: Alpinism was recognised in 2019 as shared cultural heritage of Switzerland, France and Italy. It includes knowledge about mountains, weather and safety.
40183.m: Mountaineering in the Alps is UNESCO intangible cultural heritage.

40184.q: Which knowledge from Switzerland and Austria has been on the intangible cultural heritage list since 2018?
40184.e: Switzerland and Austria jointly submitted their knowledge of protection against avalanches. UNESCO added it to the intangible cultural heritage list in 2018.
40184.m: Knowledge about avalanches is shared cultural heritage of the Alpine countries.

40185.q: Which World Heritage Site in eastern Switzerland shows especially well how mountains are formed?
40185.e: The Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008. There you can see how older rock layers were pushed over younger ones.
40185.m: In the Tectonic Arena Sardona you can see how the Alps were formed.

40186.q: Which mountain in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its fossils of marine reptiles?
40186.e: Many well-preserved fossils of marine reptiles and fish were found on Monte San Giorgio. It has been a World Heritage Site since 2003.
40186.m: Monte San Giorgio is a treasure trove of fossils.

40187.q: Which UN organisation founded the WFP together with the UN General Assembly?
40187.e: The WFP was set up jointly by the UN General Assembly and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Both still oversee it today.
40187.m: The WFP is a joint creation of the UN and the FAO.

40188.q: Which Sustainable Development Goal is at the heart of the WFP's work?
40188.e: Goal 2 of the 2030 Agenda aims to end hunger by 2030. That is exactly what the World Food Programme works for.
40188.m: The second sustainability goal is “Zero hunger”.

40189.q: For which area does the WFP take the lead within the UN in major humanitarian crises?
40189.e: In disasters, the WFP leads cooperation on logistics. It organises transport, storage and supply chains for many aid organisations.
40189.m: The WFP is the logistics expert of UN emergency aid.

40190.q: Which large organisation does the FAO belong to?
40190.e: The FAO is a specialised agency of the United Nations. It works worldwide for food and agriculture.
40190.m: The FAO is a UN organisation.

40191.q: Which UN organisation helps with food deliveries after disasters and works closely with the FAO?
40191.e: The World Food Programme (WFP) brings food to people in need. Like the FAO, it is based in Rome.
40191.m: The World Food Programme brings food to people in need.

40192.q: Which grain was at the centre of an International Year overseen by the FAO in 2023?
40192.e: The UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets. Millet is nutritious and grows even in dry conditions.
40192.m: Millet is a hardy grain for dry regions.

40193.q: Which pests does the FAO warn about with its own worldwide monitoring service?
40193.e: Swarms of desert locusts can destroy entire harvests. The FAO monitors them and warns affected countries early.
40193.m: The FAO warns of locust swarms before they destroy harvests.

40194.q: What does the UN Environment Programme show every year in a report on the climate?
a: How far the world is from its climate goals
Which country has the nicest weather
How many tourists travel to the mountains
40194.e: The Emissions Gap Report compares how many greenhouse gases countries emit with how many they should. This shows how much is still missing in climate protection.
40194.m: A UN report shows every year how much is still missing in climate protection.

40195.q: Which agreement on hazardous waste, looked after by UNEP, is named after a Swiss city?
40195.e: The 1989 Basel Convention regulates how hazardous waste may be transported across borders. Its secretariat is in Geneva.
40195.m: The Basel Convention controls the trade in hazardous waste.

40196.q: What is UNEP's highest body, in which all UN member states are represented, called?
40196.e: The UN Environment Assembly meets in Nairobi and sets the priorities of global environmental policy. All 193 UN members can take part.
40196.m: In the UN Environment Assembly, all states discuss the environment.

40197.q: Which 1992 agreement for protecting biodiversity is looked after by UNEP?
40197.e: The Convention on Biological Diversity was signed at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992. It protects the diversity of animals, plants and habitats.
40197.m: The Convention on Biological Diversity protects the variety of life.

40198.q: Which report does the WMO publish every year on the world's climate?
a: State of the Global Climate report
40198.e: In the “State of the Global Climate” report, the WMO sums up a year's temperatures, sea levels and extreme weather.
40198.m: The WMO reports every year on the state of the climate.

40199.q: Which high-altitude Swiss research station measures the air for the WMO's “Global Atmosphere Watch” programme?
40199.e: The Jungfraujoch research station is at around 3,500 metres. It is a WMO global measuring station for clean high-altitude air.
40199.m: On the Jungfraujoch, the air is measured for the whole world.

40200.q: What do weather satellites, whose data is shared through the WMO, observe?
40200.e: Weather satellites orbit the Earth and photograph clouds and storms. Their images help all countries forecast the weather.
40200.m: Weather satellites watch the weather from space.

40201.q: Over how many years is a climate normal period calculated under WMO rules?
40201.e: Climate is the average weather over a long time. The WMO uses periods of 30 years for this, for example 1991 to 2020.
40201.m: Climate describes the weather over 30 years.

40202.q: With which disease does the IAEA help poorer countries through the “Rays of Hope” initiative?
40202.e: With “Rays of Hope”, the IAEA supports countries in setting up radiotherapy against cancer. In this way the peaceful use of nuclear technology also helps in medicine.
40202.m: Nuclear technology can also help in treating cancer.

40203.q: Which UN women's fund became part of UN Women in 2010?
40203.e: UN Women was formed from four older UN bodies, including the Development Fund for Women, UNIFEM.
40203.m: UN Women brought together several UN bodies for women.

40204.q: What is the UN commission called that meets every March in New York to discuss women's rights and is supported by UN Women?
a: Commission on the Status of Women
40204.e: The Commission on the Status of Women has existed since 1946. It meets every year in New York, and UN Women prepares its sessions.
40204.m: The UN Commission on the Status of Women meets every year in New York.

40205.q: Where does Switzerland rank in the UNDP's Human Development Index?
40205.e: For years, Switzerland has been among the countries in the top places of the HDI. Health, education and income are very high here.
40205.m: Switzerland is right at the top of the HDI.

40206.q: What does the first “95” in UNAIDS's 95-95-95 targets mean?
a: 95 per cent of people with HIV know their status
95 per cent of all people are vaccinated
95 countries have no more HIV cases
95 per cent of hospitals test for HIV
40206.e: The first target means that 95 per cent of people with HIV know about their infection. The other targets concern treatment and a suppressed viral load.
40206.m: Anyone who knows about their HIV infection can get treatment.

40207.q: Why do companies have their trademark protected?
a: So that nobody may copy their name and logo
So that they do not have to pay taxes
So that they get more employees
So that customers can shop for free
40207.e: Only the company itself may use a protected trademark. That way customers can be sure they are buying the real product.
40207.m: Nobody may copy a protected trademark.

40208.q: What must you not do with a copyrighted song without permission?
40208.e: Listening and singing along are allowed. But anyone who copies a song and makes money from it needs the creators' permission.
40208.m: You may not simply copy and sell protected works.

40209.q: UNRWA has a headquarters in Amman. In which country is this city?
40209.e: Amman is the capital of Jordan. A particularly large number of Palestine refugees live in Jordan.
40209.m: Amman is the capital of Jordan.

40210.q: Why does UNRWA still exist today, although it was founded back in 1949?
a: Many refugees and their descendants still need help
It still has money left over
It is required by law forever
40210.e: No lasting solution has been found for the Palestine refugees. That is why the UN keeps extending UNRWA's mandate.
40210.m: UNRWA has been helping for many decades.

40211.q: What does International Civil Aviation Day commemorate?
a: The signing of the Convention on Civil Aviation
The first flight over the Alps
40211.e: The Convention on International Civil Aviation was signed on 7 December 1944. This world day commemorates it.
40211.m: Civil Aviation Day commemorates the 1944 Convention.

40212.q: Who is represented in the ICAO Assembly?
40212.e: The member states sit in the ICAO Assembly. It meets at least every three years.
40212.m: In the ICAO, the states decide together.

40213.q: In which city does the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have its headquarters?
40213.e: The ICRC was founded in Geneva in 1863 and still has its headquarters there today. Legally, it is a private association under Swiss law.
40213.m: The ICRC has its headquarters in Geneva.

40214.q: Which Swiss general was one of the five founders of the ICRC?
40214.e: The so-called Committee of Five included Henry Dunant, Gustave Moynier, Louis Appia, Théodore Maunoir and General Guillaume-Henri Dufour. Dufour was also the committee's first president.
40214.m: General Dufour was one of the five founders of the ICRC.

40215.q: What nationality must members of the ICRC's Committee have?
40215.e: The Committee itself, the ICRC's highest body, has 15 to 25 members, all of whom are Swiss citizens. Staff around the world, on the other hand, can come from many countries.
40215.m: Only Swiss citizens sit on the ICRC's Committee.

40216.q: Which prize has the ICRC already received three times?
40216.e: The ICRC received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917, 1944 and 1963. The first two times it was honoured for its work in the world wars.
40216.m: The ICRC has won the Nobel Peace Prize three times.

40217.q: Who do ICRC delegates regularly visit during wars to check how they are being treated?
40217.e: The ICRC visits prisoners of war and other detainees and checks whether they are treated humanely. This right is laid down in the Geneva Conventions.
40217.m: The ICRC checks whether prisoners are treated humanely in war.

40218.q: What is the ICRC's tracing service responsible for?
40218.e: The tracing service helps families separated by war or disasters to get back in touch. To do this, it collects information about prisoners, missing persons and displaced people.
40218.m: The ICRC tracing service brings separated families back together.

40219.q: What is special about Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, who became President of the ICRC in 2022?
a: She is the first woman to head the ICRC
She is also a Federal Councillor
She is the first president from Japan
40219.e: The Swiss diplomat Mirjana Spoljaric Egger took over the office from Peter Maurer in October 2022. Before her, the ICRC had only been led by men.
40219.m: Mirjana Spoljaric Egger is the first female President of the ICRC.

40220.q: Which museum in Geneva is right next to the ICRC headquarters?
a: Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum
40220.e: The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum shows the history of humanitarian aid. It stands right next to the ICRC headquarters.
40220.m: The Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum stands next to the ICRC in Geneva.

40221.q: What does the Red Cross symbol look like?
a: Red cross on a white background
White cross on a red background
Red cross on a blue background
White cross on a green background
40221.e: The protective emblem is a red cross on a white background. It is one of the best-known symbols in the world.
40221.m: The Red Cross symbol shows a red cross on a white background.

40223.q: Which protective emblem do many aid societies in mainly Muslim countries use?
40223.e: The Red Crescent was first used by the Ottoman Empire in the 1870s. In 1929 it was officially recognised as a protective emblem.
40223.m: The Red Crescent has equal status with the Red Cross.

40225.q: What is the Red Cross symbol used for as a protective emblem in an armed conflict?
a: It protects medical staff and hospitals
40225.e: Anyone or anything bearing the protective emblem, for example medical staff, ambulances or hospitals, must not be attacked. This is laid down in the Geneva Conventions.
40225.m: Helpers and hospitals with the protective emblem must not be attacked.

40226.q: Can you simply use the Red Cross symbol as a logo for your own products?
40226.e: The use of the emblem is protected by law so that it keeps its protective effect in war. Misuse can be punished.
40226.m: The Red Cross symbol may not be used however you like.

40227.q: How many officially recognised protective emblems are there in the Red Cross Movement today?
40227.e: Today there are the Red Cross, the Red Crescent and the Red Crystal. In the past, the Red Lion and Sun, which Iran used until 1980, was also recognised.
40227.m: The Red Cross, Red Crescent and Red Crystal are the three protective emblems.

40228.q: With which treaty was the red cross first set as a protective emblem in 1864?
40228.e: The First Geneva Convention of 1864 made the red cross on a white background the distinctive sign for medical services. This made the symbol internationally binding.
40228.m: Since 1864, the red cross has been an internationally recognised protective emblem.

40229.q: What does the small “Swiss Red Cross” logo on a clothing collection bag show?
a: That the collection belongs to the Red Cross
That the bag is protected in war
That a chemist's hands out the bag
40229.e: The small indicative emblem only shows that something belongs to the Red Cross Movement. The large protective emblem used in war is something different.
40229.m: The indicative emblem shows that something belongs to the Red Cross.

40230.q: In which Swiss city was Henry Dunant born?
40230.e: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva in 1828. Later, in Geneva, he founded the Red Cross together with others.

40231.q: What job did Henry Dunant do before he devoted himself to humanitarian aid?
40231.e: Dunant was a merchant and had business in Algeria. In 1859 he went to northern Italy to look for support for this business.
40231.m: Henry Dunant was originally a businessman.

40232.q: What happened to Henry Dunant in 1867, a few years after the Red Cross was founded?
40232.e: Dunant's businesses failed and he had to declare bankruptcy. After that he left Geneva and lived in poverty for a long time.
40232.m: Henry Dunant lost his entire fortune in 1867.

40233.q: Which award did Henry Dunant receive in 1901, as one of the very first ever?
40233.e: In 1901, Dunant shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. At the time he was living poor and withdrawn.
40233.m: Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize.

40234.q: In which present-day country is Solferino?
40234.e: Solferino is in northern Italy, south of Lake Garda. The battle that Henry Dunant witnessed took place there in 1859.

40235.q: Which day is marked every year on 8 May, Henry Dunant's birthday?
40235.e: On 8 May, the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement celebrates World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day. The date marks Dunant's birthday.
40235.m: 8 May is World Red Cross Day.

40236.q: In which century did the Battle of Solferino take place?
40236.e: The battle took place in 1859, so in the 19th century. A few years later, in 1863, the Red Cross was founded.
40236.m: The Battle of Solferino was in 1859.

40237.q: What did Henry Dunant do after the Battle of Solferino?
a: He organised help for the wounded
40237.e: Dunant saw thousands of wounded lying without care. In nearby Castiglione delle Stiviere, he organised help for soldiers of all sides with women from the area.
40237.m: After Solferino, Dunant helped the wounded of both sides.

40238.q: Which phrase used by the women helping in Castiglione became a symbol of helping all the wounded?
40238.e: “Tutti fratelli” means “All are brothers”. The women cared for the wounded, no matter which army they came from.
40238.m: “Tutti fratelli” means that all the wounded deserve help.

40239.q: Which countries fought against Austria at Solferino in 1859?
40239.e: The battle was part of the struggle for the unification of Italy. Austria lost it and had to give up Lombardy.
40239.m: At Solferino, France and Sardinia-Piedmont defeated Austria.

40240.q: What is the basic idea of the Geneva Conventions?
40240.e: The Geneva Conventions set out how people who do not fight, or no longer fight, are protected. These include the wounded, prisoners of war and civilians.
40240.m: The Geneva Conventions protect people who are no longer fighting.

40242.q: How many Geneva Conventions were adopted in 1949 after the Second World War?
40242.e: Four agreements were adopted on 12 August 1949. They are still considered the core of international humanitarian law today.
40242.m: There have been four Geneva Conventions since 1949.

40243.q: Which group does the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 especially protect?
40243.e: The Fourth Convention protects the civilian population in war and in occupied territories. It came about as a lesson from the suffering of civilians in the Second World War.
40243.m: The Fourth Geneva Convention protects the civilian population.

40244.q: Who is the Third Geneva Convention about?
40244.e: The Third Convention regulates the treatment of prisoners of war. They must be treated humanely and cared for, and must not be tortured.
40244.m: The Third Geneva Convention protects prisoners of war.

40245.q: What is the area of law that the Geneva Conventions belong to called?
40245.e: International humanitarian law sets rules for armed conflicts. It is meant to limit suffering, even when a war cannot be prevented.
40245.m: The Geneva Conventions are the core of international humanitarian law.

40246.q: Do rules of the Geneva Conventions also apply in a civil war?
a: Yes, there are minimum rules for civil wars too
No, only in wars between states
40246.e: An article found in all four Geneva Conventions also applies to civil wars. Everyone who is no longer fighting must be treated humanely.
40246.m: Minimum rules of the Geneva Conventions also apply in civil wars.

40248.q: What do the 1977 Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions mainly strengthen?
40248.e: Two Additional Protocols were adopted in 1977. Among other things, they better protect people who are not fighting from attacks.
40248.m: The 1977 Additional Protocols better protect the civilian population.

40249.q: Where is the UN Human Rights Council based?
40249.e: The Human Rights Council meets at the UN's European seat in Geneva. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights is also based in Geneva.
40249.m: The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva.

40250.q: What does the UN Human Rights Council work for?
40250.e: The Human Rights Council was founded in 2006. It monitors whether states respect human rights and draws attention to violations.
40250.m: The UN Human Rights Council protects human rights.

40251.q: Which UN office based in Geneva supports the work of the Human Rights Council?
a: Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights
40251.e: The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) prepares sessions and documents human rights violations. It is led by the High Commissioner for Human Rights.
40251.m: The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights supports the Human Rights Council.

40252.q: Are all UN states members of the UN Human Rights Council at the same time?
a: No, only an elected selection of states
No, only the five veto powers
40252.e: The Council has 47 members, divided among the world's regions. They are elected by the UN General Assembly.
40252.m: 47 elected states sit on the Human Rights Council.

40253.q: Does a state stay a member of the UN Human Rights Council forever?
a: No, it is elected for a set time
Yes, but only the founding states
No, it stays only one day
40253.e: The term lasts three years. A state may be elected at most twice in a row.
40253.m: Members of the Human Rights Council are elected for three years.

40254.q: Who elects the members of the UN Human Rights Council?
40254.e: The members are chosen by the General Assembly in a secret ballot. Whoever gets an absolute majority of the votes is elected.
40254.m: The UN General Assembly elects the members of the Human Rights Council.

40255.q: What is the Human Rights Council's “Universal Periodic Review” (UPR)?
a: All UN states are reviewed regularly
40255.e: In this procedure, the human rights situation in every UN member state is examined regularly. Switzerland must also undergo this review.
40255.m: In the UPR, every UN state is reviewed regularly.

40256.q: At least how many times a year does the Human Rights Council meet for regular sessions?
40256.e: The Council holds at least three sessions every year, lasting at least ten weeks in total. In crises it can also call special sessions.
40256.m: The Human Rights Council meets at least three times a year.

40257.q: What does the “Broken Chair” sculpture in front of the UN in Geneva show?
a: A chair with a broken leg
40257.e: The sculpture shows a giant wooden chair that is missing part of one leg. The broken leg is a reminder of people injured by mines.
40257.m: The Broken Chair is a giant chair with a broken leg.

40258.q: Which weapons was the Broken Chair originally a memorial against?
40258.e: The sculpture was created as a memorial against anti-personnel mines. It was meant to encourage states to sign the ban on these mines.
40258.m: The Broken Chair is a warning against landmines.

40259.q: What does the 1997 Ottawa Convention ban?
40259.e: The Ottawa Convention bans anti-personnel mines. The Broken Chair was meant to encourage states to join it.
40259.m: The Ottawa Convention bans anti-personnel mines.

40260.q: What material is the Broken Chair made of?
40260.e: The sculpture is made of wood. Despite its size, it is a piece of furniture on a giant scale.
40260.m: The Broken Chair is made of wood.

40261.q: Which organisation had the Broken Chair put up in Geneva?
40261.e: Handicap International stands up for people with disabilities, including mine victims. Today the organisation is called Humanity & Inclusion.
40261.m: Handicap International had the Broken Chair put up.

40262.q: What is the broken leg of the Broken Chair meant to remind us of?
40262.e: The broken leg stands for the injuries of mine victims. Since 2007 the sculpture has stood once again on the square in front of the UN.
40262.m: The broken leg is a reminder of mine victims.

40263.q: To which other weapons was the message of the Broken Chair extended in 2008?
40263.e: Since 2008, the Broken Chair has also stood for the fight against cluster bombs. Like mines, these can injure people long after a war.
40263.m: The Broken Chair is also a warning against cluster bombs.

40264.e: Gavi is a worldwide alliance that promotes vaccinations in poorer countries. The name originally stood for “Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunisation”.
40264.m: Gavi is a vaccine alliance for poorer countries.

40265.q: Where does the vaccine alliance Gavi have its headquarters?
40265.e: Gavi has its headquarters in Geneva. There it works with many other organisations.
40265.m: The vaccine alliance Gavi is based in Geneva.

40266.q: In which year was Gavi founded?
40266.e: Gavi was founded in 2000. It followed an earlier initiative for children's vaccinations from 1990.

40267.q: Who is Gavi's work mainly meant to benefit?
40267.e: Gavi helps poorer countries vaccinate children against dangerous diseases. According to Gavi, this has prevented many millions of deaths.
40267.m: Gavi helps vaccinate children in poorer countries.

40268.q: Which private foundation is one of Gavi's most important partners?
40268.e: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has supported Gavi with a lot of money from the start. Apart from that, it is mainly governments that pay into the alliance.
40268.m: The Gates Foundation is an important partner of Gavi.

40269.q: Which UN organisations work as partners in the vaccine alliance Gavi?
40269.e: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the children's agency UNICEF are core partners of Gavi. The World Bank is also one of the partners.
40269.m: The WHO and UNICEF are among Gavi's most important partners.

40270.q: In which worldwide initiative for distributing Covid-19 vaccines did Gavi play a leading role?
40270.e: From 2020, Gavi led the COVAX initiative together with other organisations. It was meant to share coronavirus vaccines more fairly between rich and poor countries.
40270.m: Through COVAX, Gavi helped distribute coronavirus vaccines worldwide.

40271.q: What does it mean that Gavi is a public-private partnership?
a: States and private partners work together
It belongs to a single person
40271.e: In Gavi, governments, UN organisations, foundations and vaccine makers work together. This pools money and expertise from different areas.
40271.m: In Gavi, states and private partners work together.

40272.q: What role did Switzerland have at the 1985 Geneva Summit between Reagan and Gorbachev?
a: It was a party to a war
It was not involved at all
40272.e: Switzerland made Geneva available as a meeting place and provided security. President of the Confederation Kurt Furgler welcomed the two leaders.
40272.m: Switzerland hosted the Geneva Summit in 1985.

40273.q: In which period of world history did the 1985 Geneva Summit take place?
40273.e: The summit took place during the Cold War between the USA and the Soviet Union. Both sides had huge numbers of nuclear weapons.
40273.m: The 1985 Geneva Summit took place during the Cold War.

40274.q: Which countries did Reagan and Gorbachev represent at the Geneva Summit?
40274.e: Ronald Reagan was President of the USA, and Mikhail Gorbachev was General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. The two countries were the superpowers of the Cold War.
40274.m: The USA and the Soviet Union met at the Geneva Summit.

40275.q: How long did Reagan and Gorbachev's Geneva Summit in November 1985 last?
40275.e: Reagan and Gorbachev met in Geneva on 19 and 20 November 1985. On the first day they talked at the Villa Fleur d'Eau on Lake Geneva.
40275.m: The 1985 Geneva Summit lasted two days.

40276.q: Which nickname did the Geneva Summit get because of a conversation by the fire?
40276.e: The meeting is known as the “Fireside Summit”. Reagan and Gorbachev talked there in a pool house in front of an open fire.
40276.m: The 1985 Geneva Summit is also called the Fireside Summit.

40277.q: Which topic was at the centre of the 1985 Geneva Summit?
40277.e: The two superpowers mainly talked about limiting their nuclear weapons. No disarmament treaty was reached yet, but the talks were speeded up.
40277.m: In Geneva in 1985, the talks were mainly about nuclear weapons.

40278.q: Which famous sentence about nuclear war is in the joint statement of the Geneva Summit?
a: A nuclear war cannot be won
War is the continuation of politics
40278.e: Reagan and Gorbachev declared that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. This sentence is still often quoted today.
40278.m: In Geneva in 1985 it was said that a nuclear war must never be fought.

40279.q: Where did Reagan and Gorbachev meet in 1986 for their next summit after Geneva?
40279.e: After Geneva, the two agreed on further meetings. The next one took place in October 1986 in Reykjavik in Iceland.
40279.m: The Reykjavik Summit followed Geneva in 1986.

40280.q: Where does the United Nations Conference on Disarmament meet?
40280.e: The Conference on Disarmament meets in Geneva. It is the most important negotiating body for worldwide disarmament treaties.
40280.m: The UN Conference on Disarmament meets in Geneva.

40281.q: What is the aim of the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva?
a: To negotiate treaties for fewer weapons
40281.e: Disarmament means reducing weapons. In Geneva, 65 states negotiate worldwide disarmament treaties.
40281.m: The Conference on Disarmament wants treaties for fewer weapons.

40282.q: How does the Conference on Disarmament make its decisions?
40282.e: All decisions must be taken by consensus. That is why a single state can block negotiations.
40282.m: In the Conference on Disarmament, all states must agree.

40283.q: Which type of weapon is an important topic at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva?
40283.e: In Geneva, for example, the treaty banning all nuclear weapons tests was negotiated until 1996. Nuclear weapons are among the most dangerous weapons in the world.
40283.m: The ban on nuclear weapons tests was negotiated in Geneva.

40284.q: Which type of weapon is banned by the convention that was finalised at the Geneva Conference on Disarmament in 1992 and signed in 1993?
40284.e: The Chemical Weapons Convention bans the production, storage and use of chemical weapons. It was signed in 1993.
40284.m: The ban on chemical weapons was negotiated in Geneva.

40285.q: Is Switzerland a member of the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva?
a: No, only nuclear powers are members
No, only EU states are members
No, it is only the host
40285.e: Switzerland is one of the 65 members of the Conference on Disarmament, which has existed since 1979. All the known nuclear powers are members too.
40285.m: Switzerland is a member of the Conference on Disarmament.

40286.q: Under which international organisation did the great Geneva Disarmament Conference of 1932 to 1934 take place?
40286.e: The League of Nations called the conference. Around 4,000 people from 64 countries took part.
40286.m: The League of Nations called the Geneva Disarmament Conference in 1932.

40287.q: Which country left the Geneva Disarmament Conference in October 1933 and soon afterwards also left the League of Nations?
40287.e: Nazi Germany left the conference on 14 October 1933 and a few days later gave notice of leaving the League of Nations. After that, no agreement was reached.
40287.m: Germany left the Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations in 1933.

40288.q: What is a Permanent Mission in Geneva?
a: A state's representation at international organisations
40288.e: A Permanent Mission represents a country at the UN and other international organisations in Geneva. It is a bit like an embassy for cooperation between many states.
40288.m: A Permanent Mission represents a country at international organisations.

40289.q: How many states are represented in Geneva with a Permanent Mission (as of 2025)?
40289.e: According to Genève internationale, 186 states are represented in Geneva with a Permanent Mission. That is almost every country in the world.
40289.m: Almost every state in the world has a mission in Geneva.

40290.q: What is the person who heads a Permanent Mission called?
40290.e: The head of a mission is called the Permanent Representative and usually has the rank of ambassador. He or she speaks on behalf of their own country.
40290.m: A Permanent Mission is headed by a Permanent Representative.

40291.q: How does a Permanent Mission in Geneva differ from an embassy in Bern?
a: It works with international organisations instead of with Switzerland
It belongs to the canton of Geneva
40291.e: An embassy in Bern looks after relations between two states, for example with Switzerland. A Permanent Mission, on the other hand, works with the international organisations.
40291.m: Embassies look after relations with states, missions with organisations.

40292.q: Does Switzerland itself also have a Permanent Mission in Geneva?
a: Yes, to the UN in Geneva
40292.e: Switzerland has a Permanent Mission to the UN and the other international organisations in Geneva. There it represents Switzerland's interests like any other member.
40292.m: Switzerland also has a Permanent Mission in Geneva.

40293.q: Which right protects diplomats of the Permanent Missions from arrest in the host country?
40293.e: Diplomats enjoy immunity and cannot simply be arrested or charged by the host country. This lets them work freely for their country; they must still obey the laws, though.
40293.m: Diplomatic immunity protects diplomats from arrest in the host country.

40294.q: Who works in a Permanent Mission in Geneva?
a: Only employees of the city of Geneva
40294.e: Diplomats who represent their country at the international organisations work in the Permanent Missions. In 2025 there were around 4,000 such people in Geneva.
40294.m: A country's diplomats work in a Permanent Mission.

40295.q: Why do so many states have a Permanent Mission in Geneva in particular?
a: Because many UN organisations are based there
Because there are no taxes there
Because Geneva is by the sea
40295.e: Many international organisations are based in Geneva, such as the WHO or the Human Rights Council. Anyone who wants to have a say there needs representation on the spot.
40295.m: Many states are in Geneva because many international organisations work there.

40296.q: Which organisation was based in Geneva from 1920 and is considered the forerunner of the UN?
40296.e: The League of Nations was founded after the First World War and settled in Geneva in 1920. This was the start of Geneva's history as an international city.
40296.m: From 1920, the League of Nations made Geneva an international city.

40297.q: What is the large building in Geneva that houses the UN's European seat called?
40297.e: The Palais des Nations was built in the 1930s for the League of Nations. Today it is the seat of the United Nations Office in Geneva.
40297.m: The UN in Geneva is based in the Palais des Nations.

40298.q: Who often helps international organisations in Geneva to construct their buildings?
a: Switzerland, meaning the federal government and the canton of Geneva
Nobody, they build entirely on their own
40298.e: Through the FIPOI foundation, the federal government and the canton of Geneva give low-interest loans and provide buildings. That keeps Geneva attractive for organisations.
40298.m: Switzerland supports international organisations in Geneva with buildings.

40299.q: Which UN health organisation has its headquarters in Geneva?
40299.e: The World Health Organization (WHO) is based in Geneva. UNESCO is in Paris, the FAO in Rome and UNICEF in New York.
40299.m: The WHO has its headquarters in Geneva.

40300.q: In which year did Switzerland become a full member of the UN, even though Geneva had long been a UN seat?
40300.e: Swiss voters said yes to joining the UN in March 2002. In September 2002, Switzerland became the 190th member.
40300.m: Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002.

40301.q: What does a headquarters agreement between Switzerland and an international organisation regulate?
a: Rights and duties at the location
40301.e: A headquarters agreement sets out which privileges, immunities and facilities an organisation receives in Switzerland. It forms the legal basis for its seat.
40301.m: A headquarters agreement regulates how an organisation may work in Switzerland.

40302.q: How many people in total worked in international Geneva (organisations, missions and NGOs) in 2025?
40302.e: According to Genève internationale, there were around 36,900 employees in 2025. About 29,000 of them worked in the international organisations.
40302.m: Tens of thousands of people work in international Geneva.

40303.q: Which organisation belongs to the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement?
a: The International Committee of the Red Cross
40303.e: The Movement includes the ICRC, the International Federation and the national societies such as the Swiss Red Cross.
40303.m: The ICRC belongs to the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.

40304.q: Which of these terms is a principle of the Red Cross?
40304.e: The seven principles are humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity and universality.
40304.m: Humanity is a principle of the Red Cross.

40305.q: Which principle of the Red Cross Movement means that it does not take sides in conflicts?
40305.e: Neutrality means that the Movement does not take part in hostilities or political disputes. That way it keeps the trust of all sides.
40305.m: Neutral means not taking sides in a dispute.

40306.q: Which principle means that the Red Cross helps all people solely according to how great their need is?
40306.e: Impartiality means that origin, religion or political opinion make no difference. Whoever needs help most urgently gets it first.
40306.m: Helping impartially means looking only at people's need.

40307.q: Roughly how many countries have a national Red Cross or Red Crescent society?
40307.e: The International Federation counts 191 national societies. Each country may have only one such society.
40307.m: Almost every country has its own Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

40308.q: What is Switzerland's national Red Cross society called?
40308.e: The Swiss Red Cross (SRC) was founded in 1866. It is based in Bern and is part of the worldwide Movement.
40308.m: Switzerland has the Swiss Red Cross.

40309.q: In which city is the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies based?
40309.e: The Federation was founded in Paris in 1919. Today it is based in Geneva, like the ICRC.
40309.m: The International Federation is based in Geneva.

40310.q: Which emblem do many countries use instead of the Red Cross?
40310.e: In many mainly Muslim countries, the organisation is called the Red Crescent. Both emblems are protected by the Geneva Conventions.
40310.m: As well as the Red Cross, there is the Red Crescent.

40311.q: Unlike the ICRC, what does the International Federation mainly focus on?
40311.e: The Federation coordinates the help of the national societies, especially in natural disasters and health crises. The ICRC, on the other hand, works mainly in armed conflicts.
40311.m: The Federation helps mainly in disasters, the ICRC mainly in wars.

40312.q: What are Switzerland's offers to mediate between states or to host peace talks called?
40312.e: “Good offices” means the support a state offers to parties in a conflict, for example as host, mediator or protecting power. Switzerland is known for this worldwide.
40312.m: With its good offices, Switzerland helps states in conflict.

40314.q: What does Switzerland do when it only makes peace talks possible but does not mediate?
a: It provides rooms and contacts but does not negotiate
It decides who is right in the dispute
It lends money to one side
It sends soldiers to the war zone
40314.e: This form of good offices is called facilitation. Switzerland creates good conditions, but the parties to the conflict negotiate the content themselves.
40314.m: In facilitation, Switzerland creates good conditions for talks.

40316.q: Which states took part in the 1955 Geneva Summit?
a: USA, Soviet Union, United Kingdom, France
40316.e: In 1955, the heads of government of the four victorious powers of the Second World War met in Geneva. It was one of the first big summits of the Cold War.
40316.m: The four victorious powers met at the 1955 Geneva Summit.

40317.q: Between France and which country in North Africa did Switzerland help to end a war by 1962?
40317.e: Switzerland helped France and the Algerian independence movement talk to each other. The Évian Accords ended the Algerian War in 1962.
40317.m: In 1962, Switzerland helped to end the Algerian War.

40318.q: Which of these is NOT one of Switzerland's good offices?
a: Supplying weapons to a party in a war
Mediating between parties to a conflict
Representing interests as a protecting power
40318.e: Good offices are meant to defuse conflicts and allow contact between states. Supporting a party in a war would go against neutrality.
40318.m: Good offices are meant to promote peace and not strengthen a party in a war.

40319.q: Who has to agree for Switzerland to become a protecting power for one state in another state?
40319.e: A protecting power mandate needs the consent of the state being represented and of the state in which Switzerland will be active.
40319.m: For a protecting power mandate, both states concerned must agree.

40320.q: In which building in Geneva do international UN conferences and peace talks often take place?
40320.e: The Palais des Nations is the seat of the UN Office in Geneva. Many negotiations and conferences are held there.
40320.m: The Palais des Nations in Geneva is an important place for peace talks.

40321.q: Between which two states was Switzerland a mutual protecting power until they restored relations in 2023?
40321.e: After the break in 2016, Switzerland represented Saudi Arabia's interests in Iran and Iran's interests in Saudi Arabia. In 2023 the two countries restored their relations.
40321.m: As protecting power, Switzerland represented the interests of Saudi Arabia and Iran.

40322.q: When is a protecting power usually needed?
a: When two states break off diplomatic relations
When a state chooses a new capital
When two states sign a trade agreement
When a state joins an organisation
40322.e: Without diplomatic relations, there are no more embassies. A protecting power then takes over the most essential tasks, such as passing on messages.
40322.m: After relations are broken off, a protecting power helps keep contact.

40323.q: Whose interests has Switzerland represented as protecting power in Iran since 1980?
40323.e: The USA and Iran have had no diplomatic relations since 1980. Since then Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Tehran.
40323.m: Switzerland represents the USA in Iran.

40324.q: Why is Switzerland in particular often chosen as a protecting power?
a: Because it has the largest army
Because it is by the sea
Because it is in the EU
40324.e: As a neutral country, Switzerland does not take sides in conflicts. That is why both sides often trust it.
40324.m: As a neutral country, Switzerland is a popular protecting power.

40325.q: Whose interests did Switzerland represent in the USA from 1991 to 2015?
40325.e: From 1991, Switzerland was also the protecting power for Cuba in Washington. In 2015, Cuba and the USA opened their own embassies again.
40325.m: Until 2015, Switzerland represented Cuba's interests in the USA.

40326.q: After which war did Switzerland begin to represent Russia's interests in Georgia and Georgia's in Russia?
40326.e: After the war in August 2008, Georgia and Russia broke off diplomatic relations. Switzerland then took on the protecting power mandate for both sides.
40326.m: Since the Caucasus war, Switzerland has been protecting power for Russia and Georgia.

40327.q: What are Switzerland's offers to mediate between states or to represent them as a protecting power called?
40327.e: With its good offices, Switzerland helps states that are not talking to each other. These include mediation and protecting power mandates.
40327.m: Protecting power mandates are among Switzerland's good offices.

40328.q: Roughly since when has Switzerland taken on protecting power mandates?
40328.e: As early as the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and 1871, Switzerland represented other states. It has kept up this tradition ever since.
40328.m: Switzerland has been a protecting power for over 150 years.

40329.q: Which federal department is responsible for protecting power mandates today?
40329.e: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs looks after relations with other states. This includes protecting power mandates.
40329.m: The FDFA looks after Switzerland's protecting power mandates.

40330.q: Which Federal Councillor has headed Switzerland's foreign affairs department since 2017 (as of 2026)?
40330.e: Ignazio Cassis of the FDP has been head of the FDFA since 1 November 2017. This makes him Switzerland's foreign minister.
40330.m: Ignazio Cassis has been Switzerland's foreign minister since 2017.

40331.q: Which canton does foreign minister Ignazio Cassis come from?
40331.e: Ignazio Cassis is from Ticino and, before his election to the Federal Council, was a member of the National Council for the canton of Ticino. He is a doctor by profession.

40332.q: Who was the first woman to head the Swiss foreign affairs department?
40332.e: Micheline Calmy-Rey of the SP headed the FDFA from 2003 to 2011. She was Switzerland's first female foreign minister.
40332.m: Micheline Calmy-Rey was Switzerland's first female foreign minister.

40333.q: What is the full name of the Swiss federal department abbreviated EDA in German (FDFA in English)?
40333.e: The FDFA is one of the seven federal departments. It is responsible for Switzerland's foreign policy.
40333.m: The FDFA is Switzerland's foreign affairs department.

40334.q: In which city does the FDFA have its headquarters?
40334.e: The FDFA is based in the Federal Palace in Bern. From there, Switzerland's embassies and consulates abroad are run.
40334.m: The FDFA has its headquarters in Bern.

40335.q: What is the Federal Councillor who heads the FDFA often called?
40335.e: Whoever heads the FDFA is responsible for foreign policy. That is why people often speak of the foreign minister.
40335.m: The head of the FDFA is often called the foreign minister.

40336.q: How many departments does the Swiss federal administration have, one of them being the FDFA?
40336.e: Each of the seven members of the Federal Council heads a department. The FDFA is the department for foreign policy.
40336.m: Switzerland has seven departments, one for each Federal Councillor.

40337.q: Which two principles have shaped Swiss foreign policy since the Second World War?
40337.e: Switzerland stays neutral but helps other countries, for example with humanitarian aid. Federal Councillor Max Petitpierre coined this guiding principle.
40337.m: Swiss foreign policy is based on neutrality and solidarity.

40338.q: What do you call a person who represents a country in a city on a voluntary basis without being a career diplomat?
40338.e: Honorary consuls usually have another job. They help travellers and maintain contacts where there is no embassy.
40338.m: An honorary consul represents a country on a voluntary basis.

40339.q: What is a state's most important representation in another state's capital called?
40339.e: The embassy represents a state to the government of the host country. It is headed by an ambassador.
40339.m: The embassy is a state's most important representation abroad.

40340.q: What is a typical task of a Swiss consulate?
a: Writing laws for the host country
Collecting taxes in the host country
40340.e: Consulates help their own citizens, for example with lost passports or in emergencies. They also issue documents.

40341.q: In which capital does the Swiss embassy stand right next to the Federal Chancellery?
40341.e: The Swiss embassy building in Berlin survived the Second World War. Today it stands right next to the German Federal Chancellery in the government district.
40341.m: The Swiss embassy in Berlin stands next to the Chancellery.

40342.q: What does it mean that an embassy is “inviolable”?
a: The host country's authorities may not enter it without permission
The embassy may never be closed
The embassy must have its own army
The building is protected against earthquakes
40342.e: Under the Vienna Convention, the host country's police and authorities may only enter an embassy with the consent of the head of mission. The host country must also protect it.
40342.m: An embassy may not be entered by the host country without permission.

40343.q: What does a new ambassador hand to the head of state of the host country at the start of her term?
40343.e: With the letter of credence, the sending state confirms that the person officially represents it. Only then can she fully carry out her duties.
40343.m: New ambassadors present a letter of credence.

40344.q: What is the FDFA app called with which travellers can get advice and register their trip?
40344.e: With the “Travel Admin” app, travellers can read travel advice and register their trip with the FDFA. That way the FDFA can reach them more easily in a crisis.
40344.m: The Travel Admin app helps Swiss travellers abroad.

40345.q: Roughly how many Swiss people live abroad (as of 2024)?
40345.e: Over 800,000 Swiss citizens live abroad, most of them in Europe. They are called the Swiss Abroad or the “Fifth Switzerland”.

40346.q: Why is Switzerland often asked to mediate in conflicts?
a: Because it has the largest army
Because it is by the sea
Because it belongs to the EU
40346.e: Switzerland does not take sides in conflicts. That is why both sides often trust it, for example Armenia and Turkey in 2009.
40346.m: Neutral Switzerland often mediates in conflicts.

40347.q: What does a mediator do in a conflict?
a: Helps the parties find a solution themselves
Decides like a judge who is right
Fights on the side of the weaker party
Punishes the party that started it
40347.e: In mediation, a neutral third party supports the talks. But the parties to the conflict must find and accept the solution themselves.
40347.m: Mediators help with talks; the parties find the solution themselves.

40348.q: What must be the case for Switzerland to mediate in a conflict?
a: All parties to the conflict must agree
The UN must ban the war
One party must have won the war
40348.e: Mediation only works if everyone involved accepts the mediator. Nobody can be forced into mediation.
40348.m: You can only mediate if all parties agree.

40349.q: What is another word for helping as a neutral go-between in a conflict?
40349.e: In mediation, a neutral person helps the people in dispute to talk to each other. Switzerland, for example, was active in this way on the Bürgenstock in 2002.
40349.m: Helping as a go-between is also called mediation.

40350.q: In which Swiss city do international peace talks often take place?
40350.e: Many international organisations are based in Geneva, including a large UN seat. That is why parties to conflicts often meet there.
40350.m: Geneva is an important place for peace talks.

40351.q: What is a ceasefire, as is often agreed during mediation?
40351.e: In a ceasefire, the fighting stops. That gives time to negotiate a lasting peace.
40351.m: A ceasefire is a pause in the fighting.

40352.q: The reunification of which island was negotiated on the Bürgenstock in 2004?
40352.e: In March 2004, negotiations on the UN plan for Cyprus took place on the Bürgenstock. The plan later failed in a referendum on the island.
40352.m: In 2004, Cyprus was negotiated on the Bürgenstock.

40353.q: Which FDFA division is responsible, among other things, for peacebuilding and mediation?
40353.e: The Peace and Human Rights Division supports peace processes and mediation. It also works to protect human rights.
40353.m: The Peace and Human Rights Division promotes peace.

40354.q: Which UN body elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council?
40354.e: In the General Assembly, all UN member states have one vote. Every year it elects five of the ten non-permanent members.
40354.m: The UN General Assembly elects the non-permanent members.

40355.q: As what kind of member did Switzerland sit on the UN Security Council?
40355.e: Besides the five permanent members, there are ten non-permanent members. Switzerland was one of them.
40355.m: Switzerland was a non-permanent member of the Security Council.

40356.q: How many countries sit on the UN Security Council in total?
40356.e: The Security Council has 5 permanent and 10 non-permanent members, making 15 altogether. Switzerland was one of the non-permanent members in 2023 and 2024.
40356.m: The UN Security Council has 15 members.

40357.q: For how long is a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council elected?
40357.e: Non-permanent members stay on the Council for two years and cannot be re-elected immediately.
40357.m: Non-permanent members sit on the Security Council for two years.

40358.q: With which slogan did Switzerland campaign for its seat on the Security Council?
40358.e: The slogan “A plus for peace” refers to the cross on the Swiss flag, which looks like a plus sign.
40358.m: Switzerland campaigned with the slogan “A plus for peace”.

40359.q: What is the main task of the UN Security Council?
a: To maintain world peace and international security
To set the UN budget on its own
40359.e: Under the UN Charter, the Security Council has the main responsibility for peace and security. For example, it can decide on sanctions or peace missions.
40359.m: The Security Council is responsible for world peace.

40360.q: Which of these countries is a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
40360.e: The five permanent members are China, France, the United Kingdom, Russia and the USA. Germany, Italy and Switzerland have only been non-permanent members at times.
40360.m: France is a permanent member of the Security Council.

40361.q: In which city is the UN Security Council based?
40361.e: The Security Council meets at the UN headquarters in New York. During its membership, Switzerland had its own ambassador there.
40361.m: The UN Security Council meets in New York.

40362.q: Which special right did Switzerland NOT have on the Security Council?
40362.e: Only the five permanent members, China, France, the United Kingdom, Russia and the USA, can block decisions with a veto. Non-permanent members vote normally.
40362.m: Only the permanent members have a veto on the Security Council.

40363.q: Which federal office is responsible for Switzerland’s humanitarian aid?
a: The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC)
40363.e: The SDC is part of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA). It runs the federal government’s humanitarian aid and development cooperation.
40363.m: The SDC is responsible for Switzerland’s humanitarian aid.

40364.q: How did the emblem of the Red Cross come about?
a: By reversing the colours of the Swiss flag
From the coat of arms of the city of Paris
From a flag of the Roman army
40364.e: In honour of Switzerland, a red cross on a white background was chosen. It is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped.
40364.m: The Red Cross is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped.

40365.q: Which man from Geneva is regarded as the founder of the Red Cross movement?
40365.e: Henry Dunant proposed founding the Red Cross. In 1901 he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy.
