40365.m: Henry Dunant is the founder of the Red Cross.

40366.q: Which battle of 1859 gave Henry Dunant the idea of helping the wounded neutrally?
40366.e: Dunant saw the suffering of the wounded at Solferino in northern Italy. He wrote about it in the book “A Memory of Solferino”.
40366.m: The Battle of Solferino inspired Henry Dunant.

40368.q: What is the Swiss Rescue team used for?
a: Searching for people buried after earthquakes
40368.e: Swiss Rescue is made up of specialists and search dogs. After severe earthquakes abroad it flies out to locate and rescue people buried under rubble.
40368.m: Swiss Rescue saves people buried after earthquakes.

40369.q: What is the name of the Swiss foundation that collects donations after disasters at home and abroad?
40369.e: Swiss Solidarity was founded in 1946 and collects donations for people in need. It works together with Swiss aid organisations.
40369.m: Swiss Solidarity collects donations for people in need.

40370.q: Which foreign army did Switzerland take in and look after in the winter of 1871?
40370.e: During the Franco-Prussian War, around 87,000 French soldiers under General Bourbaki fled to Switzerland. They were disarmed, interned and cared for.
40370.m: In 1871 Switzerland took in the Bourbaki army.

40371.q: What does the abbreviation SHA stand for?
40371.e: The SHA is the operational unit of the federal government’s humanitarian aid. Its specialists help with disasters and crises abroad.
40371.m: The SHA is the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit.

40372.q: When is the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit sent into action?
a: For elections in the Federal Palace
For road accidents on Swiss motorways
40372.e: The SHA helps abroad, for example after earthquakes, floods or in war zones. It is one of the tools of the federal government’s humanitarian aid.
40372.m: The SHA helps with disasters abroad.

40373.q: What was the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit called in the past?
40373.e: Originally the unit was called the Swiss Disaster Relief Corps. It was later renamed the Humanitarian Aid Unit.
40373.m: The SHA used to be called the Swiss Disaster Relief Corps.

40374.q: Who belongs to the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit?
a: Specialists who can travel abroad at short notice
Only soldiers of the Swiss Army
40374.e: Around 700 specialists are ready in the SHA, for example in construction, medicine, logistics or rescue. They can be sent abroad quickly for a mission.
40374.m: The SHA has specialists who can help abroad quickly.

40375.q: What does it mean that the SHA is a militia unit?
a: Its members have other jobs and go on missions when needed
Its members are all professional soldiers
Its members are elected by the people
Its members only work in Switzerland
40375.e: As in the Swiss militia system, members normally work in their own jobs. When a disaster happens, they are called up for a mission.
40375.m: SHA members go on missions alongside their normal jobs.

40376.q: Which specialist group exists in the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit?
40376.e: The SHA is divided into specialist groups such as construction, health, logistics, rescue, and water and hygiene. Clean water is especially important after disasters.
40376.m: The SHA has a specialist group for water and hygiene.

40377.q: Whose projects does the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit mainly carry out?
40377.e: The SHA comes under the FDFA and carries out projects of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation. It helps wherever the federal government provides humanitarian aid.
40377.m: The SHA carries out projects of the SDC.

40378.q: To whom does the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit also lend specialists?
a: UN organisations such as the World Food Programme
40378.e: The SHA also lends specialists to UN organisations, for example the World Food Programme. Such postings are called secondments.
40378.m: SHA specialists also work for UN organisations.

40379.q: In which year were the Hague Conventions that set out the law of neutrality agreed?
40379.e: At the Second Hague Peace Conference in 1907, the rights and duties of neutral states were set down in writing. They still apply today.
40379.m: The law of neutrality was set down in The Hague in 1907.

40380.q: In which country is the city of The Hague, after which the 1907 conventions are named?
40380.e: The Hague is the seat of the Dutch government. The Hague Peace Conferences met there in 1899 and 1907.
40380.m: The Hague is in the Netherlands.

40381.q: For which two kinds of war do the 1907 Hague Conventions regulate neutrality?
a: War on land and war at sea
40381.e: One convention covers neutrality in war on land, another covers neutrality in war at sea. Aircraft did not yet play a role in 1907.
40381.m: The Hague Conventions regulate neutrality in war on land and at sea.

40382.q: What is a neutral state NOT allowed to do under the law of neutrality?
a: Let its own soldiers fight for one side in a war
40382.e: A neutral state must not take part in a war between other states. It must not use troops or weapons to help one side.
40382.m: A neutral state does not take part in other states’ wars.

40383.q: What are warring parties forbidden to do on the territory of a neutral state?
40383.e: The territory of a neutral state is inviolable. Warring parties may not move troops or convoys of ammunition through it.
40383.m: Warring parties may not march through neutral territory.

40384.q: What must a neutral state do with soldiers of a warring party who flee onto its territory?
a: Take them into its own army
Hand them over to the enemy
40384.e: Under the Hague Convention, a neutral state must intern foreign troops on its territory. That way they can no longer take part in the war.
40384.m: Foreign soldiers are interned in a neutral state.

40385.q: Under the law of neutrality, what applies if a neutral state restricts exports of war material?
a: It must treat all warring parties equally
It may supply only one side
It must give weapons to all sides
It must leave exports to the warring party
40385.e: A neutral state must apply restrictions on war material equally to all warring parties. It must not favour either side.
40385.m: A neutral state must treat the warring parties equally.

40386.q: Under the law of neutrality, may a neutral state defend itself against an attack?
a: Yes, that does not count as a hostile act
No, it must put up with the attack
Only with permission from the UN
Only if a neighbour fights too
40386.e: The Hague Convention states that resisting a violation of neutrality is not a hostile act. That is also why Switzerland has an army.
40386.m: A neutral state may defend itself.

40387.q: In which year did the European great powers recognise Switzerland’s permanent neutrality?
40387.e: After the Congress of Vienna, the great powers recognised Switzerland’s perpetual neutrality in 1815. This recognition still applies today.

40388.q: At which great meeting of the European powers in 1814 and 1815 was the future of Switzerland also discussed?
40388.e: At the Congress of Vienna, the great powers reorganised Europe after Napoleon. Switzerland’s borders and neutrality were also discussed there.
40388.m: Decisions about Switzerland were also made at the Congress of Vienna.

40389.q: What does Switzerland’s neutrality, recognised in 1815, mean?
a: Switzerland does not fight in wars between other states
40389.e: A neutral state does not take sides in other countries’ wars. Switzerland still has an army to defend itself.
40389.m: Neutral means not taking part in other countries’ wars.

40390.q: Which three cantons joined the Swiss Confederation in 1815?
40390.e: After the Congress of Vienna, Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva were admitted to the Confederation as new cantons. This made Geneva a full canton for the first time.
40390.m: In 1815 Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined Switzerland.

40391.q: How many cantons did the Confederation have after 1815?
40391.e: Three new cantons were added in 1815 to the 19 cantons of the Mediation period. This created the federation of 22 cantons.

40392.q: Which canton received the territory of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel at the Congress of Vienna?
40392.e: Bern received the area of today’s Jura and the Laufen valley as compensation for losing Vaud and Aargau.
40392.m: In 1815 Bern received the territory of the Prince-Bishopric of Basel.

40393.q: The Valtellina used to belong to the Grisons. Which country does it belong to today?
40393.e: The Grisons lost the Valtellina in 1797. It did not get the area back at the Congress of Vienna. Today the Valtellina is in Italy.
40393.m: The Valtellina belongs to Italy today.

40394.q: Which war was the conference on the Bürgenstock in June 2024 about?
40394.e: The Summit on Peace in Ukraine took place on the Bürgenstock on 15 and 16 June 2024. It was meant to look for a path towards a peace process.
40394.m: The 2024 Bürgenstock summit dealt with peace in Ukraine.

40395.q: Above which lake is the Bürgenstock?
40395.e: The Bürgenstock is a ridge above Lake Lucerne in central Switzerland. A large hotel resort stands there.
40395.m: The Bürgenstock lies above Lake Lucerne.

40396.q: Who was the host of the 2024 Bürgenstock conference?
a: President of the Confederation Viola Amherd
President of the National Council Eric Nussbaumer
40396.e: Viola Amherd was President of the Confederation in 2024 and issued the invitation to the summit. Switzerland organised the meeting at Ukraine’s request.
40396.m: Viola Amherd hosted the Bürgenstock summit in 2024.

40397.q: Roughly how many states took part in the 2024 Bürgenstock conference?
40397.e: According to the figures, 92 states and 8 international organisations took part. Together that made about 100 delegations.
40397.m: About 90 states came to the Bürgenstock in 2024.

40398.q: Which country was not invited to the 2024 Bürgenstock conference?
40398.e: Russia was not invited to this phase of the talks. However, Switzerland stressed that Russia would have to be included in a later peace process.
40398.m: Russia was not invited to the Bürgenstock in 2024.

40399.q: Which large country stayed away from the 2024 Bürgenstock conference, giving Russia’s absence as the reason?
40399.e: China did not take part in the summit. It criticised the fact that both sides in the war were not at the table.
40399.m: China did not take part in the Bürgenstock summit.

40400.q: Which topic did the joint communiqué of the Bürgenstock conference deal with?
40400.e: The communiqué dealt with three topics: nuclear safety, food security, and the release of prisoners and deported people.
40400.m: Nuclear safety was a topic at the Bürgenstock.

40401.q: In which canton is the hotel resort on the Bürgenstock where the 2024 summit took place?
40401.e: The resort is in the canton of Nidwalden, high above Lake Lucerne. Most of the Bürgenstock belongs to the Nidwalden municipality of Ennetbürgen.
40401.m: The Bürgenstock resort is in the canton of Nidwalden.

40402.q: What does a country holding the OSCE chairmanship do?
a: It leads the organisation and its meetings
It becomes the new OSCE headquarters
It decides all elections in Europe
It gets its own OSCE army
40402.e: The chairing country leads the OSCE, chairs meetings and mediates in conflicts. After Switzerland, Serbia took on this role in 2015.
40402.m: The chairing country leads the OSCE.

40403.q: Which department of the Federal Council deals with relations with other countries?
40403.e: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) is responsible for foreign policy. In 2014 its head, Didier Burkhalter, chaired the OSCE.
40403.m: The FDFA is responsible for Switzerland’s foreign policy.

40404.q: In which city does the OSCE have its headquarters?
40404.e: The OSCE Secretariat is in Vienna. The Permanent Council also meets there regularly.
40404.m: The OSCE is based in Vienna.

40405.q: Which area of work belongs to the OSCE?
40405.e: The OSCE works in three areas: security, economy and environment, and the human dimension with human rights and democracy.
40405.m: The OSCE also works for human rights and democracy.

40406.q: How long does an OSCE chairmanship last?
40406.e: The OSCE chairmanship passes to a different participating state every year. Switzerland held it, for example, in 2014.
40406.m: The OSCE chairmanship changes every year.

40407.q: Which crisis especially marked the year of Switzerland’s OSCE chairmanship in 2014?
a: The crisis in and around Ukraine
40407.e: In 2014 Russia annexed Crimea, and fighting broke out in eastern Ukraine. The OSCE became an important forum for talks.
40407.m: In 2014 the Ukraine crisis was at the centre of the OSCE chairmanship.

40408.q: What did the OSCE deploy in Ukraine in March 2014?
40408.e: The OSCE Special Monitoring Mission observed the situation in Ukraine and reported on it. Its members were unarmed civilians.
40408.m: In 2014 the OSCE sent a civilian monitoring mission to Ukraine.

40409.q: Why are international meetings often held in Switzerland?
a: Because Switzerland is by the sea
Because it is the largest country in Europe
40409.e: As a neutral country, Switzerland is seen as a good place for talks. In 2014, for example, the foreign ministers of the OSCE states met in Basel.
40409.m: Neutral Switzerland often hosts international meetings.

40410.q: In which period was the CSCE, which later became the OSCE, created?
40410.e: During the Cold War, the CSCE brought states from East and West to the same table. In 1975 they signed the Helsinki Final Act, and so did Switzerland.
40410.m: The OSCE has its roots in the Cold War.

40411.q: Who are the members of the European Council?
a: The heads of state or government of the EU countries
All members of the European Parliament
The foreign ministers of the EU countries
The judges of the EU courts
40411.e: The heads of state or government of the member states meet in the European Council. They are joined by the President of the European Council and the President of the Commission.
40411.m: The European Council is made up of the EU’s heads of government and state.

40412.q: What is the main task of the European Council?
a: It sets the general political direction
It gives judgements on EU law
It elects the members of parliament
40412.e: The European Council decides the EU’s big goals and priorities. It does not pass laws itself.
40412.m: The European Council sets the EU’s political direction.

40413.q: In which city do the members of the European Council usually meet?
40413.e: European Council summits usually take place in Brussels, where many EU institutions are based.
40413.m: The European Council usually meets in Brussels.

40414.q: Who, for example, takes part in a meeting of the European Council?
a: The Swiss President of the Confederation
40414.e: The heads of state or government of the EU countries meet in the European Council. Germany is represented by the Federal Chancellor.
40414.m: The heads of government of the EU countries meet in the European Council.

40415.q: How often, at least, does the European Council meet?
40415.e: According to the EU Treaty, the European Council meets twice every six months, so at least four times a year. In a crisis there are extra special summits.
40415.m: The European Council meets for a summit at least four times a year.

40416.q: What are meetings of the European Council often called in the media?
40416.e: Because the countries’ top politicians meet there, people speak of EU summits. They usually take place in Brussels.
40416.m: A meeting of the European Council is called an EU summit.

40417.q: Which organisation is often confused with the European Council, even though it is not part of the EU?
40417.e: The Council of Europe in Strasbourg is a separate organisation with 46 members that works for human rights. Switzerland is a member, even though it is not in the EU.
40417.m: The Council of Europe is different from the EU’s European Council.

40418.q: How many countries do the heads of state or government in the European Council come from?
40418.e: Each of the 27 EU countries is represented in the European Council by its head of government or head of state.
40418.m: All 27 EU countries are represented in the European Council.

40419.q: Who sits in the Council of the European Union?
a: Specialist ministers of the member states
The heads of state or government
Elected Members of the European Parliament
40419.e: Depending on the topic, the responsible ministers meet in the Council of the EU, for example the agriculture or environment ministers. That is why it is also called the Council of Ministers.
40419.m: In the Council of the European Union, the countries’ specialist ministers negotiate.

40420.q: What other name does the Council of the European Union have?
40420.e: Because the ministers of the member states meet there, the Council of the EU is often called the Council of Ministers. Officially it is simply called “the Council”.
40420.m: The Council of the European Union is also called the Council of Ministers.

40421.q: Together with which body does the Council of the EU pass most laws?
40421.e: In the ordinary legislative procedure, both the Council and Parliament must agree to a law. They are called the EU’s two lawmakers.
40421.m: The Council and Parliament pass EU laws together.

40422.q: For how long does each member state hold the presidency of the Council of the EU?
40422.e: The presidency of the Council passes to another country every six months. This way every country gets its turn.
40422.m: The Council presidency changes every six months.

40423.q: How are most decisions taken in the Council of the EU?
a: With a large majority of the countries
By a referendum in all countries
40423.e: Most decisions need a qualified majority. This means many countries representing a large share of the EU population must agree.
40423.m: The Council of the EU usually needs a large, qualified majority.

40424.q: How many countries send their ministers to the Council of the EU (as of 2025)?
40424.e: The EU has 27 member states. Depending on the topic, each country sends its responsible minister.
40424.m: All 27 member states are represented in the Council of the EU.

40425.q: How must decisions on foreign and security policy usually be taken in the Council of the EU?
40425.e: In foreign and security policy, unanimity usually applies. So any single country can block a decision.
40425.m: In EU foreign policy, all countries usually have to agree.

40426.q: In which city does the Council of the EU usually meet?
40426.e: The Council of the EU usually meets in Brussels. In some months the meetings take place in Luxembourg.
40426.m: The Council of the EU usually meets in Brussels.

40427.q: In which city does the Court of Justice of the European Union have its seat?
40427.e: The Court of Justice of the EU is in the city of Luxembourg. Both the Court of Justice and the General Court of the EU work there.
40427.m: The Court of Justice of the EU is in Luxembourg.

40428.q: What is the main task of the Court of Justice of the European Union?
a: It makes sure EU law is applied the same way everywhere
It sets the key interest rate
40428.e: The Court interprets EU law and checks that it is followed. This way it applies in the same way in all member states.
40428.m: The Court of Justice of the EU ensures EU law is applied uniformly.

40429.q: How many judges does each member state provide to the Court of Justice (the highest court) of the EU?
40429.e: Each of the 27 member countries sends one judge to the Court of Justice. There are also eleven Advocates General who give the judges expert opinions.
40429.m: The Court of Justice of the EU has one judge from each member state.

40430.q: For how long are judges at the Court of Justice of the EU appointed?
40430.e: The judges are appointed jointly by the governments of the member states for six years. After that they can be reappointed.
40430.m: Judges at the Court of Justice of the EU serve for six years.

40431.q: What can a court in an EU country do if it is not sure what an EU law means?
a: It asks the Court of Justice of the EU
40431.e: The court puts its question to the Court of Justice of the EU in Luxembourg. Its answer then applies to all courts in the EU.
40431.m: Courts in the EU can ask the Court of Justice of the EU for guidance.

40432.q: Which court is often confused with the Court of Justice of the EU?
a: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea
40432.e: The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg belongs to the Council of Europe, not the EU. Cases from Switzerland can also be heard there.
40432.m: The Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg is not part of the EU.

40433.q: Who, for example, can bring a case before the General Court of the EU in Luxembourg?
a: A company that disagrees with an EU decision
40433.e: The Court of Justice of the EU also includes the General Court of the European Union. Companies, for example, bring cases there against EU decisions.
40433.m: Companies can also challenge decisions before the General Court of the EU.

40434.q: Who can take a member state to the Court of Justice of the EU if it does not apply EU law?
40434.e: The Commission can start infringement proceedings and take a member state to the Court. If the country loses, it must apply the law or face fines.
40434.m: The Commission can take countries to court if they do not follow EU law.

40435.q: What is the most important goal of the European Central Bank?
40435.e: The ECB is meant to ensure price stability in the euro area. So money should keep its value as far as possible.
40435.m: The ECB mainly ensures stable prices in the euro area.

40436.q: What does inflation, which the ECB wants to keep as low as possible, mean?
a: Prices rise and money loses value
40436.e: With inflation, many things become more expensive and you can buy less with the same money. The ECB wants to keep prices in the euro area stable.
40436.m: Inflation means that prices are rising.

40438.q: Which currency is the European Central Bank responsible for?
40438.e: The ECB was founded in 1998. It makes sure the euro keeps its value in the countries of the eurozone.
40438.m: The ECB is responsible for the euro.

40439.q: What does the ECB usually do when prices are rising too quickly?
40439.e: When interest rates rise, loans become more expensive. People and companies spend less, and prices rise more slowly.
40439.m: The ECB slows rising prices with higher interest rates.

40440.q: What is the name of the central bank that has a similar job in Switzerland to the ECB in the euro area?
40440.e: Switzerland is not part of the euro area and has its own currency, the franc. The Swiss National Bank is responsible for it.
40440.m: The Swiss National Bank, not the ECB, is responsible for the franc.

40441.q: What is the name of the bank responsible for the euro?
40441.e: The European Central Bank, or ECB for short, is the central bank for all countries that use the euro.
40441.m: The ECB is the central bank of the euro.

40442.q: Which office has Ursula von der Leyen held since December 2019?
40442.e: Ursula von der Leyen has been President of the European Commission since 1 December 2019. She was the first woman in this office.
40442.m: Ursula von der Leyen leads the European Commission.

40443.q: Which country does Ursula von der Leyen come from?
40443.e: Ursula von der Leyen is a German politician from the CDU. However, she was born in Brussels in 1958.
40443.m: Ursula von der Leyen is German.

40444.q: Which ministerial post did Ursula von der Leyen hold in Germany before moving to the EU Commission?
40444.e: From 2013 to 2019 she was Germany’s Federal Minister of Defence. Before that she had been, among other things, Minister for Families and Minister of Labour.
40444.m: Before her EU role, Ursula von der Leyen was Germany’s Minister of Defence.

40445.q: In which year was Ursula von der Leyen elected for a second term as Commission President?
40445.e: After the 2024 European elections, the European Parliament confirmed her in July 2024 for another five years.
40445.m: Ursula von der Leyen was elected for a second term in 2024.

40446.q: Which party does Ursula von der Leyen belong to in Germany?
40446.e: Ursula von der Leyen is a member of the Christian Democratic Union. In the European Parliament, the CDU belongs to the European People’s Party.
40446.m: Ursula von der Leyen is a member of the CDU.

40447.q: Which institution must elect the Commission President before she can take office?
a: The Court of Justice of the EU
40447.e: The European Council proposes a person. Then the European Parliament must agree with a majority of its members.
40447.m: The Commission President is elected by the European Parliament.

40448.q: What is the name of the big climate protection programme that the Commission under Ursula von der Leyen presented in 2019?
40448.e: The Green Deal is meant to make the EU climate neutral by 2050. It was presented in December 2019.
40448.m: The European Green Deal aims to make the EU climate neutral by 2050.

40449.q: How many members does the EU Commission under Ursula von der Leyen have, including the President?
40449.e: Each member state provides one Commission member. With 27 countries, the Commission therefore has 27 members, counting the President.
40449.m: Each EU country provides one member of the Commission.

40450.q: Which city is regarded as the unofficial capital of the European Union?
40450.e: The Commission, the Council of the EU and the European Council are based in Brussels. That is why the city is often called the capital of Europe.
40450.m: Brussels is regarded as the capital of the EU.

40451.q: What is the name of the famous market square in the centre of Brussels that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
40451.e: The Grand-Place is surrounded by splendid guildhalls and the Gothic town hall. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
40451.m: The Grand-Place is the most famous square in Brussels.

40452.q: Which EU institution has its headquarters in Brussels?
a: The Court of Justice of the EU
40452.e: The Commission works in the star-shaped Berlaymont building in Brussels. The Central Bank is in Frankfurt, and the Court of Justice and the Court of Auditors are in Luxembourg.
40452.m: The European Commission is based in Brussels.

40453.q: Which two languages are official languages in the city of Brussels?
40453.e: The Brussels-Capital Region is officially bilingual. In everyday life, French is mostly spoken there.
40453.m: French and Dutch are the official languages in Brussels.

40454.q: What is the area of Brussels called where many EU buildings stand?
40454.e: The European Quarter includes the Berlaymont, the Europa building and offices of the European Parliament. Thousands of EU officials work there.
40454.m: Most EU buildings in Brussels are in the European Quarter.

40455.q: What is the name of the well-known structure in Brussels that is an enlarged model of an iron crystal?
40455.e: The Atomium was built for the 1958 World Exhibition. It shows nine atoms of an iron crystal, hugely enlarged.
40455.m: The Atomium is a landmark of Brussels.

40456.q: Which military alliance, besides the EU, also has its headquarters in Brussels?
40456.e: NATO has its headquarters in Brussels. It is a defence alliance, not an EU institution.
40456.m: NATO also has its headquarters in Brussels.

40457.q: Apart from Strasbourg, where else does the European Parliament meet, for example in committees and shorter sessions?
40457.e: Parliament’s committees and political groups usually meet in Brussels. Extra shorter plenary sessions are also held there.
40457.m: Many sessions of the European Parliament take place in Brussels.

40458.q: In which city does the European Parliament have its official seat?
40458.e: According to the EU treaties, Strasbourg is Parliament’s official seat. Most of the big plenary sessions take place there.
40458.m: The European Parliament has its seat in Strasbourg.

40459.q: Why do Members of the European Parliament regularly travel back and forth between two cities?
a: Because Parliament meets in Strasbourg and in Brussels
Because they have to live in Bern and Geneva
Because they go to a football match every week
40459.e: The big sessions take place in Strasbourg, many other meetings in Brussels. That is why the members commute between the two cities.
40459.m: The European Parliament meets in Strasbourg and in Brussels.

40461.q: From what age can people vote in the European elections in Austria?
40461.e: Each country sets its own voting age for the European elections. Austria allows voting from the age of 16; in most other countries it is 18.
40461.m: In Austria, 16-year-olds can already vote for the European Parliament.

40462.q: Which EU body is elected directly by the citizens?
40462.e: Only Parliament is elected directly by the people. The other bodies are appointed by governments or made up of government members.
40462.m: The European Parliament is the only directly elected EU body.

40463.q: What are the groups called in which Members of the European Parliament with similar political views join together?
40463.e: Members sit not by country but by political group. For years the largest group has been the European People’s Party.
40463.m: In the European Parliament, members form political groups by political direction.

40464.q: What does the European Parliament award the Sakharov Prize for every year?
a: For work for human rights and freedom
For the best song in Europe
40464.e: Since 1988 the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought has been awarded to people who bravely stand up for human rights.
40464.m: The Sakharov Prize honours work for human rights.

40465.q: Which EU country is on a divided island in the eastern Mediterranean?
40465.e: Cyprus joined the EU in 2004. Since 1974 the north of the island has been controlled by Turkey, and EU law does not apply there in practice.
40465.m: Cyprus is an EU country on a divided island.

40466.q: Which EU country has the most inhabitants?
40466.e: Germany has over 80 million inhabitants, making it the most populous country in the EU.
40466.m: Germany is the most populous country in the EU.

40467.q: Which EU country has the largest area?
40467.e: With its territory in Europe, France is the largest EU country by area. Spain and Sweden come next.
40467.m: France is the largest country in the EU by area.

40468.q: Which is the smallest member country of the EU, both by area and by population?
40468.e: The island state of Malta in the Mediterranean is only about 316 square kilometres in size. It also has the fewest inhabitants of all EU countries.
40468.m: Malta is the smallest country in the EU.

40469.q: How many founding states did the European Economic Community have in 1957?
40469.e: The founders were Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. They signed the Treaties of Rome in 1957.
40469.m: European unification began with six founding states.

40470.q: Which EU member country is a grand duchy?
40470.e: Luxembourg has a Grand Duke as head of state. It is the only grand duchy in the world.
40470.m: Luxembourg is the only grand duchy in the world.

40471.q: How does Switzerland manage its relations with the EU without being a member?
a: With a seat on the European Council
Not at all, there are no agreements
40471.e: Switzerland has concluded many bilateral agreements with the EU, for example on the free movement of persons or Schengen. This gives it access to the single market in certain areas.
40471.m: Switzerland works with the EU through bilateral agreements.

40472.q: Which countries joined the EU together in the largest enlargement in 2004?
a: Ten countries, including Poland and the Czech Republic
40472.e: On 1 May 2004 ten countries joined, mainly from Central and Eastern Europe, plus Malta and Cyprus. It was the largest enlargement in the history of the EU.
40472.m: In 2004 ten countries joined the EU at the same time.

40473.q: In which year did the Treaty of Lisbon come into force?
40473.e: The treaty was signed in December 2007 and came into force on 1 December 2009, after all countries had approved it.
40473.m: The Treaty of Lisbon has applied since 2009.

40474.q: In which country is the city after which the Treaty of Lisbon is named?
40474.e: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal. The treaty was signed there in 2007, when Portugal held the Council presidency.
40474.m: The Treaty of Lisbon was signed in Portugal’s capital.

40475.q: Which country used the exit rule in the Treaty of Lisbon to leave the EU?
40475.e: The Treaty of Lisbon was the first to set out how a country can leave the EU. The United Kingdom used this rule for Brexit and left in 2020.
40475.m: The United Kingdom left the EU with Brexit.

40476.q: What do citizens collect for a European Citizens’ Initiative?
40476.e: With enough signatures from several EU countries, citizens can ask the EU Commission to propose a law. This option has existed since the Treaty of Lisbon.
40476.m: For a European Citizens’ Initiative you collect signatures.

40477.q: Which new foreign policy post did the Treaty of Lisbon create?
a: High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy
40477.e: The High Representative leads the EU’s foreign policy and is also a Vice-President of the Commission. This person is often called the EU’s foreign policy chief.
40477.m: The High Representative is, in effect, the EU’s foreign minister.

40478.q: Which document became legally binding with the Treaty of Lisbon?
a: Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU
40478.e: The Charter of Fundamental Rights has existed since 2000. Since the Treaty of Lisbon it has been just as binding as the EU treaties.
40478.m: Since the Treaty of Lisbon the Charter of Fundamental Rights has been binding.

40479.q: Which planned treaty failed in referendums in 2005 and was later replaced by the Treaty of Lisbon?
a: Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe
40479.e: France and the Netherlands rejected the planned EU constitution in referendums in 2005. Many of its contents were then taken over into the Treaty of Lisbon.
40479.m: The Treaty of Lisbon replaced the failed EU constitution.

40480.q: What can the EU as a whole do since the Treaty of Lisbon?
a: Conclude its own treaties with other states
Recruit its own soldiers in all countries
40480.e: Since the Treaty of Lisbon, the EU has had its own legal personality. That is why it can conclude agreements with other countries itself.
40480.m: Since Lisbon, the EU as a whole can conclude treaties with other states.

40481.q: Who decides the outcome of a case at the Court of Justice of the EU?
40481.e: At the Court, independent judges give the judgement. Before that, Advocates General can give an opinion, but the judges must decide.
40481.m: Independent judges decide at the Court of Justice of the EU.

40482.q: What does the European Central Bank make sure of?
a: That the euro keeps its value
That the European Football Championship takes place
40482.e: The ECB is meant to keep prices in the euro area stable. That way money keeps its value as far as possible.
40482.m: The ECB ensures a stable euro.

40483.q: What does the EU single market mean?
a: Goods, people, money and services can move freely across borders
Each country may only sell its own goods
You may only shop in Brussels
All shops have the same prices
40483.e: The EU single market has existed since 1993. Within the EU there are in principle no more customs checks on goods.
40483.m: In the single market, borders are open for trade.

40484.q: How many fundamental freedoms does the EU single market have?
40484.e: The single market is based on the free movement of goods, persons and other areas. People speak of the four fundamental freedoms.
40484.m: The single market is based on four fundamental freedoms.

40485.q: Which of these freedoms is one of the fundamental freedoms of the single market?
a: Free choice of where to live outside Europe
Free access to all universities worldwide
40485.e: Capital, meaning money, may flow freely between the member states. The other fundamental freedoms concern goods, persons and services.
40485.m: Money may flow freely between countries in the single market.

40486.q: What does free movement of persons in the single market mean?
a: You may live and work in another EU country
You no longer need an identity card
You may travel everywhere for free
You may vote in every country
40486.e: EU citizens may live and work in any member state. Thanks to an agreement, free movement of persons also applies between Switzerland and the EU.
40486.m: Thanks to free movement of persons, you may work in other EU countries.

40487.q: What is the name of the economic area through which Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein take part in the single market?
40487.e: The European Economic Area, or EEA for short, links the EU with these three countries.
40487.m: Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are in the single market through the EEA.

40488.q: In which year did Swiss voters reject joining the European Economic Area?
40488.e: On 6 December 1992 the people and the cantons narrowly said no to the EEA. After that, Switzerland chose the path of bilateral agreements.
40488.m: Switzerland said no to the EEA in 1992.

40489.q: What is a customs union, like the one within the EU?
a: No customs duties between members and common duties towards outsiders
Each country sets its own customs duties
Customs duties only within the union
40489.e: There are no customs duties within the EU. Towards other countries, all members charge the same external duties.
40489.m: In the EU customs union, common duties apply towards other countries.

40490.q: Which mark shows that a product meets the safety rules of the EU single market?
40490.e: Many products such as toys or electrical devices carry the CE mark. With it, the manufacturer declares that the product meets EU requirements.
40490.m: The CE mark shows that a product meets EU rules.

40491.q: Which of these countries is part of the eurozone?
40491.e: In Italy you pay with the euro. Switzerland, the United Kingdom and Norway have their own currencies.
40491.m: Italy is part of the eurozone.

40494.q: Why don’t you need to change money when travelling from Germany to Italy?
a: Because both countries use the euro
Because you can only pay with francs there
Because everything in Italy is free
Because you can only pay with gold
40494.e: Germany and Italy both belong to the eurozone. So you can pay with the same money in both countries.
40494.m: In the eurozone you pay with the euro everywhere.

40495.q: Which EU country pays not with the euro but with the krone?
40495.e: Denmark is in the EU but keeps its Danish krone. It secured this right by treaty.

40496.q: Which country introduced the euro on 1 January 2023?
40496.e: Croatia introduced the euro on 1 January 2023, replacing the kuna.
40496.m: Croatia has paid with the euro since 2023.

40497.q: Which tiny state uses the euro even though it is not a member of the EU?
40497.e: Vatican City may use the euro and mint its own coins thanks to an agreement with the EU. Liechtenstein, on the other hand, uses the Swiss franc.
40497.m: The Vatican uses the euro without being part of the EU.

40498.q: Among other things, what must a country show before it may introduce the euro?
a: That its prices are stable and it does not have too much debt
That it is by the sea
That it has more than 10 million inhabitants
40498.e: To adopt the euro, a country must meet conditions, for example low inflation and sound public finances.
40498.m: To adopt the euro, a country needs stable prices and healthy finances.

40499.q: What is the currency Switzerland uses, even though it is surrounded almost entirely by euro countries?
40499.e: Switzerland is not in the EU and has never introduced the euro. However, many shops near the border also accept euros.

40500.q: Which large country, lying partly in Europe and partly in Asia, has wanted to join the EU for a very long time?
40500.e: Turkey has been an official candidate for membership since 1999. But the negotiations have hardly made progress for years.
40500.m: Turkey has long wanted to join the EU.

40501.q: Which country applied to join the EU in 2022 after the Russian attack?
40501.e: After the Russian attack, Ukraine applied for membership in 2022. In June 2022 it became a candidate country.
40501.m: Ukraine has been an EU candidate country since 2022.

40502.q: Among other things, what must a country have to be allowed to join the EU?
40502.e: A country that wants to join the EU needs, among other things, a stable democracy, independent courts and a working economy.
40502.m: An EU country must be a stable democracy.

40503.q: Which of these countries is an EU candidate country (as of 2026)?
40503.e: Montenegro has been a candidate since 2010 and has been negotiating membership since 2012. It is seen as one of the countries that has made the most progress.
40503.m: Montenegro is one of the EU candidate countries.

40504.q: Georgia would like to join the EU. In which mountain range is the country?
40504.e: Georgia lies in the Caucasus between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. It has been an EU candidate country since the end of 2023.
40504.m: Georgia lies in the Caucasus and would like to join the EU.

40505.q: In which region of Europe are many of today’s candidate countries, such as Serbia, Albania and North Macedonia?
40505.e: Several countries of the Western Balkans are seeking to join the EU. They also include Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro.
40505.m: Many EU candidate countries are in the Western Balkans.

40506.q: What do you call a country that is officially allowed to negotiate with the EU about joining?
40506.e: A candidate country officially has permission to work towards joining. But it often takes many years before it is admitted.
40506.m: Countries that want to join the EU are called candidate countries.

40507.q: What happened in 2016 to Switzerland’s 1992 application to join the EU?
a: It was accepted by the EU
It was confirmed by the people
It was handed to the UN
40507.e: The Federal Council had submitted an application in 1992, which then lay dormant. In 2016 Switzerland told the EU that it should be regarded as withdrawn.
40507.m: Switzerland withdrew its EU application in 2016.

40508.q: In which Swiss city did Winston Churchill give a famous speech about the future of Europe in 1946?
40508.e: Churchill spoke in Zurich on 19 September 1946. The speech is seen as an important push for European unification.
40508.m: Churchill’s famous speech on Europe took place in Zurich in 1946.

40509.q: To which audience did Winston Churchill give his Zurich speech?
40509.e: In Zurich, Churchill addressed the “academic youth”, meaning students. Above all, he wanted to win over the young generation for Europe.
40509.m: Churchill addressed his Zurich speech to young people.

40510.q: Which goal did Churchill call for in his Zurich speech?
a: A shared army for the whole world
40510.e: Churchill called for the creation of a kind of “United States of Europe”. This was meant to prevent new wars.
40510.m: Churchill dreamed of a United States of Europe.

40511.q: In which building in Zurich did Churchill give his speech on Europe in 1946?
40511.e: The speech was given in the great hall of the University of Zurich. It is one of the best-known speeches ever given in Switzerland.
40511.m: In 1946 Churchill spoke in the great hall of the University of Zurich.

40512.q: According to Churchill’s Zurich speech, which two countries should form a partnership first?
40512.e: Churchill said the first step had to be a partnership between France and Germany. The two countries had fought each other in several wars.
40512.m: According to Churchill, the unification of Europe should start with France and Germany.

40513.q: Which country did Winston Churchill lead as Prime Minister in the Second World War?
40513.e: Churchill was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 and led the country through the Second World War. After the war he spoke about Europe in Zurich in 1946.
40513.m: Churchill led the United Kingdom through the Second World War.

40514.q: With which well-known call did Churchill end his Zurich speech?
40514.e: At the end, Churchill called out “Let Europe arise!”.
40514.m: Churchill ended his speech with the call “Let Europe arise!”.

40515.q: Which institution did Churchill propose in Zurich as the first step towards uniting Europe?
40515.e: Churchill said the first practical step was to found a Council of Europe. The Council of Europe was then created in 1949.
40515.m: In Zurich Churchill proposed a Council of Europe, which was founded three years later.

40516.q: What does Europe Day on 9 May commemorate?
a: The end of the First World War
40516.e: On 9 May 1950 Robert Schuman presented his plan. That is why the EU celebrates Europe Day on this date.
40516.m: Europe Day on 9 May commemorates the Schuman Declaration.

40517.q: Which office did Robert Schuman hold when he presented his declaration in 1950?
40517.e: Robert Schuman was France’s Foreign Minister at the time. He presented the plan on behalf of the French government.
40517.m: Robert Schuman was French Foreign Minister.

40518.q: Which two raw materials did the Schuman Plan want to be managed jointly?
40518.e: Coal and steel were important for making weapons. Countries that manage them jointly can hardly wage war against each other any more.
40518.m: The Schuman Plan aimed to control coal and steel jointly.

40519.q: What was the main aim of the 1950 Schuman Declaration?
a: To make war between France and Germany impossible
To found a European football team
40519.e: Schuman wrote that a war between France and Germany should become “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible”.
40519.m: The Schuman Declaration was meant to secure peace between France and Germany.

40520.q: In which city was the Schuman Declaration presented?
40520.e: Schuman presented the declaration in the Clock Room of the Foreign Ministry at the Quai d’Orsay. This building is in the French capital.
40520.m: The Schuman Declaration was presented in Paris.

40521.q: After which war did Robert Schuman present his plan?
40521.e: The plan came in 1950, five years after the end of the Second World War. It was meant to prevent a new war in Europe.
40521.m: The Schuman Plan was created after the Second World War.

40522.q: Which community grew out of the Schuman Plan in 1951?
40522.e: The European Coal and Steel Community was the first step towards today’s EU.
40522.m: The Coal and Steel Community grew out of the Schuman Plan.

40523.q: Which German Federal Chancellor quickly agreed to the Schuman Plan in 1950?
40523.e: Konrad Adenauer was Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany at the time and supported the plan immediately.
40523.m: Konrad Adenauer said yes to the Schuman Plan.

40524.q: Which country did Jean Monnet, one of the founding fathers of Europe, come from?
40524.e: Jean Monnet was born in Cognac, France, in 1888. After the First World War he worked for the League of Nations in Geneva.

40525.q: What did the Frenchman Jean Monnet work for after the Second World War?
40525.e: Jean Monnet wanted the countries of Europe to work closely together so that there would be no more war. He is regarded as one of the founding fathers of the EU.
40525.m: Jean Monnet worked for a united Europe.

40526.q: In which European organisation did Jean Monnet play an important role?
a: In the European Coal and Steel Community
40526.e: The European Coal and Steel Community was founded in 1951. Monnet was the first President of its High Authority.
40526.m: Jean Monnet shaped the European Coal and Steel Community.

40527.q: Which special honorary title did Jean Monnet receive in 1976 as the first person ever?
40527.e: In 1976 the heads of state or government of the European Communities made Monnet the first Honorary Citizen of Europe.
40527.m: Jean Monnet was the first Honorary Citizen of Europe.

40528.q: What is Jean Monnet often called?
a: One of the founding fathers of Europe
The inventor of the European Parliament
40528.e: Together with Robert Schuman, Konrad Adenauer and others, Monnet is one of the so-called founding fathers of European unification.
40528.m: Jean Monnet is regarded as a founding father of Europe.

40529.q: Why did Jean Monnet want the countries of Europe to work together?
a: So that there would be no more war between them
So that everyone would speak the same language
So that there would be only one king
So that Europe would conquer the world
40529.e: After two world wars, Monnet wanted peace through cooperation. Countries whose economies work together do not go to war against each other.
40529.m: Monnet wanted peace through cooperation in Europe.

40530.q: In which famous building in Paris was Jean Monnet honoured and laid to rest?
40530.e: For the 100th anniversary of his birth, Monnet’s remains were moved to the Panthéon in 1988. There France honours its most important figures.
40530.m: Jean Monnet rests in the Panthéon in Paris.

40531.q: Which way of working is typical of Jean Monnet’s path to uniting Europe?
a: One big treaty all at once
40531.e: Monnet relied on step-by-step cooperation in individual areas such as coal and steel. More unity was meant to grow from this over time.
40531.m: Monnet wanted to unite Europe step by step.

40532.q: In German, what is the European Coal and Steel Community often called for short?
40532.e: The word “Montan” refers to mining. That is why the ECSC is also called the Montanunion in German.
40532.m: In German the ECSC is also called the Montanunion.

40533.q: How many founding states did the European Coal and Steel Community have?
40533.e: The founders were Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
40533.m: The European Coal and Steel Community began with six states.

40534.q: Which country was NOT one of the founding states of the European Coal and Steel Community?
40534.e: The United Kingdom did not take part in the Coal and Steel Community. It only joined the European Communities in 1973.
40534.m: The United Kingdom was not there when the Coal and Steel Community was founded.

40535.q: Which two things did the European Coal and Steel Community manage jointly?
40535.e: Its official name was the European Coal and Steel Community. At that time coal and steel were important for industry and weapons.
40535.m: The Coal and Steel Community managed coal and steel jointly.

40536.q: Why did France and Germany want to manage coal and steel jointly?
a: So that no country could secretly arm itself for war
So that coal would become more expensive
So that fewer trains would run
So that they would find gold
40536.e: Weapons were made from coal and steel at that time. If both countries control them jointly, a new war between them becomes almost impossible.
40536.m: Joint control of coal and steel was meant to prevent wars.

40537.q: Does the European Coal and Steel Community still exist today?
a: No, its tasks passed to the EU in 2002
Yes, it is bigger than the EU
Yes, it only applies in Switzerland now
No, it was banned as early as 1953
40537.e: The treaty on the Coal and Steel Community was valid for 50 years. It expired in 2002, and its tasks passed to the European Community.
40537.m: The Coal and Steel Community became part of the EU in 2002.

40538.q: What was a lot of coal and steel needed for after the Second World War?
40538.e: Coal was the most important source of energy, and steel was needed for machines, rails and houses. So both were very important for rebuilding Europe.
40538.m: Coal and steel were important for rebuilding Europe.

40539.q: Why is the European Coal and Steel Community regarded as the forerunner of today’s EU?
a: It was the first European community with a joint authority
It created the European Parliament in Bern
40539.e: With the ECSC, states for the first time handed over powers to a joint European authority. Later communities built on this.
40539.m: The Coal and Steel Community was the first building block of today’s EU.

40540.q: In which city were important treaties on European unification signed in 1957?
40540.e: On 25 March 1957, the treaties establishing the EEC and Euratom were signed in Rome.
40540.m: The Treaties of Rome were signed in Rome in 1957.

40541.q: How many countries signed the Treaties of Rome in 1957?
40541.e: Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed the treaties. They are regarded as the founding states.
40541.m: Six countries signed the Treaties of Rome.

40542.q: Which economic community was founded with the Treaties of Rome?
40542.e: The EEC was meant to create a common market. It is an important forerunner of today’s EU.
40542.m: The EEC was created with the Treaties of Rome.

40543.q: Which second community was created in 1957 with the Treaties of Rome?
40543.e: Euratom is the European Atomic Energy Community. It was meant to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
40543.m: Besides the EEC, Euratom was founded in 1957.

40544.q: Which present-day community developed, among other things, out of the EEC?
40544.e: The EEC later became the European Community and finally the European Union. The Treaties of Rome are an important foundation stone of the EU.
40544.m: The EEC is a forerunner of the EU.

40545.q: According to the Treaties of Rome, what was to be gradually removed between the EEC states?
40545.e: The EEC planned a customs union. Goods were to be traded between the member states without customs duties.
40545.m: The EEC wanted to abolish customs duties between its members.

40546.q: Which common policy for agriculture did the Treaties of Rome set up?
40546.e: The EEC Treaty provided for a common agricultural policy. It was meant to secure food supplies and support farmers’ incomes.
40546.m: The Common Agricultural Policy goes back to the Treaties of Rome.

40547.q: Which organisation did Switzerland, Austria and the United Kingdom, among others, found in 1960 as a counterpart to the EEC?
40547.e: The European Free Trade Association, EFTA, was founded in 1960. Switzerland is still a member today.
40547.m: Switzerland was a co-founder of EFTA in 1960.

40548.q: In which country is the city of Maastricht?
40548.e: Maastricht is in the south of the Netherlands, near the borders with Belgium and Germany.
40548.m: Maastricht is a city in the Netherlands.

40549.q: In which year was the Maastricht Treaty signed?
40549.e: The treaty was signed on 7 February 1992.

40550.q: What was founded with the Maastricht Treaty?
a: The European Coal and Steel Community
40550.e: The European Union was created with the Maastricht Treaty. That is why it is regarded as the founding treaty of the EU.
40550.m: The Maastricht Treaty created the European Union.

40551.q: Roughly since when has the European Union existed?
40551.e: The Maastricht Treaty came into force in 1993. That is when the European Union was created.

40552.q: Which common currency was prepared in the Maastricht Treaty?
40552.e: The treaty set out the path to economic and monetary union. This led to the euro, as notes and coins from 2002.
40552.m: The Maastricht Treaty paved the way for the euro.

40553.q: Which new citizenship did the Maastricht Treaty introduce?
40553.e: Every person who is a national of an EU country is also a citizen of the Union. This rule came with Maastricht.
40553.m: Citizenship of the Union has existed since Maastricht.

40554.q: Which country first rejected the Maastricht Treaty in a referendum?
40554.e: The Danes narrowly said no in the first vote. After special arrangements, they agreed in a second vote.
40554.m: Denmark first said no to the Maastricht Treaty.

40555.q: How is the structure of the EU after the Maastricht Treaty often described in a picture?
40555.e: The EU rested on three pillars: the European Communities, foreign and security policy, and cooperation in justice and home affairs.
40555.m: After Maastricht the EU stood on three pillars.

40556.q: Under the Maastricht Treaty, which condition did countries have to meet for the euro?
a: They must not take on too much new debt
They had to be by the sea
They had to have a queen
They had to have more than 50 million inhabitants
40556.e: The Maastricht criteria require healthy public finances. For example, a country may only take on a little new debt each year.
40556.m: To adopt the euro, a country needs healthy public finances.

40557.q: Shortly after which event was the Council of Europe founded in 1949?
a: After the fall of the Berlin Wall
After the introduction of the euro
40557.e: After the Second World War, the states of Europe wanted to protect peace, democracy and human rights together. So in 1949 they founded the Council of Europe.
40557.m: The Council of Europe was created shortly after the Second World War.

40559.q: Is the Council of Europe part of the European Union?
a: No, it is a separate organisation
Yes, it is an EU body
Yes, it is the EU government
No, it belongs to the UN
40559.e: The Council of Europe is an independent international organisation. Countries such as Switzerland, which are not in the EU, are also members.
40559.m: The Council of Europe is not part of the EU.

40560.q: Which statement about the members of the Council of Europe is true?
a: It has more members than the EU
It has exactly as many members as the EU
Only EU countries may be members
40560.e: Almost all the states of Europe belong to the Council of Europe, including Switzerland. It has 46 members, while the EU has 27.
40560.m: The Council of Europe has more members than the EU.

40561.q: Which Swiss politician became Secretary General of the Council of Europe in 2024?
40561.e: Former Federal Councillor Alain Berset was elected by the Parliamentary Assembly in 2024 and took office in September 2024.
40561.m: Alain Berset has headed the Council of Europe as Secretary General since 2024.

40562.q: Which country was expelled from the Council of Europe in 2022?
40562.e: After the attack on Ukraine, Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe in March 2022.
40562.m: Russia has not been in the Council of Europe since 2022.

40563.q: Which organisation originally introduced the blue European flag with the circle of stars?
40563.e: The Council of Europe adopted the flag in 1955. Later the European Communities also took over the same flag.
40563.m: The European flag originally comes from the Council of Europe.

40564.q: Which piece of music did the Council of Europe choose as the European anthem in 1972?
40564.e: The melody comes from the last movement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s 9th Symphony.
40564.m: The European anthem is Beethoven’s Ode to Joy.

40565.q: What does the European Convention on Human Rights protect?
a: The fundamental rights of people in Europe
The rights of companies to high profits
40565.e: The European Convention on Human Rights of 1950 protects important rights such as the right to life or freedom of expression.
40565.m: The ECHR protects the fundamental rights of people in Europe.

40566.q: Which organisation does the European Convention on Human Rights come from?
40566.e: The ECHR was drawn up within the Council of Europe. All members of the Council of Europe have signed it.
40566.m: The ECHR is a treaty of the Council of Europe.

40567.q: Does the European Convention on Human Rights also apply in Switzerland?
a: No, it only applies in the EU
No, it only applies in France
Only in the cantons on Lake Geneva
40567.e: Switzerland is a member of the Council of Europe and recognised the ECHR in 1974. That is why it also applies here.
40567.m: The ECHR also applies in Switzerland.

40568.q: What does the European Convention on Human Rights forbid without any exception?
40568.e: The ECHR forbids torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, without any exception.
40568.m: The ECHR forbids torture without exception.

40569.q: Which freedom does the European Convention on Human Rights protect?
a: The freedom not to pay taxes
The freedom to drive without a licence
The freedom not to go to school
40569.e: The ECHR protects freedom of expression. This includes receiving and passing on information and ideas.
40569.m: The ECHR protects freedom of expression.

40570.q: What was abolished in Europe with additional protocols to the ECHR?
40570.e: Protocol No. 6 banned the death penalty in peacetime, and Protocol No. 13 bans it in all circumstances.
40570.m: The ECHR protocols forbid the death penalty.

40571.q: Which of these rights does the European Convention on Human Rights protect?
a: The right to your own car
The right to a high wage
The right to a holiday by the sea
40571.e: The ECHR protects every person’s right to life. It comes first among the guaranteed rights.
40571.m: The ECHR protects the right to life.

40572.q: Which area of life does the European Convention on Human Rights especially protect?
40572.e: The ECHR protects a person’s private life, family life, home and letters and messages.
40572.m: The ECHR protects private and family life.

40573.q: Compliance with which treaty does the European Court of Human Rights watch over?
40573.e: The Court examines whether states have violated the rights guaranteed in the ECHR.
40573.m: The Court in Strasbourg watches over the ECHR.

40574.q: Who may bring a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights?
40574.e: With an individual application, single people can also bring a case, once they have gone through all the courts in their own country.
40574.m: Individual people can also bring a case in Strasbourg.

40575.q: How many judges does each member state provide to the European Court of Human Rights?
40575.e: The number of judges equals the number of member states of the Council of Europe. Each state provides one person.
40575.m: Each Council of Europe state provides one judge.

40576.q: In which city is the European Court of Human Rights?
40576.e: The Court has its seat in Strasbourg, France, like the Council of Europe.
40576.m: The Court of Human Rights is in Strasbourg.

40577.q: Which organisation does the European Court of Human Rights belong to?
40577.e: The Court belongs to the Council of Europe. That is why cases can also be brought against Switzerland, even though it is not in the EU.
40577.m: The Court of Human Rights belongs to the Council of Europe.

40578.q: Which Swiss group won a climate protection case at the European Court of Human Rights in 2024?
a: The KlimaSeniorinnen (Senior Women for Climate Protection)
40578.e: In April 2024 the Court ruled that Switzerland had violated the rights of the KlimaSeniorinnen by doing too little to protect the climate.
40578.m: The KlimaSeniorinnen won against Switzerland in Strasbourg in 2024.

40579.q: When may a person complain to the Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg?
a: When they have gone through all the courts in their own country
Immediately, without asking another court first
Only if the government allows it
40579.e: First the courts in your own country must decide. Only after that can you complain in Strasbourg.
40579.m: You only go to Strasbourg after the courts in your own country.

40580.q: How many states joined the EU on 1 May 2004?
40580.e: On 1 May 2004 ten states became EU members at once. It was the largest enlargement in EU history.
40580.m: On 1 May 2004 ten new states joined the EU.

40581.q: How many members did the EU have after the enlargement of 1 May 2004?
40581.e: Before, the EU had 15 members; after the enlargement there were 25.
40581.m: After 2004 the EU had 25 member states.

40582.q: Which country did NOT join the EU in 2004?
40582.e: Romania only joined in 2007, together with Bulgaria. Poland, Hungary and Slovenia joined in 2004.
40582.m: Romania and Bulgaria only followed in 2007.

40583.q: Which three Baltic states joined the EU in 2004?
a: Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia
40583.e: The three Baltic states were part of the Soviet Union until 1991 and became EU members in 2004.
40583.m: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have been in the EU since 2004.

40584.q: Which two island states in the Mediterranean joined the EU in 2004?
40584.e: Malta and Cyprus are in the Mediterranean and used to be British colonies. Both became EU members in 2004.
40584.m: Malta and Cyprus became EU members in 2004.

40585.q: Which of the new EU countries had the largest population in 2004?
40585.e: Poland had about 38 million inhabitants at the time, more than all the other new members.
40585.m: Poland was the largest country in the 2004 enlargement.

40586.q: Which two countries, which formed a single state until 1993, joined the EU in 2004?
40586.e: Czechoslovakia split peacefully in 1993. Both successor states became EU members in 2004.
40586.m: The Czech Republic and Slovakia joined the EU together in 2004.

40587.q: Which of the countries that joined in 2004 was the first to introduce the euro?
40587.e: Slovenia has paid with the euro since 1 January 2007. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary still have their own currencies (as of 2025).
40587.m: Slovenia was the first of the 2004 newcomers to use the euro.

40588.q: On which day does the EU celebrate Europe Day each year?
40588.e: Europe Day is on 9 May. On that day in 1950 Robert Schuman presented his declaration.

40589.q: Which event does the EU’s Europe Day commemorate?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
40589.e: In his declaration, Robert Schuman proposed managing coal and steel jointly. European cooperation grew out of this.
40589.m: Europe Day commemorates the Schuman Declaration.

40590.q: How many stars does the European flag have, which flies on many buildings on Europe Day?
40590.e: The flag shows a circle of twelve golden stars. The number twelve stands for perfection, not for the number of members.
40590.m: The European flag has twelve stars.

40591.q: Where is Europe Day mainly celebrated?
a: In the countries of the EU
40591.e: Europe Day is a celebration of the European Union. In many EU countries there are festivals and open days on this day.
40591.m: Europe Day is mainly celebrated in the EU.

40592.q: What do many EU institutions often offer around Europe Day?
40592.e: Around 9 May, the European Parliament and the Commission, for example, open their buildings to visitors.
40592.m: On Europe Day you can often visit EU buildings.

40593.q: Which day of remembrance in several Eastern European countries also falls on 9 May?
a: Victory Day in the Second World War
40593.e: In Russia and some other countries, the end of the war in 1945 is remembered on 9 May. This is linked to the time difference at the moment of surrender.
40593.m: 9 May is Victory Day in Russia.

40594.q: How many years after the end of the Second World War in Europe was the Schuman Declaration, which Europe Day commemorates, presented?
40594.e: The war in Europe ended in May 1945, and the declaration followed in May 1950. 1950 minus 1945 = 5.
40594.m: Five years after the end of the war, European unification began with the Schuman Declaration.

40595.q: The Schuman Declaration dates from 1950, and Europe Day was set in 1985. How many years are there in between?
40595.e: You calculate 1985 minus 1950 = 35. So Europe Day was officially decided 35 years after the declaration.
40595.m: There are 35 years between the Schuman Declaration and the official Europe Day.

40596.q: In which German city is the Charlemagne Prize awarded?
40596.e: The Charlemagne Prize is awarded every year in Aachen town hall.
40596.m: The Charlemagne Prize comes from Aachen.

40597.q: Who is the Charlemagne Prize named after?
40597.e: Charlemagne often stayed in Aachen and ruled over large parts of Europe. He is regarded as the “Father of Europe”.
40597.m: The Charlemagne Prize honours the memory of Charlemagne.

40598.q: What is the Charlemagne Prize awarded for?
a: For services to the unification of Europe
40598.e: The prize honours people or institutions that have worked especially hard for the unification of Europe.
40598.m: The Charlemagne Prize rewards work for a united Europe.

40599.q: When was the Charlemagne Prize awarded for the first time?
a: Shortly after the Second World War
40599.e: The Charlemagne Prize was first awarded in 1950, five years after the end of the Second World War. Europe was meant to grow together after the war.
40599.m: The Charlemagne Prize has existed since 1950, shortly after the Second World War.

40600.q: Who usually receives the Charlemagne Prize?
40600.e: The Charlemagne Prize mainly goes to politicians who have worked for a united Europe. Sometimes an institution is honoured too.
40600.m: The Charlemagne Prize usually goes to politicians.

40601.q: Roughly when did Charlemagne, after whom the Charlemagne Prize is named, live?
40601.e: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in the year 800. He ruled over large parts of Europe and often stayed in Aachen.
40601.m: Charlemagne became emperor in the year 800.

40603.q: What received the Charlemagne Prize in 2002, even though it is not a person?
40603.e: In 2002 the euro was honoured because it was introduced as notes and coins that year.
40603.m: In 2002 the euro currency received the Charlemagne Prize.

40604.q: In which Swiss city did Winston Churchill give a famous speech for a united Europe in 1946?
40604.e: Churchill spoke at the University of Zurich in 1946 and called for a kind of “United States of Europe”. For this and his further efforts he received the Charlemagne Prize in 1955.
40604.m: Churchill gave a famous speech on Europe in Zurich in 1946.

40605.q: What must a state do if the Court of Human Rights rules against it?
a: It must carry out the judgement
It must move out of Europe
Nothing, the judgement is only advice
40605.e: The states have committed themselves to following the judgements. Often they have to change laws or pay compensation.
40605.m: States must carry out the judgements from Strasbourg.

40606.q: With which community did Switzerland conclude a free trade agreement in 1972?
40606.e: In 1972 Switzerland concluded a free trade agreement with the European Economic Community, or EEC for short. It later became the EU.
40606.m: In 1972 Switzerland concluded a free trade agreement with the EEC.

40607.q: Who decided on the free trade agreement with the EEC in Switzerland in 1972?
a: The people and the cantons in a vote
40607.e: On 3 December 1972 the people and the cantons voted on the agreement. About 72 per cent of voters said yes.
40607.m: In 1972 voters clearly said yes to the free trade agreement.

40608.q: Does the 1972 free trade agreement still apply today?
a: Yes, it is still important today
40608.e: The agreement has applied without interruption since 1973. It is still an important basis for trade with the EU today.
40608.m: The 1972 free trade agreement still applies today.

40609.q: Which goods are, in principle, NOT covered by the 1972 free trade agreement?
40609.e: The agreement removed customs duties on industrial products. Separate rules apply to agriculture so that farmers remain protected.
40609.m: Agricultural products are, in principle, not part of the 1972 free trade agreement.

40610.q: Which free trade organisation did Switzerland already belong to as a founding member before 1972?
40610.e: The European Free Trade Association, EFTA, was founded in 1960, and Switzerland was there from the start. The agreement with the EEC followed in 1972.
40610.m: Switzerland was a founding member of EFTA in 1960.

40611.q: What is removed between the partners in a free trade agreement?
40611.e: Free trade means that goods are traded across the border without customs duties and without quotas. Otherwise the countries remain independent.
40611.m: A free trade agreement removes customs duties and quantity limits.

40612.q: Why did the free trade agreement become especially important for Switzerland in the early 1970s?
a: Important EFTA partners such as the United Kingdom joined the EEC
40612.e: In 1973 the United Kingdom and Denmark moved from EFTA to the EEC. Without an agreement, Swiss exports there would have faced customs duties again.
40612.m: The free trade agreement secured Switzerland duty-free access to important markets.

40613.q: Membership of which European economic area did Switzerland vote on in December 1992?
40613.e: The EEA is the European Economic Area. Shortly before the vote, the Federal Council had also submitted an application to join the European Community.
40613.m: Switzerland voted on the EEA in 1992.

40614.q: What happened to the application to join after the no to the EEA in December 1992?
a: It was withdrawn the very same day
40614.e: After the no to the EEA, the Federal Council did not pursue the application any further. It lay “frozen” in Brussels for decades.
40614.m: After the no to the EEA, the application stayed frozen.

40615.q: What was the result of the vote on joining the EEA in December 1992?
40615.e: The no was very narrow: 50.3 per cent voted no. A clear majority of the cantons rejected it.
40615.m: Joining the EEA was narrowly rejected in 1992.

40616.q: Which parts of the country mostly voted for the EEA in 1992?
40616.e: All the cantons of French-speaking Switzerland and the two Basels said yes. The divide between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland was often called the “Röstigraben”.
40616.m: French-speaking Switzerland voted for the EEA in 1992.

40617.q: Is Switzerland a member of the European Union today?
a: Only the cantons of French-speaking Switzerland
40617.e: Switzerland is not in the EU. It officially withdrew its old application in 2016. It manages its relations with bilateral agreements.
40617.m: Switzerland is not a member of the EU.

40618.q: What was the result of the 2001 popular initiative “Yes to Europe!”?
40618.e: The initiative wanted rapid membership negotiations with the EU. On 4 March 2001 about 77 per cent rejected it.
40618.m: The “Yes to Europe!” initiative was clearly rejected in 2001.

40619.q: What majority would joining the EU need in Switzerland, because it affects the constitution?
40619.e: Joining a supranational community is subject to a mandatory referendum. So it needs the double majority of the people and the cantons.
40619.m: Joining the EU would need the approval of the people and the cantons.

40620.q: How many agreements make up the Bilateral Agreements I?
40620.e: The Bilateral Agreements I include seven agreements, for example on air transport and research. They were signed in 1999.
40620.m: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven agreements.

40621.q: What does the “guillotine clause” in the Bilateral Agreements I do?
a: If one agreement ends, the others end too
The EU can punish Switzerland at any time
Each agreement expires after ten years
The cantons can cancel individual agreements
40621.e: The agreements of the Bilateral Agreements I are linked to each other. If one is terminated, the others also lapse.
40621.m: Because of the guillotine clause, the Bilateral Agreements I are linked.

40622.q: How did the Swiss people vote on the Bilateral Agreements I in May 2000?
a: A clear yes, with about two thirds
40622.e: On 21 May 2000, 67.2 per cent of voters agreed. A referendum had been called against the agreements.
40622.m: The Bilateral Agreements I were accepted by two thirds in 2000.

40623.q: Why did the Bilateral Agreements I only come into force in 2002, even though the people agreed in 2000?
a: All EU states still had to agree
The Federal Council was against them
The agreements had to be rewritten
40623.e: After the referendum, all EU states still had to agree. That is why the agreements only came into force on 1 June 2002.
40623.m: The Bilateral Agreements I have applied since 2002.

40624.q: Which agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements I?
40624.e: The air transport agreement gives Swiss airlines access to the European air transport market. It is part of the first package of 1999.
40624.m: Air transport is part of the Bilateral Agreements I.

40625.q: What is the agreement on public procurement about?
a: Contracts from public authorities to companies
40625.e: Larger contracts from municipalities, cantons and public companies are advertised across Europe. Companies from Switzerland and the EU can apply on equal terms.
40625.m: Public procurement is about contracts from public authorities.

40626.q: What does the agreement on technical barriers to trade make easier?
a: A product only has to be tested once
All products need a Swiss stamp
40626.e: Tests on products such as machines are mutually recognised. This saves double testing and costs.
40626.m: Thanks to the agreement on technical barriers to trade, products do not have to be tested twice.

40627.q: How was free movement of persons with the EU introduced?
a: Step by step over several years
All at once on a single day
Only for children and young people
Only for people from neighbouring countries
40627.e: Free movement of persons was introduced gradually. For the 15 old EU states, the quotas ended in June 2007.
40627.m: Free movement of persons was introduced step by step.

40628.q: Which popular initiative of 2020 wanted to end free movement of persons?
40628.e: The Limitation Initiative demanded an end to free movement of persons. The people rejected it in September 2020 with about 62 per cent.
40628.m: The Limitation Initiative was rejected in 2020.

40629.q: In which year were the Bilateral Agreements II signed?
40629.e: The Bilateral Agreements II were signed in Luxembourg on 26 October 2004. They build on the first package.
40629.m: The Bilateral Agreements II were signed in 2004.

40630.q: Which agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements II?
40630.e: Schengen/Dublin is the best-known agreement of the Bilateral Agreements II. It governs cooperation on borders, police and asylum.
40630.m: Schengen/Dublin is part of the Bilateral Agreements II.

40631.q: What was the result of the 2005 referendum on Schengen/Dublin?
a: Only the cantons were allowed to vote
40631.e: On 5 June 2005, 54.6 per cent of voters agreed to join Schengen/Dublin.
40631.m: In 2005 the people said yes to Schengen/Dublin.

40632.q: What makes the Bilateral Agreements II different from the Bilateral Agreements I?
40632.e: The agreements of the Bilateral Agreements II are not linked to each other. If one ends, the others remain.
40632.m: The Bilateral Agreements II are not linked by a guillotine clause.

40633.q: Which goods does the agreement on processed agricultural products cover?
40633.e: Processed agricultural products are foods made by industry, such as chocolate, coffee or biscuits. The agreement lowered customs duties on these products.
40633.m: Chocolate is one of the processed agricultural products.

40634.q: What does the European Environment Agency, in which Switzerland takes part, do?
a: It collects data on the environment in Europe
It collects rubbish from all countries
40634.e: Through one of the Bilateral Agreements II, Switzerland is a member of the European Environment Agency in Copenhagen. It collects data on the environment in Europe.
40634.m: Switzerland takes part in the European Environment Agency.

40635.q: What was the agreement on the taxation of savings about?
a: Taxes on interest earned by EU citizens in Switzerland
The level of mortgage interest rates
The interest of the National Bank
40635.e: Swiss banks deducted a withholding tax on interest earned by people from the EU and passed it on. In 2017 the agreement was replaced by the automatic exchange of information.
40635.m: The savings tax agreement concerned interest earned by EU citizens on Swiss accounts.
