40636.q: Thanks to the Bilateral Agreements II, which federal office works closely with Eurostat?
40636.e: The statistics agreement makes sure Swiss data can be compared with EU data. Eurostat is the EU’s statistics office.
40636.m: The Federal Statistical Office works with Eurostat.

40637.q: What do the Dublin rules govern in Europe?
a: Which country examines an asylum application
Which language you learn at school
40637.e: The Dublin rules set out which state is responsible for an asylum application. Switzerland has taken part since 2008.
40637.m: The Dublin rules decide which country examines an asylum application.

40638.q: Under the Dublin rules, which country is usually responsible for an asylum application?
a: The country the person first entered
The country with the most inhabitants
Always the country of the EU Commission
40638.e: Often the state through which a person first entered the Dublin area is responsible. But there are exceptions, for example for families.
40638.m: Usually the country of first entry examines an asylum application.

40639.q: What is stored for asylum seekers in the European database Eurodac?
40639.e: Fingerprints are compared in Eurodac. This shows whether someone has already applied for asylum in another state.
40639.m: Eurodac stores the fingerprints of asylum seekers.

40640.q: Which city is the Dublin agreement named after?
40640.e: The first Dublin Convention was signed in Dublin in 1990. Dublin is the capital of Ireland.
40640.m: The Dublin agreement is named after the capital of Ireland.

40641.q: Does Switzerland take part in the Dublin rules?
a: Yes, even though it is not in the EU
No, only EU countries may take part
Only the canton of Geneva takes part
40641.e: Switzerland is not an EU member but has concluded an agreement with the EU on Schengen and Dublin. It has applied the Dublin rules since 2008.
40641.m: Switzerland takes part in Dublin even though it is not in the EU.

a: Returning a person to the responsible Dublin state
A flight to Ireland for students
40642.e: If another state is responsible, Switzerland can transfer the asylum seeker there. The asylum application is then examined there.
40642.m: In a Dublin transfer, a person goes back to the responsible state.

40643.q: Which Swiss federal office is responsible for Dublin procedures?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
The Federal Office for the Environment
40643.e: The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) decides on asylum applications. It also checks whether another Dublin state is responsible.
40643.m: In Switzerland, the State Secretariat for Migration is responsible for Dublin procedures.

40644.q: What advantage does Switzerland get from taking part in Dublin?
a: It can send second applications back to other states
It no longer has to guard any borders
It receives money for every asylum seeker
It may decide EU asylum laws on its own
40644.e: Anyone who has already applied in another Dublin state is usually sent back there. This prevents multiple procedures.
40644.m: Thanks to Dublin, Switzerland does not have to examine every second application itself.

40645.q: Since the land transport agreement, what is the maximum weight of lorries in Switzerland?
40645.e: The limit used to be 28 tonnes. With the land transport agreement it was raised step by step to 40 tonnes, as in the EU.
40645.m: In Switzerland lorries may now weigh up to 40 tonnes.

40646.q: What is the charge called that heavy lorries pay in Switzerland for every kilometre driven?
40646.e: The HVC depends on weight, kilometres and emissions standard. The EU recognised it in the land transport agreement.
40646.m: Heavy lorries in Switzerland pay the HVC.

40647.q: What is part of the money from the heavy vehicle charge used for?
40647.e: The heavy vehicle charge is meant to move freight onto the railway. That is why a large part of the money goes into expanding the railway, for example the NRLA.
40647.m: Money from the heavy vehicle charge is used to expand the railway.

40648.q: What goal does Switzerland pursue with its transport policy in the Alps?
a: Moving freight from road to rail
Building more motorways over the passes
40648.e: Switzerland wants transit traffic through the Alps to go by train as far as possible. This protects the environment and the people.
40648.m: Switzerland wants to move freight through the Alps onto the railway.

40649.q: Which 1994 popular initiative demanded that the Alpine region be protected from transit traffic?
40649.e: The Alpine Initiative was accepted on 20 February 1994. Since then, protection of the Alps has been in the Federal Constitution.
40649.m: The 1994 Alpine Initiative protects the Alps from too much transit traffic.

40650.q: Which NRLA tunnel was opened in 2016?
40650.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long and was opened in June 2016. It helps move freight onto the railway.
40650.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel was opened in 2016.

40651.q: May a lorry from the EU deliver goods from Basel to Zurich in Switzerland?
40651.e: Transport within a foreign country is called cabotage. It is forbidden for foreign lorries in Switzerland. This protects Swiss transport companies.
40651.m: Foreign lorries may not transport goods within Switzerland.

40652.q: What still applies to lorries in Switzerland even after the land transport agreement?
a: The ban on driving at night and on Sundays
A driving ban on all working days
40652.e: Switzerland was able to keep the night and Sunday driving ban for lorries. It protects people from noise.
40652.m: In Switzerland lorries are generally not allowed to drive at night or on Sundays.

40653.q: What was the institutional framework agreement meant to regulate?
a: How the bilateral agreements are updated and disputes settled
40653.e: The agreement was meant to form a common roof for several market access agreements. It was about adopting law, monitoring and settling disputes.
40653.m: The framework agreement was meant to regulate how the bilateral agreements develop.

40654.q: With whom did Switzerland negotiate the institutional framework agreement?
40654.e: Switzerland negotiated with the EU from 2014. The agreement was meant to put the bilateral agreements with the EU on a common basis.
40654.m: The framework agreement was negotiated with the EU.

40655.q: Who ended the negotiations on the framework agreement in May 2021?
40655.e: On 26 May 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations. There was no referendum on it.
40655.m: The Federal Council broke off the negotiations on the framework agreement in 2021.

40656.q: Which point of the framework agreement was especially controversial in Switzerland?
40656.e: Trade unions feared that Swiss wages would be less well protected. The Citizens’ Rights Directive and state aid were also controversial.
40656.m: Wage protection was a main point of dispute in the framework agreement.

40657.q: What would Switzerland have had to do regularly under the framework agreement?
a: Adopt new EU law in certain areas
Make a new constitution every year
40657.e: If the EU changed its law in an area covered by the agreements, Switzerland would have adapted its law. This is called dynamic adoption of law. However, the people could still have called a referendum.
40657.m: Under the framework agreement, Switzerland would have adopted new EU law.

40658.q: What worry did many opponents of the framework agreement have?
a: Foreign judges could have a say
Switzerland would have to introduce the euro
The army would have to belong to the EU
40658.e: On questions of EU law, the Court of Justice of the EU in Luxembourg would have had a say. So many people feared “foreign judges”.
40658.m: Many feared foreign judges under the framework agreement.

40659.q: What was a consequence of breaking off the framework agreement in 2021?
a: The EU stopped updating some agreements
Switzerland had to move out of Europe
The borders were closed for ever
40659.e: The EU no longer updated some existing agreements. Since then Swiss companies, for example in medical technology, have needed extra approvals in the EU.
40659.m: After the break-off, the EU stopped updating some agreements.

40660.q: With whom did Switzerland negotiate the Bilateral Agreements III package?
40660.e: The negotiations with the EU began in March 2024 and were concluded in substance in December 2024.
40660.m: The Bilateral Agreements III are a package of agreements with the EU.

40661.q: What normally happens in Switzerland before big agreements like the Bilateral Agreements III apply?
a: Parliament debates them, and often the people vote
The President of the Confederation decides alone
Nothing, they apply immediately after signing
40661.e: After signing, Parliament debates the agreements. With important agreements, the people often have the last word.
40661.m: Parliament and often the people decide on big agreements.

40662.q: Which new agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements III?
40662.e: The electricity agreement is meant to let Switzerland take part in the European internal electricity market. Until now there has been no such agreement.
40662.m: The Bilateral Agreements III include an electricity agreement.

40663.q: What is the food safety agreement in the Bilateral Agreements III meant to create?
a: A common area for safe food
40663.e: Switzerland and the EU are to apply common rules on food safety. This makes it easier to trade food.
40663.m: The Bilateral Agreements III create a common food safety area.

40664.q: Under the Bilateral Agreements III, who is to decide disputes between Switzerland and the EU if no agreement is reached?
a: An arbitration tribunal with members from both sides
The Swiss Federal Supreme Court alone
40664.e: First there are negotiations in the Joint Committee. If no agreement is reached, an arbitration tribunal with equal numbers of members from both sides decides.
40664.m: An arbitration tribunal is to settle disputes over the Bilateral Agreements III.

40665.q: What does the safeguard clause in the package between Switzerland and the EU allow?
a: Measures in case of serious problems caused by immigration
40665.e: If there are serious economic or social problems caused by free movement of persons, Switzerland can take protective measures. The clause was newly negotiated.
40665.m: With the safeguard clause, Switzerland can react to big immigration problems.

40666.q: What is a “dispatch” from the Federal Council to Parliament, like the one on the Bilateral Agreements III?
a: A report that explains a proposal
A letter to a foreign state
40666.e: In a dispatch, the Federal Council explains a proposal to Parliament. It adopted the one on the Bilateral Agreements III in March 2026.
40666.m: With a dispatch, the Federal Council explains a proposal to Parliament.

40667.q: What could cantons, parties and associations do about the Bilateral Agreements III between June and October 2025?
a: Give their views in the consultation
40667.e: In the consultation, cantons, parties and associations can give their opinion on a proposal. The Federal Council then evaluates the responses.
40667.m: In the consultation, cantons, parties and associations give their views.

40668.q: Which cooperation is planned in the new health agreement of the Bilateral Agreements III?
a: A single health insurance fund for everyone
A ban on medicines from the EU
40668.e: Switzerland is to work with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, for example. This way it can fight pandemics better together with others.
40668.m: The health agreement strengthens cooperation against cross-border health threats.

40669.q: What does Switzerland pay the so-called cohesion contribution for?
a: To reduce differences between poor and rich EU regions
40669.e: The money supports projects in economically weaker EU states. Switzerland chooses the projects together with the partner countries.
40669.m: The cohesion contribution is meant to reduce differences in Europe.

40670.q: Who decided in 2006 on the legal basis for the first Swiss enlargement contribution?
40670.e: In 2006 the people voted on the law on cooperation with Eastern Europe and accepted it with about 53 per cent.
40670.m: Swiss voters said yes to the enlargement contribution in 2006.

40671.q: How much money did the second Swiss contribution amount to in total?
40671.e: The second contribution amounts to 1.302 billion francs. It is spread over about ten years.
40671.m: The second Swiss contribution amounts to about 1.3 billion francs.

40672.q: What are the two main focuses of the second Swiss contribution?
40672.e: About 1.1 billion francs are planned for cohesion. About 200 million francs help states that are strongly affected by migration.
40672.m: The second Swiss contribution strengthens cohesion and migration management.

40673.q: Which states receive the cohesion part of the Swiss contribution?
a: The EU states that have joined since 2004
The founding states of the EU
40673.e: The 13 states that have joined the EU since 2004 are supported. They include, for example, Poland, Hungary and Romania.
40673.m: The cohesion contribution goes to the EU states that joined from 2004 onwards.

40674.q: Why does Switzerland pay a contribution to EU countries even though it is not an EU member?
a: Because it benefits greatly from trade with the EU
Because it will soon join the EU
Because the EU belongs to Switzerland
40674.e: Thanks to agreements, Switzerland has good access to the EU single market. With the contribution it helps to reduce differences in Europe.
40674.m: Switzerland benefits from trade with the EU and supports poorer EU countries.

40675.q: Which country received the most money from the first enlargement contribution?
40675.e: Poland is the largest of the new EU countries and received the biggest share. Small states such as Malta received much less.
40675.m: Poland received the biggest share of the first enlargement contribution.

40676.q: Which example is one of the projects of the Swiss contribution?
a: Vocational training in Eastern European countries
40676.e: Many projects strengthen vocational training, for example in Bulgaria, Romania or Slovakia. Switzerland contributes its experience with apprenticeships.
40676.m: Among other things, the Swiss contribution supports vocational training in Eastern Europe.

a: An EU programme for exchanges in education, youth and sport
40677.e: With Erasmus+, students, apprentices and teachers can spend time abroad. From 2014 Switzerland was only a third country, but it is meant to take part fully again.
40677.m: Erasmus+ is the EU exchange programme for education.

40678.q: What can students do with an exchange programme like Erasmus+?
a: Study for a semester at a university abroad
Have a free holiday by the sea
40678.e: With Erasmus+, young people study for a while at a university in another country. Switzerland currently funds its own programme for this.
40678.m: With Erasmus+ you can study abroad.

40679.q: What is the name of the Swiss agency for exchange and mobility in education?
40679.e: Movetia promotes exchanges in schools, vocational training and higher education. It manages the Swiss mobility programmes.
40679.m: Movetia is the Swiss agency for exchange and mobility.

40680.q: From which year is Switzerland to take part fully in Erasmus+ again?
40680.e: As part of the package with the EU, participation in Erasmus+ from 2027 was agreed. That is when a new programme generation begins.
40680.m: Switzerland is to take part fully in Erasmus+ again from 2027.

40681.q: The scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam, after whom the programme is named, lived for a long time in which Swiss city?
40681.e: Erasmus of Rotterdam lived in Basel for many years and died there in 1536. He travelled all over Europe, so his name suits the exchange programme.
40681.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam lived and died in Basel.

40682.q: Apart from students and apprentices, who can take part in Erasmus+?
40682.e: Erasmus+ also supports teachers, trainers, youth work and sport. It is the EU programme for education, youth and sport.
40682.m: Erasmus+ is also for teachers and youth groups.

40683.e: Horizon Europe is the EU’s biggest programme for research and innovation. It runs from 2021 to 2027.
40683.m: Horizon Europe is the EU’s research and innovation programme.

40684.q: What have researchers in Switzerland been able to do again since 2025?
a: Take part fully in Horizon Europe
Travel to the USA without a passport
40684.e: Switzerland has been associated with Horizon Europe again since 2025. Researchers can apply for all projects again.
40684.m: Switzerland has been part of Horizon Europe again since 2025.

40685.q: How did Switzerland take part in Horizon Europe from 2021 to 2024?
a: Only to a limited extent, like a country outside Europe
As leader of the whole programme
40685.e: After the negotiations on the framework agreement were broken off, the EU no longer let Switzerland take part fully. It was treated as a so-called third country.
40685.m: From 2021 to 2024 Switzerland took part in Horizon Europe only to a limited extent.

40686.q: Who paid for Swiss researchers’ projects when Switzerland was not associated with Horizon Europe?
40686.e: The federal government funded projects directly, and the Swiss National Science Foundation created replacement programmes. This allowed many projects to continue.
40686.m: While not associated, the federal government funded the research itself.

40687.q: What was difficult for Swiss researchers when Switzerland was not fully part of Horizon Europe?
a: They could not apply for all EU funding
They were not allowed to do research at all
40687.e: Some sought-after funding, such as European Research Council grants, was only open to researchers from participating countries. So the federal government paid replacement money.
40687.m: Without full participation, Swiss researchers missed out on important EU funding.

40688.q: Which EU programme for exchanges in school, apprenticeships and studies does Switzerland want to rejoin from 2027?
40688.e: Besides Horizon Europe, the agreement on EU programmes also covers Erasmus+. This makes it easier for young people to go on an exchange abroad.
40688.m: With Erasmus+, young people can learn abroad.

40689.q: What are cross-border commuters called in Italian in Ticino?
40689.e: In Ticino people speak of “frontalieri”. The word comes from “frontiera”, the border.
40689.m: In Ticino cross-border commuters are called “frontalieri”.

40690.q: What are cross-border commuters called in French in Geneva?
40690.e: In French-speaking Switzerland people speak of “frontaliers”. Many live in the French border area around Geneva.
40690.m: In Geneva cross-border commuters are called “frontaliers”.

a: Someone who lives abroad and works in Switzerland
Someone who guards the Swiss border
Someone who likes hiking along borders
Someone who lives and works in Switzerland
40691.e: Cross-border commuters live, for example, in France, Italy or Germany and travel to work in Switzerland. They return home at least once a week.
40691.m: Cross-border commuters live abroad and work in Switzerland.

40692.q: Which rail service has linked Geneva with the surrounding French area since 2019?
40692.e: The Léman Express is a cross-border suburban rail network around Geneva. It opened in December 2019 and takes pressure off the roads.
40692.m: The Léman Express links Geneva with France.

40693.q: Where do cross-border commuters from Germany pay most of their taxes?
a: They pay no taxes at all
40693.e: Cross-border commuters from Germany only pay a small withholding tax of at most 4.5 per cent in Switzerland. They pay most of their taxes in Germany, where they live.
40693.m: Cross-border commuters from Germany pay most of their taxes in Germany.

40694.q: From which neighbouring country do most cross-border commuters working in Geneva come?
40694.e: Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France. Many people live in the French border area and work in Geneva.
40694.m: Most cross-border commuters in Geneva come from France.

40695.q: Thanks to an agreement, what have cross-border commuters been able to do since 2023 without changing the country of their social insurance?
a: Live abroad indefinitely without a permit
40695.e: Since July 2023, cross-border commuters may work less than half of their working time from home in the country where they live. They still remain insured in Switzerland.
40695.m: Cross-border commuters may work partly from home.

40696.q: Which agreement made it easier for EU citizens to work in Switzerland as cross-border commuters?
a: The agreement on free movement of persons
40696.e: Since the agreement on free movement of persons, there have been no more quotas or strict border zones. The number of cross-border commuters then rose sharply.
40696.m: The agreement on free movement of persons made working as a cross-border commuter easier.

40698.q: What does it mean that Switzerland and Liechtenstein form a common customs area?
a: Goods can be transported between the two countries without customs duties
You need a visa for Liechtenstein
There are no taxes in Liechtenstein
40698.e: The customs treaty has applied since 1924. So there is no customs border between Switzerland and Liechtenstein, but Liechtenstein remains a separate state.
40698.m: There are no customs duties between Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

40699.q: With which country did Liechtenstein have a customs treaty before Switzerland?
40699.e: From 1852 to 1919 Liechtenstein was linked to Austria by a customs treaty. After the First World War, Liechtenstein ended it.
40699.m: Before Switzerland, Liechtenstein was in a customs union with Austria.

40700.q: Where do customs checks for Liechtenstein take place today?
a: On the Rhine between Switzerland and Liechtenstein
40700.e: Because Switzerland and Liechtenstein form one customs area, there are no customs checks between them. Checks take place at the border with Austria.
40700.m: Liechtenstein’s customs border is at the border with Austria.

40701.q: Which administration looks after customs in Liechtenstein?
40701.e: Because of the customs treaty, Switzerland takes on border protection and customs tasks. Today the responsible body is called the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security.
40701.m: Switzerland carries out the customs tasks for Liechtenstein.

40703.q: Which economic area did Liechtenstein join in 1995, but Switzerland did not?
40703.e: Liechtenstein said yes to the EEA. The customs treaty was adjusted so that Liechtenstein can be linked to both Switzerland and the EEA at the same time.
40703.m: Liechtenstein has been a member of the European Economic Area since 1995.

40704.q: What does it mean that Liechtenstein belongs to the Schengen Area?
a: There are no regular passport checks at the borders
You pay with the euro there
Liechtenstein is part of the EU
40704.e: In the Schengen Area, travellers are not systematically checked at the borders between member countries. Liechtenstein is part of it, but not in the EU.
40704.m: There are no regular border checks in the Schengen Area.

40705.q: In which city was the North Atlantic Treaty signed in 1949?
40705.e: The founding states signed the treaty in Washington, the capital of the USA.
40705.m: The NATO treaty was signed in Washington.

40706.q: Which two parts of the world does NATO link?
40706.e: NATO was founded in 1949 by twelve states, including the USA and Canada and ten countries from Europe. That is why it is also called the North Atlantic Alliance.
40706.m: NATO links countries from North America and Europe.

40707.q: What does the abbreviation NATO stand for?
40707.e: Written out in full, NATO means North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
40707.m: NATO means North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

40708.q: In which city does NATO have its headquarters today?
40708.e: NATO headquarters is in Brussels, the capital of Belgium.

40709.q: Which military alliance did the Soviet Union and its allies found in 1955?
40709.e: The Warsaw Pact was NATO’s counterpart during the Cold War. It was dissolved in 1991.
40709.m: The Warsaw Pact was the alliance of the Eastern Bloc.

40710.q: Who is Secretary General of NATO (as of 2025)?
40710.e: Mark Rutte, former Prime Minister of the Netherlands, has been Secretary General of NATO since October 2024.
40710.m: Mark Rutte has led NATO as Secretary General since 2024.

40711.q: Which of these countries was one of NATO’s founding members in 1949?
40711.e: Canada founded NATO together with the USA and ten European states. Greece joined in 1952, Spain in 1982 and Poland in 1999.
40711.m: Canada is a founding member of NATO.

40712.q: What does Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty say?
a: An attack on one member counts as an attack on all
Members may not have an army
Every member pays the same amount
40712.e: Article 5 is the mutual defence clause. If one member is attacked, the other members help with its defence.
40712.m: Under Article 5 it is one for all and all for one.

40713.q: What is it called when NATO triggers Article 5?
40713.e: When NATO decides that a member has been attacked and Article 5 applies, this is called a case of collective defence.
40713.m: Triggering Article 5 is called a case of collective defence.

40714.q: How many times has Article 5 been triggered so far (as of 2025)?
40714.e: In the whole history of NATO, Article 5 has been triggered only once.
40714.m: Collective defence has only been triggered once so far.

40715.q: After which event was Article 5 triggered?
a: The building of the Berlin Wall in 1961
The fall of the Wall in 1989
40715.e: The day after the attacks in New York and Washington, NATO declared a case of collective defence to support the USA.
40715.m: After the attacks of 11 September 2001, collective defence applied.

40716.q: In a case of collective defence, does every NATO country have to send soldiers?
a: No, each country decides for itself what kind of help to give
Yes, every country must send the same number of soldiers
Yes, but only the founding members
No, only the USA must help
40716.e: Article 5 requires assistance but leaves it to each member to decide which measures it considers necessary.
40716.m: Each member decides for itself how it helps in a case of collective defence.

40717.q: What do NATO members do when one member feels threatened?
40717.e: Under Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the members consult each other if one sees its security threatened. This has happened several times.
40717.m: When threatened, NATO members consult each other.

40718.q: What is needed for a new country to join NATO?
a: Only the agreement of the USA
Nothing, any country can simply join
40718.e: Under Article 10 of the treaty, all members must agree. That is why a single country was able to delay a membership for a long time.
40718.m: All members must agree for a country to join NATO.

40719.q: Which right is NATO’s mutual defence clause based on?
40719.e: The UN Charter allows states to defend themselves against an attack, alone or together with others. Article 5 of the NATO treaty is based on this.
40719.m: NATO’s mutual defence clause is based on the right of self-defence.

40720.q: Which three former Eastern Bloc states were the first to join NATO in 1999?
a: Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary
40720.e: Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary became members on 12 March 1999. This started the eastward enlargement.
40720.m: Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary joined NATO in 1999.

40721.q: What does NATO’s eastward enlargement mean?
a: Countries in eastern Europe joined NATO
40721.e: After the end of the Cold War, many countries in eastern Europe joined NATO. In 2004 there were even seven states at once.
40721.m: In the eastward enlargement, eastern European countries joined NATO.

40722.q: Which three Baltic states became NATO members in 2004?
40722.e: The three Baltic states used to be part of the Soviet Union and were admitted to NATO in 2004.
40722.m: The Baltic states have been in NATO since 2004.

40723.q: Which alliance did Poland and Hungary belong to before they joined NATO?
40723.e: During the Cold War, Poland and Hungary belonged to the Warsaw Pact led by the Soviet Union. After it was dissolved in 1991, they joined NATO in 1999.
40723.m: Many new NATO countries used to be in the Warsaw Pact.

40724.q: Which country criticises NATO’s eastward enlargement especially strongly?
40724.e: Russia sees it as a threat that NATO has grown right up to its borders. The countries of eastern Europe, on the other hand, wanted to protect themselves from Russia.

40725.q: Which of these countries is a member of NATO today?
40725.e: Poland joined NATO in 1999. Switzerland, Austria and Ireland are neutral and not members.
40725.m: Poland has been in NATO since 1999.

40726.q: How did the territory of the former GDR become part of NATO?
a: By joining on its own in 1999
It is still not NATO territory today
40726.e: With reunification on 3 October 1990, the whole of united Germany belonged to NATO.
40726.m: East Germany became part of NATO with reunification in 1990.

40727.q: To which two countries did NATO hold out the prospect of future membership in Bucharest in 2008?
40727.e: At the 2008 Bucharest summit, NATO declared that Ukraine and Georgia would become members, without setting a timetable.
40727.m: In 2008 NATO promised Ukraine and Georgia future membership.

40728.q: In which year did Finland join NATO?
40728.e: Finland became a member of NATO on 4 April 2023.
40728.m: Finland has been in NATO since 2023.

40729.q: What was Finland’s position before joining NATO?
a: It was in the Warsaw Pact
40729.e: For a long time Finland did not belong to any military alliance. After the Russian attack on Ukraine, it joined NATO in 2023 as the 31st member.

40730.q: In which year did Sweden become a member of NATO?
40730.e: Sweden joined on 7 March 2024, almost a year after Finland.
40730.m: Sweden has been in NATO since 2024.

40731.q: Which event led Finland and Sweden to apply for NATO membership?
a: The Russian attack on Ukraine in 2022
40731.e: After Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, both countries applied in May 2022.
40731.m: The war in Ukraine led Finland and Sweden into NATO.

40732.q: Which two NATO countries were the last to agree to Sweden joining?
40732.e: All members must agree to a country joining. Turkey and finally Hungary delayed ratification until 2024.
40732.m: Joining needs the agreement of all members.

40733.q: Roughly how long is the border between Finland and Russia?
40733.e: Finland shares a border of about 1,340 km with Russia. With its membership, NATO’s land border with Russia roughly doubled.
40733.m: Finland has a long border with Russia.

40734.q: How long was Sweden militarily non-aligned before joining NATO?
40734.e: Sweden has not fought a war since 1814 and remained non-aligned for over two centuries. Joining NATO ended this policy.
40734.m: Sweden was non-aligned for over 200 years.

40735.q: Finland’s NATO membership fell on the anniversary of which event?
a: The signing of the North Atlantic Treaty
The end of the Second World War
The fall of the Berlin Wall
40735.e: Finland joined on 4 April. Exactly on that date, years earlier, the treaty on which NATO is based had been signed.

40736.q: What does the abbreviation OSCE stand for?
a: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe
Organisation for States and Customs in Europe
Order for Safety and Civil Protection in Europe
Organisation for Sport and Cohesion in Europe
40736.e: The OSCE is an organisation in which states talk about security, human rights and cooperation.
40736.m: The OSCE works for security and cooperation in Europe.

40737.q: How many participating states does the OSCE have (as of 2025)?
40737.e: The OSCE has 57 participating states, making it the largest regional security organisation in the world.

40738.q: Which conference did the OSCE grow out of?
40738.e: The OSCE grew out of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, or CSCE for short.
40738.m: The OSCE used to be the CSCE.

40739.q: In which city was the CSCE Final Act signed in 1975?
40739.e: The 1975 Helsinki Final Act set out important principles, such as the inviolability of borders and respect for human rights.
40739.m: The CSCE Final Act was signed in Helsinki in 1975.

40741.q: Which country holds the OSCE chairmanship in 2026?
40741.e: In 2026 Switzerland chairs the OSCE for the third time, after 1996 and 2014. The head of the Department of Foreign Affairs takes on the chairmanship.
40741.m: Switzerland holds the OSCE chairmanship in 2026.

40742.q: Which task, for example, does the OSCE take on?
40742.e: The OSCE sends observers to elections to check whether they are free and fair.

40743.q: Which two North American states belong to the OSCE?
40743.e: The OSCE includes states from North America through Europe to Central Asia. From North America, the USA and Canada belong to it, but not Mexico.
40743.m: The USA and Canada are also in the OSCE.

40744.q: When was NATO’s Partnership for Peace created?
a: Shortly after the end of the Cold War
40744.e: The Partnership for Peace was founded in 1994, a few years after the end of the Cold War. It was meant to bring former opponents together.
40744.m: The Partnership for Peace was created after the Cold War.

40745.q: Does Switzerland take part in the Partnership for Peace?
a: No, only EU countries may take part
40745.e: Switzerland has been a partner country since 1996. It works with NATO without becoming a member.
40745.m: Switzerland is a partner of NATO, but not a member.

40746.q: What is the Partnership for Peace?
a: A NATO programme for cooperation with non-members
A UN treaty against nuclear weapons
An army of the European Union
An alliance of neutral states against NATO
40746.e: In the Partnership for Peace, non-NATO states voluntarily work with NATO, for example on training and peacebuilding.
40746.m: The Partnership for Peace links NATO with partner countries.

40747.q: As a partner country, does Switzerland have to give other countries military help in a war?
a: No, there is no obligation to assist
Only if the UN demands it
40747.e: The Partnership for Peace contains no obligation to assist. Each partner decides for itself what it takes part in.
40747.m: Partner countries have no obligation to assist.

40748.q: In what, for example, does Switzerland take part in the Partnership for Peace?
40748.e: Switzerland takes part, for example, in courses, exercises and peacebuilding. It does not take part in combat missions.
40748.m: Switzerland helps with training and peacebuilding.

40749.q: Which neutral neighbouring country of Switzerland joined the Partnership for Peace in 1995?
40749.e: Like Switzerland, Austria is neutral and has taken part in the Partnership for Peace since 1995.
40749.m: Austria also takes part in the Partnership for Peace.

40750.q: Which principle applies to Switzerland when taking part in the Partnership for Peace?
a: The army is placed under NATO
40750.e: Switzerland only chooses activities that are compatible with its neutrality, such as training and peacebuilding.
40750.m: Switzerland remains neutral in the Partnership for Peace.

40751.q: Which large country also joined the Partnership for Peace in 1994?
40751.e: Russia joined the partnership in 1994. Cooperation with NATO was later largely stopped because of conflicts.
40751.m: Russia was also a partner in the NATO partnership.

40752.q: According to the Federal Constitution, which task belongs to the Swiss Army?
a: Defending the country and its people
40752.e: According to Article 58 of the Federal Constitution, the army defends the country and its people and helps to keep the peace.
40752.m: The army defends Switzerland and its people.

40753.q: When can the Swiss Army support civilian authorities?
40753.e: The army helps, for example, with floods, avalanches or big events when civilian resources are not enough.
40753.m: The army helps civilian authorities in disasters.

40754.q: On which principle is the Swiss Army organised?
40754.e: Most members of the army are citizens who do military service alongside their normal jobs.
40754.m: The Swiss Army is a militia army.

40755.q: Who is subject to compulsory military service in Switzerland?
40755.e: The Federal Constitution requires every Swiss man to do military service. Women can serve voluntarily.
40755.m: Swiss men are required to do military service.

40756.q: How long does basic military training last for most recruits?
40756.e: Normal basic training lasts 18 weeks. For some roles it is longer.

40757.q: Since which year has Switzerland had civilian service as an alternative to military service?
40757.e: Since 1996, people liable for service who cannot square military service with their conscience have been able to do civilian service.

40758.q: Who elects a general in Switzerland in the event of war?
40758.e: There is only a general in times of serious threat. He is elected by the United Federal Assembly.
40758.m: The Federal Assembly elects the general.

40759.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the initiative to abolish the army in 1989?
40759.e: The initiative was rejected with about 64 per cent voting no. The high yes vote of about 36 per cent surprised many people at the time.
40759.m: The initiative to abolish the army was rejected in 1989.

40760.q: In which country is Swisscoy deployed?
40760.e: Swisscoy is the Swiss Army contingent in the international peacekeeping force in Kosovo.
40760.m: Swisscoy works for peace in Kosovo.

40761.q: What is Swisscoy’s task in Kosovo?
a: It helps to keep the peace
It fights wars against neighbouring countries
It is building a ski resort there
40761.e: Swisscoy has been in Kosovo since 1999. It is part of an international peacekeeping force and helps keep things safe and peaceful.
40761.m: Swisscoy keeps the peace in Kosovo.

40762.q: Which international peacekeeping force does Swisscoy belong to?
40762.e: Swisscoy is part of KFOR, the Kosovo Force led by NATO.

40763.q: Which organisation leads KFOR, to which Swisscoy belongs?
40763.e: KFOR is led by NATO and is based on a UN Security Council resolution. Switzerland is not in NATO but takes part in KFOR voluntarily.
40763.m: KFOR in Kosovo is led by NATO.

40764.q: Since 2024, what is the normal maximum number of army personnel in Swisscoy?
40764.e: Since 1 January 2024 the contingent has numbered up to 215 people. Before that it was at most 195.
40764.m: Swisscoy has up to 215 army personnel.

40765.q: How do Swiss army members come to serve in Swisscoy?
40765.e: Missions in military peace support are voluntary in Switzerland.

40766.q: What may Swisscoy members carry weapons for?
40766.e: Swisscoy members are armed for self-protection, for example with a pistol and an assault rifle.
40766.m: Swisscoy is armed only for self-protection.

40767.q: Who in Switzerland must approve an extension of the Swisscoy mission?
40767.e: Armed missions abroad with more than 100 people or lasting more than three weeks must be approved by the Federal Assembly.

40768.q: What does the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty aim to prevent?
40768.e: The 1968 treaty is meant to stop the spread of nuclear weapons. States without nuclear weapons promise not to build any.
40768.m: The Non-Proliferation Treaty aims to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.

40769.q: How many states take part in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
a: Almost all the states in the world
40769.e: Over 190 states are parties to the treaty. Only a few countries, such as India, Pakistan and Israel, have never joined.
40769.m: Almost all the states in the world take part in the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

40770.q: How many states are official nuclear-weapon states under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
40770.e: The treaty only recognises as nuclear-weapon states those countries that had exploded a nuclear weapon before 1967.
40770.m: The treaty recognises five official nuclear powers.

40771.q: Which country is an official nuclear power under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
40771.e: China is one of the recognised nuclear powers because it had exploded a nuclear weapon before 1967. India, Pakistan and Israel have never joined the treaty.
40771.m: China is one of the official nuclear powers.

40772.q: Which country announced its withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 2003?
40772.e: North Korea left the treaty in 2003 and carried out nuclear weapons tests from 2006.
40772.m: North Korea withdrew from the Non-Proliferation Treaty in 2003.

40773.q: Which organisation checks that states do not use their nuclear material for weapons?
40773.e: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), based in Vienna, carries out inspections at nuclear facilities.
40773.m: The IAEA monitors compliance with the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

40774.q: What do states without nuclear weapons promise in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
a: Not to build or buy nuclear weapons
40774.e: States without nuclear weapons give up making or acquiring them. Since 1995 the treaty has applied indefinitely.
40774.m: In the treaty, states without nuclear weapons give them up.

40775.q: Under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, what may states without nuclear weapons use peacefully?
40775.e: The treaty rests on three pillars: non-proliferation, disarmament and the right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
40775.m: Nuclear energy may be used peacefully.

40776.q: Does Switzerland take part in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
a: Yes, it is a state party
Only as an observer without obligations
No, because it has nuclear weapons itself
40776.e: Switzerland signed the treaty in 1969 and ratified it in 1977. It has no nuclear weapons.
40776.m: Switzerland is a state party and has no nuclear weapons.

40777.q: What does the Ottawa Convention ban?
40777.e: The Ottawa Convention bans the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of mines aimed at people.
40777.m: The Ottawa Convention bans landmines aimed at people.

40778.q: In which country is the city after which the Ottawa Convention is named?
40778.e: The convention was signed in December 1997 in Ottawa, the capital of Canada.
40778.m: Ottawa is the capital of Canada.

40779.q: Why are landmines still dangerous even after a war?
a: They stay in the ground and can explode years later
They move around in the ground
40779.e: Mines often lie hidden in the ground and still explode many years after a war. That is why the Ottawa Convention has banned mines aimed at people since 1999.
40779.m: Landmines remain dangerous even after a war.

40780.q: Which famous person drew attention to landmines with a visit to Angola in 1997?
40780.e: Princess Diana walked through a minefield in Angola and so drew worldwide attention to the suffering caused by mines.

40781.q: Which of these states has NOT joined the Ottawa Convention?
40781.e: The USA, Russia and China are not among the states parties. Most European countries have joined.
40781.m: Not all the great powers take part in the Ottawa Convention.

40782.q: In which Swiss city does the Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining have its seat?
40782.e: The centre was founded in Geneva in 1998 and supports the clearing of mines around the world.
40782.m: The centre for humanitarian demining is in Geneva.

40783.q: What must states parties to the Ottawa Convention do with their stocks of anti-personnel mines?
40783.e: The states must destroy their stockpiles and clear mined areas.
40783.m: States parties must destroy their mines.

40784.q: Which type of mine does the Ottawa Convention NOT ban?
40784.e: The convention only applies to mines aimed at people. Mines aimed at vehicles are not covered.
40784.m: Anti-tank mines are not covered by the Ottawa Convention.

40785.q: What does the Chemical Weapons Convention ban?
a: Poison gas and other chemical weapons
40785.e: The Chemical Weapons Convention bans making, stockpiling and using chemical weapons. There are other treaties for nuclear weapons.
40785.m: The Chemical Weapons Convention bans chemical weapons such as poison gas.

40786.q: Under the Chemical Weapons Convention, what must countries do with their old chemical weapons?
40786.e: Countries must destroy their stocks of chemical weapons under supervision. Experts from the OPCW check this.
40786.m: Under the convention, chemical weapons must be destroyed.

40787.q: Where does the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) have its seat?
40787.e: The OPCW monitors compliance with the convention and is based in The Hague in the Netherlands.
40787.m: The OPCW is based in The Hague.

40788.q: Which award did the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons receive in 2013?
40788.e: The OPCW received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work to eliminate chemical weapons.
40788.m: The OPCW was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013.

40789.q: Which country joined the Chemical Weapons Convention in 2013 after a poison gas attack?
40789.e: After the poison gas attack near Damascus in August 2013, Syria joined the convention under international pressure.
40789.m: Syria joined the Chemical Weapons Convention in 2013.

40790.q: Why are poison gases especially terrible as weapons?
a: They hit everyone in an area, including bystanders
They only work when it rains
40790.e: Poison gas spreads with the wind and hits soldiers and civilians alike. That is why the Geneva Protocol banned the use of poison gas in war as early as 1925.
40790.m: Poison gas also hits bystanders, which is why it is banned.

40791.q: Which Swiss laboratory is recognised by the OPCW as a special laboratory for analysing warfare agents?
40791.e: Spiez Laboratory in the canton of Bern tests samples for chemical warfare agents on behalf of the OPCW.
40791.m: Spiez Laboratory tests samples for the OPCW.

40792.q: Which substance is a chemical warfare agent?
40792.e: Sarin is a nerve agent that is deadly even in the tiniest amounts. It is banned by the convention.
40792.m: Sarin is a banned nerve agent.

40793.q: In which war was poison gas first used on a large scale?
40793.e: In 1915 chlorine gas was used near Ypres in Belgium. After that, several armies used poison gas.
40793.m: Poison gas was used on a massive scale in the First World War.

40794.q: What is the aim of arms control?
a: To limit weapons and make them verifiable
40794.e: Arms control uses treaties to limit the number and type of weapons and to build trust between states.
40794.m: Arms control limits weapons through treaties.

40795.q: Which two countries have the most nuclear weapons?
40795.e: Together, the USA and Russia have most of the world’s nuclear weapons. That is why they make arms control treaties.
40795.m: The USA and Russia have the most nuclear weapons.

40797.q: Which two states concluded the New START disarmament treaty in 2010?
40797.e: New START limited the number of strategic nuclear warheads of the two biggest nuclear powers.
40797.m: New START is a treaty between the USA and Russia.

40798.q: What does the Biological Weapons Convention ban?
40798.e: Biological weapons deliberately spread germs such as bacteria or viruses. The 1972 Biological Weapons Convention bans them.
40798.m: Biological weapons using germs are banned.

40799.q: In which city does the states’ Conference on Disarmament meet?
40799.e: The Conference on Disarmament is the most important negotiating forum for disarmament and meets in Geneva.
40799.m: The Conference on Disarmament meets in Geneva.

40800.q: Has Switzerland signed the 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (as of 2025)?
40800.e: The Federal Council decided not to sign the treaty for the time being. It came into force in 2021 without Switzerland.
40800.m: Switzerland has not joined the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

40801.q: Why are cluster munitions especially dangerous?
a: Many small explosives are left lying around and explode later
40801.e: Cluster munitions scatter many small explosives. Some do not explode straight away and still endanger people years later, often children.
40801.m: Cluster munitions endanger people long after the war.

40802.q: What did the Treaty on Open Skies allow?
a: Observation flights over other states parties
40802.e: With unarmed observation flights, states could check other countries’ military activities and so build trust.
40802.m: The Treaty on Open Skies allowed observation flights.

40803.q: What does the UN Arms Trade Treaty of 2013 regulate?
a: The international trade in conventional weapons
The trade in nuclear power stations
40803.e: The Arms Trade Treaty sets rules for exporting weapons such as tanks or rifles. Its secretariat is in Geneva.
40803.m: The Arms Trade Treaty regulates the arms trade.

40805.q: What role did Eleanor Roosevelt have from 1933 to 1945?
40805.e: While her husband was President, she was First Lady. She used this role actively, for example with newspaper columns and press conferences only for women journalists.
40805.m: Eleanor Roosevelt was First Lady of the USA for twelve years.

40806.q: Which UN body did Eleanor Roosevelt chair from 1946?
40806.e: Eleanor Roosevelt was the first chair of the UN Commission on Human Rights. This commission drew up a shared text on the rights of all people.
40806.m: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the UN’s first Commission on Human Rights.

40807.q: Which document did Eleanor Roosevelt call a “Magna Carta” for all humanity?
a: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Charter of the United Nations
40807.e: Eleanor Roosevelt compared the Declaration of Human Rights with the Magna Carta, a famous English charter of liberties from 1215. She wanted to show how important the text is for all people.
40807.m: Eleanor Roosevelt saw the Declaration of Human Rights as a charter of liberties for all people.

40808.q: In which city did the UN General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
40808.e: At that time the General Assembly met in the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. The UN headquarters in New York had not yet been finished.
40808.m: The Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in Paris.

40809.q: Which other Roosevelt from Eleanor’s family was also President of the USA?
40809.e: Theodore Roosevelt was President of the USA from 1901 to 1909. He was Eleanor Roosevelt’s uncle.
40809.m: Theodore Roosevelt was Eleanor’s uncle and also President.

40810.q: How many states voted against the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in the UN General Assembly in 1948?
40810.e: 48 states voted for it and 8 abstained. There were no votes against, which Eleanor Roosevelt saw as a great success.
40810.m: No state voted against the Declaration of Human Rights.

40811.q: What happened in April 1945 to Eleanor’s husband, President Franklin D. Roosevelt?
40811.e: Franklin D. Roosevelt died in April 1945, shortly before the end of the Second World War. After that, Eleanor Roosevelt represented the USA at the UN.
40811.m: Franklin D. Roosevelt died as President in 1945.

40812.q: Which 1924 document is regarded as the forerunner of the Convention on the Rights of the Child?
a: The Geneva Declaration of the Rights of the Child
The Charter of the United Nations
40812.e: In 1924 the League of Nations adopted the Geneva Declaration, written by the British woman Eglantyne Jebb. It was the first international declaration on children’s rights.
40812.m: The 1924 Geneva Declaration was the first international text on children’s rights.

40813.q: What is the name of the UN body in Geneva that monitors how the Convention on the Rights of the Child is put into practice?
a: The Committee on the Rights of the Child
40813.e: The committee is made up of 18 independent experts. It examines the states’ reports and gives them recommendations.
40813.m: A UN committee in Geneva monitors children’s rights.

40814.q: What is the 2000 optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on armed conflict about?
a: Protection from being used as child soldiers
40814.e: The protocol requires that people under 18 do not take a direct part in fighting. They must not be forced into armies.
40814.m: Children should not have to fight as soldiers.

40815.q: What does the third optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, from 2011, make possible?
a: Children can complain to the UN committee
Children can choose their own school
40815.e: With this protocol, children or their representatives can report a violation of their rights to the UN committee. But first they must try the courts in their own country.
40815.m: Children can complain to the UN if their rights are violated.

40816.q: What does Article 28 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child require of states?
a: Primary school should be compulsory and free for all
Every child should learn a musical instrument
All children should wear a uniform
Every child should study a foreign language
40816.e: Article 28 covers the right to education. States should make primary school compulsory and free of charge for all children.
40816.m: Primary school should be free for all children.

40817.q: What does Article 32 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child protect children from?
40817.e: Children must not be made to do work that is dangerous or harms their education and health. States must set a minimum age for work.
40817.m: Children must be protected from exploitative work.

40818.q: What does Article 19 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child protect children from?
40818.e: Article 19 requires states to protect children from every form of physical and mental violence. This also applies within the family.
40818.m: Children have a right to protection from violence.

40819.q: According to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, what must be a primary consideration in all decisions affecting children?
a: The best interests of the child
40819.e: Article 3 requires that the best interests of the child are a primary consideration in all actions by authorities, courts and schools.
40819.m: The child’s best interests come first in decisions about children.

40820.q: What does Article 2 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child say?
a: The rights apply to all children without distinction
Only children with a passport have rights
The rights only apply from age 10
40820.e: Article 2 bans discrimination. Origin, sex, religion, language or disability must play no part.
40820.m: Children’s rights apply to every child.

40821.q: Which organisation adopted the women’s rights convention CEDAW?
40821.e: The UN General Assembly adopted the convention in 1979. It is the most important international agreement on women’s rights.
40821.m: The women’s rights convention CEDAW is a UN agreement.

40822.q: What is the women’s rights convention CEDAW directed against?
40822.e: CEDAW requires states to eliminate every form of discrimination against women. Women should have the same rights as men in all areas of life.
40822.m: CEDAW is meant to end discrimination against women.

40824.q: What does equality between women and men mean?
a: Both have the same rights and opportunities
Both must have the same job
Both must be the same height
Both must wear the same clothes
40824.e: Equality means that no one is disadvantaged because of their sex, for example in pay or training.
40824.m: Equality means equal rights and opportunities.

40825.q: What is an example of disadvantaging women?
a: A woman is paid less than a man for the same work
A woman chooses her own job
A woman is elected to the Federal Council
A woman does sport in a club
40825.e: Equal work deserves equal pay. Even so, women sometimes still earn less today. CEDAW requires such disadvantages to be removed.
40825.m: There should be equal pay for equal work.

40826.q: What must states that have ratified CEDAW regularly submit to the committee?
a: A list of all female inhabitants
40826.e: States regularly report on the measures they have taken for equality. The committee examines the reports and makes recommendations.
40826.m: States must report on their progress on equality.

40827.q: What does the 1999 optional protocol to CEDAW make possible?
a: Individuals can complain to the committee
Women may vote in every country
40827.e: With the optional protocol, women who feel their rights have been violated can send a communication to the committee. First they must have used up the route through the courts in their own country.
40827.m: With the optional protocol, women can turn directly to the CEDAW committee.

40828.q: Which large state has signed CEDAW but never ratified it (as of 2025)?
40828.e: The USA signed the convention in 1980, but the Senate never approved ratification. Almost all other states in the world are parties.
40828.m: The USA has never ratified CEDAW.

40829.q: Who must abide by the UN Convention against Torture?
a: All states that have ratified it
40829.e: The UN adopted the convention in 1984. States that have ratified it must ban and prevent torture.
40829.m: States that have ratified the Convention against Torture must abide by it.

40830.q: Has Switzerland ratified the UN Convention against Torture?
a: No, because it is not in the UN
40830.e: Switzerland ratified the convention in December 1986, even before it came into force internationally.
40830.m: Switzerland ratified the Convention against Torture in 1986.

40831.q: Under the Convention against Torture, may a state torture as an exception in a war or emergency?
a: Yes, if there is a threat of terrorism
40831.e: The ban on torture is absolute. The convention says explicitly that neither war nor emergency nor an order from a superior can justify torture.

40832.q: What is the name of the UN body that monitors compliance with the Convention against Torture?
40832.e: The Committee against Torture is made up of ten independent experts and meets in Geneva. It examines the states’ reports.
40832.m: The UN Committee against Torture monitors the ban on torture.

40833.q: What does Article 3 of the Convention against Torture forbid?
a: Deporting people to a country where they face torture
40833.e: No one may be sent back to a state where they face torture. This principle is called non-refoulement.
40833.m: No one may be sent to a country where they face torture.

40834.q: Which Swiss commission has visited prisons and other places where people are detained since 2010?
a: The National Commission for the Prevention of Torture
The Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs
40834.e: The commission was set up on the basis of an optional protocol to the Convention against Torture. It checks detention conditions and writes reports with recommendations.
40834.m: The National Commission for the Prevention of Torture checks places of detention in Switzerland.

40835.q: To whom is the international day on 26 June dedicated?
40835.e: The UN Convention against Torture came into force on 26 June 1987. Since 1998 this day has commemorated victims of torture.
40835.m: On 26 June people remember the victims of torture.

40836.q: What counts as torture under the Convention against Torture?
a: When an official deliberately causes severe pain, for example to get a confession
When a child has to do homework
When someone has to pay a fine
When a prisoner has to go to bed early
40836.e: Article 1 describes torture as deliberately causing severe physical or mental pain by state authorities. Typical aims are confessions, punishment or intimidation.
40836.m: Torture means the state deliberately causes severe pain.

40837.q: What do states that join the UN convention against racism commit themselves to?
40837.e: The UN adopted the convention in 1965. States promise to ban and fight racism.
40837.m: The convention against racism commits states to fighting racism.

40838.q: Which of these UN human rights conventions was adopted first?
a: The Convention on the Rights of the Child
40838.e: The convention against racism is the oldest of the major UN human rights conventions. The other three only followed years later.
40838.m: The convention against racism is the oldest major UN human rights convention.

40839.q: What did Switzerland have to change before joining the convention against racism?
40839.e: Switzerland joined the convention in 1994. Before that, it added a criminal provision against racism to the Criminal Code.
40839.m: For the convention against racism, Switzerland changed its criminal law.

40840.q: Which new rule did Swiss voters accept in a vote in 1994?
40840.e: With the anti-racism provision in the Criminal Code, racist incitement is punished. Voters accepted it with about 55 per cent voting yes.
40840.m: The anti-racism criminal provision has applied in Switzerland since a vote in 1994.

40841.q: On which day is the International Day against Racism?
40841.e: The UN declared 21 March the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. In Switzerland, action weeks against racism take place around this day.
40841.m: 21 March is the International Day against Racism.

40842.q: In which country did the 1960 massacre that the International Day against Racism commemorates take place?
40842.e: In Sharpeville, South Africa, the police shot many people on 21 March 1960 who were protesting peacefully against apartheid.
40842.m: The Day against Racism commemorates a massacre in South Africa.

40843.q: According to the convention against racism, what counts as racial discrimination?
a: Disadvantage because of skin colour, descent or ethnic origin
Disadvantage because of bad school marks
Disadvantage because of your favourite music
Disadvantage because you live in a city
40843.e: The convention lists characteristics such as race, colour, descent and national and ethnic origin. Anyone treated worse because of these is being discriminated against.
40843.m: Racial discrimination is disadvantage because of origin or skin colour.

40844.q: What does the Federal Commission against Racism do?
a: It advises the federal government and informs people about racism
40844.e: The commission was founded in 1995. It advises the federal government and informs the public about racism.
40844.m: The Federal Commission against Racism advises the federal government.

40845.q: What does the name Human Rights Watch mean?
40845.e: “Watch” here means observing or keeping guard. The organisation watches whether human rights are respected.
40845.m: Human Rights Watch keeps watch over human rights.

40846.q: What kind of organisation is Human Rights Watch?
a: An independent organisation that does not belong to any state
A department of the US government
40846.e: Human Rights Watch is a non-governmental organisation. It belongs to no state and works independently.
40846.m: Human Rights Watch is an independent organisation.

40847.q: In which city does Human Rights Watch have its headquarters?
40847.e: Human Rights Watch has its headquarters in New York. It also has offices in many other cities around the world.
40847.m: Human Rights Watch has its headquarters in New York.

40848.q: What does Human Rights Watch publish every year?
a: A world report on the state of human rights
A ranking of the richest countries
40848.e: In its World Report, Human Rights Watch describes the human rights situation in about 100 countries. It comes out at the start of each year.
40848.m: Human Rights Watch publishes a world report every year.

40849.q: According to Human Rights Watch itself, from whom does it not accept money?
40849.e: Human Rights Watch wants to stay independent and is funded by private donations and foundations. It refuses money from governments.
40849.m: Human Rights Watch does not accept money from governments.

40850.q: What did Human Rights Watch campaign for with other organisations in the 1990s?
40850.e: Human Rights Watch was a founding member of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. The campaign received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1997.
40850.m: Human Rights Watch helped to outlaw landmines.

40851.q: How does Human Rights Watch mainly work?
a: It investigates human rights violations and makes them public
It sends soldiers to crisis areas
It builds hospitals in war zones
40851.e: Experts travel to crisis areas, interview witnesses and collect evidence. The reports are meant to put pressure on governments so that things change.
40851.m: Human Rights Watch uncovers human rights violations.

40852.q: Which UN body in Geneva does Human Rights Watch try to influence with its reports?
40852.e: The UN Human Rights Council meets several times a year in Geneva. Organisations such as Human Rights Watch present their investigations there.
40852.m: The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva.

40853.q: What does the organisation Reporters Without Borders work for?
a: Press freedom and the protection of journalists
40853.e: Reporters Without Borders helps persecuted journalists and makes attacks on press freedom public. The organisation is independent of governments.
40853.m: Reporters Without Borders fights for press freedom.

40854.q: What kind of organisation is Reporters Without Borders?
a: An independent organisation, not run by the state
40854.e: Reporters Without Borders is a non-governmental organisation. It is independent of governments and stands up for journalists.
40854.m: Reporters Without Borders is independent of governments.

40855.q: In which city does Reporters Without Borders have its headquarters?
40855.e: The organisation was founded in the south of France, but its international headquarters is now in Paris.
40855.m: Reporters Without Borders has its headquarters in Paris.

40856.q: What is Reporters Without Borders called in French?
40856.e: The French abbreviation RSF is also used internationally. It stands for Reporters sans frontières.
40856.m: In French the organisation is called Reporters sans frontières.

40857.q: How often does the Reporters Without Borders press freedom ranking come out?
40857.e: The ranking has come out every year since 2002. This shows whether press freedom in a country is getting better or worse.
40857.m: The press freedom ranking comes out every year.

40858.q: What does the Reporters Without Borders press freedom ranking show?
a: How freely journalists can work in about 180 countries
Which country has the most TV channels
How many books are published per country
40858.e: The ranking compares how independently the media in a country can report. It assesses things such as political interference and violence against journalists.
40858.m: The press freedom ranking compares media freedom around the world.

40859.q: Which country was in first place in the press freedom ranking every year from 2017 to 2024?
40859.e: Norway always came first in these years. The media there are regarded as especially free and independent.
40859.m: Norway is regarded as a country with great press freedom.

40861.q: What does Malala Yousafzai mainly campaign for?
40861.e: Even as a child, Malala wrote online about girls wanting to go to school. Today her Malala Fund supports education projects for girls.
40861.m: Malala fights for all girls to be able to go to school.

40862.q: In which year was Malala Yousafzai shot by the Taliban on her way to school?
40862.e: In October 2012 a Taliban fighter shot at her on the school bus. Malala survived with serious injuries.
40862.m: Malala survived an attack by the Taliban in 2012.

40863.q: To which country was Malala Yousafzai flown for treatment after the attack?
40863.e: Malala was taken to a hospital in Birmingham, England. Her family later moved there too.
40863.m: Malala was treated in the United Kingdom.

40864.q: What is the name of the 2013 book in which Malala Yousafzai tells her life story?
40864.e: She wrote the book together with the journalist Christina Lamb. It has been translated into many languages.
40864.m: Malala tells her story in the book “I Am Malala”.

40865.q: Which prize did Malala Yousafzai receive in 2014 as the youngest winner of all time?
40865.e: Malala was only 17 when she received the Nobel Peace Prize. She shared it with Kailash Satyarthi from India, who fights against child labour.
40865.m: Malala received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.

40866.q: At which university did Malala Yousafzai finish her studies in 2020?
40866.e: Malala studied philosophy, politics and economics at Oxford. She graduated in 2020.
40866.m: Malala studied at the University of Oxford.

40869.q: In which year did Martin Luther King receive the Nobel Peace Prize?
40869.e: Martin Luther King received the prize in 1964, aged 35, for his non-violent struggle against racism. At the time he was the youngest Nobel Peace Prize winner.
40869.m: Martin Luther King received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

40870.q: What did Martin Luther King march for in 1965 on the march from Selma to Montgomery?
a: The right of Black people to vote
40870.e: In the southern states, many Black people were prevented by tricks from registering to vote. After the marches, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in 1965.
40870.m: The Selma march fought for the right to vote.

40872.q: Who was Martin Luther King’s great role model for non-violent resistance?
40872.e: Gandhi had led India to independence through non-violent resistance. Martin Luther King travelled to India in 1959 to learn more about him.
40872.m: Martin Luther King learned non-violence from Mahatma Gandhi.

40873.q: When is the holiday in honour of Martin Luther King in the USA?
a: On the third Monday in January
On the last Thursday in November
On the first Monday in September
40873.e: Martin Luther King Day falls near his birthday on 15 January. It has been a public holiday in the USA since 1986.
40873.m: Martin Luther King Day is in January.

40875.q: Which country did Desmond Tutu come from?
40875.e: Desmond Tutu was born in Klerksdorp in 1931. He became one of his country’s best-known churchmen.

40876.q: Which system did Desmond Tutu mainly fight against?
40876.e: Apartheid was the state system of racial segregation in South Africa, under which Black people had hardly any rights. Tutu called non-violently for it to end.

40877.q: Which famous prize did Desmond Tutu receive for his non-violent struggle against apartheid?
40877.e: Tutu received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984. The prize made his fight against racial segregation known around the world.
40877.m: Desmond Tutu received the Nobel Peace Prize.

40878.q: Which church office did Desmond Tutu receive in 1986 as the first Black person?
a: President of the World Council of Churches
40878.e: As Archbishop of Cape Town he led his church in southern Africa. Before him, only white people had held this office.
40878.m: Desmond Tutu became the first Black Archbishop of Cape Town.

40879.q: Which church did Desmond Tutu belong to?
40879.e: Desmond Tutu was a priest and later a bishop of the Anglican Church. This church began in England.
40879.m: Desmond Tutu was an Anglican clergyman.

40880.q: Which commission did Desmond Tutu lead from 1996 after the end of apartheid?
40880.e: The commission heard victims and perpetrators in order to uncover the crimes of apartheid. The aim was for the country to be reconciled.
40880.m: Desmond Tutu led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

40881.q: Which expression did Desmond Tutu coin for the new, diverse South Africa?
40881.e: By “rainbow nation” Tutu meant that people of all skin colours form one country together. The term became very popular in South Africa.
40881.m: Desmond Tutu called South Africa a rainbow nation.

40882.q: In which year did Desmond Tutu die?
40882.e: Desmond Tutu died in Cape Town on 26 December 2021, aged 90. Many people around the world mourned him.

40883.q: Since which year has the death penalty been abolished in Swiss civilian criminal law?
40883.e: On 1 January 1942 the new Swiss Criminal Code came into force, which no longer includes the death penalty. Before that, some cantons could still impose it.
40883.m: There has been no death penalty in Swiss civilian criminal law since 1942.

40884.q: May Switzerland still use the death penalty today in war or in the military?
a: No, it has been completely abolished
Yes, it is allowed in war
40884.e: Military criminal law still provided for the death penalty in wartime until 1992. Since then it has been completely abolished in Switzerland.
40884.m: Since 1992 the death penalty has been completely abolished in Switzerland.

40885.q: What does the Swiss Federal Constitution say about the death penalty?
a: It is only allowed in war
The people can vote on it
40885.e: Article 10 of the Federal Constitution says clearly: “The death penalty is prohibited.” It protects the right to life.
40885.m: The Federal Constitution forbids the death penalty.

40886.q: Which country in Europe still carries out the death penalty (as of 2025)?
40886.e: Belarus is the only country in Europe that still carries out executions. It is also not a member of the Council of Europe.
40886.m: Belarus is the last country in Europe with executions.

40887.q: On which continent have almost all countries abolished the death penalty?
40887.e: In Europe only Belarus still carries out the death penalty. The first state in the world to abolish it was Tuscany in Italy, as early as 1786.
40887.m: In Europe the death penalty has been abolished almost everywhere.

40888.q: What is the World Day against the Death Penalty for?
a: To call for the abolition of the death penalty worldwide
40888.e: Since 2003, organisations have called every year on 10 October for the death penalty to be abolished everywhere.
40888.m: On the World Day against the Death Penalty, people call for its abolition.

40889.q: How many of the world’s states have abolished the death penalty in law or in practice (as of 2024)?
40889.e: According to Amnesty International, about 145 states have abolished the death penalty or no longer carry out executions. That is clearly more than two thirds of all countries.
40889.m: Most states in the world no longer execute anyone.

40890.q: According to estimates, which country executes the most people each year?
40890.e: In China, thousands of people are probably executed every year. The exact figures are a state secret.
40890.m: China carries out the most death sentences.

40891.q: Roughly when did the last execution under civilian law take place in Switzerland?
40891.e: In October 1940 a murderer was executed in Sarnen in the canton of Obwalden. Shortly afterwards, in 1942, the new Criminal Code without the death penalty came into force.
40891.m: Switzerland’s last civilian execution was in 1940.

40892.q: Which Caribbean country became independent in 1804 after an uprising of enslaved people?
40892.e: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up from 1791. In 1804 they founded the free state of Haiti.
40892.m: Haiti grew out of a successful uprising of enslaved people.

40893.q: Across which ocean were millions of people taken from Africa to America in the slave trade?
40893.e: From the 16th to the 19th century, people from West Africa were taken across the Atlantic on ships. Many died on the crossing.
40893.m: The slave trade went across the Atlantic.

40894.q: Which war in the USA was also about slavery?
40894.e: From 1861 to 1865 the northern states fought against the southern states. After the North won, slavery was banned throughout the USA.
40894.m: The American Civil War was also about slavery.

40895.q: Which US President issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863?
40895.e: With the Emancipation Proclamation, Abraham Lincoln declared the enslaved people in the southern states free during the Civil War.
40895.m: Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation.

40896.q: Which side wanted to keep slavery in the American Civil War?
40896.e: Many enslaved people worked on the plantations of the southern states. The South lost the war, and slavery was abolished in 1865.
40896.m: The southern states wanted to keep slavery.

40897.q: What were enslaved people in America mainly used for?
40897.e: Enslaved people had to grow and harvest cotton, sugar cane or tobacco on plantations. They received no pay and had no rights.
40897.m: Enslaved people had to work on plantations.

40898.q: What is counted as modern slavery today?
40898.e: Slavery is banned everywhere today. Even so, millions of people around the world are forced to work without being free to leave.
40898.m: Forced labour is a form of modern slavery.

40899.q: Who does the Geneva Refugee Convention protect?
a: People who are persecuted in their home country
People who move for a new job
40899.e: The convention protects people who had to flee their country because they are persecuted there. It sets out which rights these refugees have.
40899.m: The Geneva Refugee Convention protects persecuted people.

40900.q: In which year was the Geneva Refugee Convention adopted?
40900.e: The convention was adopted in Geneva in 1951, a few years after the Second World War. At that time millions of people in Europe had fled their homes.
40900.m: The Geneva Refugee Convention dates from 1951.

40901.q: What does the Geneva Refugee Convention forbid states to do?
a: Send refugees back to a country where they face persecution
40901.e: No one may be sent back to a country where they face persecution. This important principle is called non-refoulement, from the French word for pushing back.
40901.m: Refugees must not be sent back to a country where they face persecution.

40902.q: Which UN organisation works for refugees worldwide and watches over the Refugee Convention?
40902.e: The UNHCR is based in Geneva. It helps refugees all over the world and makes sure states keep to the Refugee Convention.
40902.m: The UNHCR is the UN’s refugee agency.

40903.q: Which of these is a ground for persecution under the Geneva Refugee Convention?
40903.e: Anyone persecuted because of their political opinion can be recognised as a refugee. Poverty or natural events alone, on the other hand, are not grounds for persecution.
40903.m: Persecution because of political opinion is a recognised reason for fleeing.

40904.q: Roughly how many countries have signed the Geneva Refugee Convention?
40904.e: Almost 150 states have joined the convention or its protocol. This makes it one of the most important treaties for protecting refugees.
40904.m: About 150 countries are bound by the Refugee Convention.

40905.q: Does Switzerland have to keep to the Geneva Refugee Convention?
a: Yes, it has been a state party since 1955
Only in the canton of Geneva
40905.e: Switzerland ratified the convention in 1955. Since then it has had to give persecuted people protection according to these rules.
40905.m: Switzerland has been bound by the Refugee Convention since 1955.

40906.q: Under the Geneva Refugee Convention, where must a person be to count as a refugee?
40906.e: A refugee within the meaning of the convention has left their country of origin. Anyone who flees within their own country does not fall under this definition.
40906.m: A refugee under the convention has left their home country.

40907.q: Under the Geneva Refugee Convention, who is excluded from refugee protection?
a: Anyone who has committed war crimes
Anyone who enters without a passport
Anyone who does not speak English
40907.e: The exclusion clause in Article 1F excludes people who have committed serious crimes such as war crimes. The protection is not meant to benefit perpetrators.
40907.m: Anyone who has committed serious crimes does not receive refugee protection.

a: A request for protection in another country
An application for a holiday trip
