40908.e: Anyone persecuted in their home country can ask for protection in another country. In Switzerland, the State Secretariat for Migration examines every application.
40908.m: With an asylum application you ask for protection from persecution.

40909.q: Since the 2019 reform, what do asylum seekers in Switzerland receive free of charge?
40909.e: Because the procedure is faster, asylum seekers get free advice and legal representation. This is meant to ensure fair procedures.
40909.m: Asylum seekers in Switzerland are entitled to free legal representation.

40910.q: Which court decides on appeals against asylum decisions in Switzerland?
40910.e: You can appeal against a negative asylum decision to the Federal Administrative Court in St Gallen. In asylum matters its decision is usually final.
40910.m: Asylum appeals go to the Federal Administrative Court.

40911.q: Which European agreement regulates which state is responsible for an asylum application?
40911.e: Under the Dublin rules, the state a person first entered is usually responsible. Switzerland takes part, even though it is not in the EU.
40911.m: The Dublin system decides which country examines an asylum application.

40913.q: What does the N permit confirm in Switzerland?
a: That someone has applied for asylum
That someone is a Swiss citizen
That someone may drive a car
That someone was born in Switzerland
40913.e: The N permit confirms that a person has applied for asylum. It is only valid while the procedure is running.
40913.m: Asylum seekers in Switzerland hold the N permit.

40914.q: What does it mean if someone is provisionally admitted in Switzerland?
a: The person does not get asylum but may stay for the time being
The person must leave the next day
The person may only stay as a tourist
40914.e: Provisional admission is for people who do not get asylum but cannot be sent back, for example because of war. These people receive the F permit.
40914.m: Provisionally admitted people may stay in Switzerland for the time being.

40915.q: Why are fingerprints taken from asylum seekers in Europe?
a: To see whether they have already applied in another country
To work out their exact age
To open a bank account for them
To issue them a driving licence
40915.e: The fingerprints are stored in the Eurodac database. This shows whether a person has already applied in another Dublin state.
40915.m: Fingerprints show whether someone has already applied for asylum elsewhere.

40916.q: What does a decision not to consider an application mean in the asylum procedure?
a: The application is not examined on its merits
40916.e: With a decision not to consider an application, the authorities do not examine the reasons for fleeing, for example because another Dublin state is responsible.
40916.m: With a non-consideration decision, the reasons for fleeing are not examined at all.

40917.q: Which department does the State Secretariat for Migration belong to?
a: The Department of Justice and Police
40917.e: The SEM is part of the Federal Department of Justice and Police (FDJP). This department is also responsible for police and justice.
40917.m: The SEM belongs to the FDJP.

40918.q: What is the State Secretariat for Migration responsible for?
a: Asylum, and the entry and residence of foreign nationals
40918.e: The SEM decides, for example, on asylum applications and regulates who may enter Switzerland and live here. It has had this name since 2015.
40918.m: The SEM is responsible for migration and asylum.

40919.q: What was the name of the authority that the State Secretariat for Migration grew out of?
40919.e: The Federal Office for Migration (FOM) was responsible until the end of 2014. After that it became the State Secretariat.
40919.m: The SEM grew out of the Federal Office for Migration.

40920.q: Near which city does the State Secretariat for Migration have its headquarters?
40920.e: The SEM headquarters is in Wabern near Bern, close to the Federal Palace. The federal asylum centres are also run from there.
40920.m: The SEM is based near Bern.

40921.q: Which federal permit does the SEM issue for naturalisation?
40921.e: For ordinary naturalisation, the approval of the federal government is needed as well as that of the municipality and canton. The SEM issues it.
40921.m: There is no ordinary naturalisation without a federal permit.

40922.q: What support does the SEM offer people who return voluntarily to their country of origin?
40922.e: With return assistance, people receive, for example, money or help for a fresh start in their country of origin. This is meant to make voluntary return easier.
40922.m: Return assistance supports a fresh start in the country of origin.

40923.q: Which travel document does the SEM regulate for people from many countries who want to enter Switzerland?
40923.e: People from certain countries need a visa to enter. The SEM decides who needs one and works with the Schengen states on this.
40923.m: To enter from many countries you need a visa.

40924.q: What title does the person who heads the State Secretariat for Migration have?
40924.e: A State Secretariat is headed by a State Secretary. This person reports to the head of the department.
40924.m: A State Secretariat is headed by a State Secretary.

40925.q: Where do asylum seekers in Switzerland go first?
40925.e: Asylum seekers are first housed in a federal asylum centre. For this purpose Switzerland is divided into six asylum regions.
40925.m: Asylum seekers first go to a federal asylum centre.

40926.q: Who runs the federal asylum centres in Switzerland?
40926.e: As the name says, the centres are the responsibility of the federal government. The SEM runs them and works with partners for care and security.
40926.m: The federal asylum centres are the federal government’s responsibility.

40927.q: What is the longest time asylum seekers stay in a federal asylum centre?
40927.e: The law sets a maximum of 140 days, about four and a half months. After that the people are assigned to a canton or leave Switzerland.
40927.m: Asylum seekers stay at most a few months in a federal asylum centre.

40928.q: What happens in a federal asylum centre with a processing function?
40928.e: Asylum applications are examined in the centres with a processing function. For eastern Switzerland, such a centre is in Altstätten.
40928.m: Asylum applications are examined in centres with a processing function.

40929.q: Where do asylum seekers go if their application is examined in the extended procedure?
40929.e: If a case needs more investigation, the person is assigned to a canton. They live there until the decision is made.
40929.m: In the extended procedure, asylum seekers live in a canton.

40930.q: What mainly determines how many asylum seekers a canton must take in?
40930.e: Distribution among the cantons is basically in proportion to the number of inhabitants. Large cantons such as Zurich therefore take in more people.
40930.m: Cantons with more inhabitants take in more asylum seekers.

40931.q: What can happen to asylum seekers who seriously disrupt security in a centre?
a: They go to a special centre with stricter rules
They may move into a hotel
40931.e: Asylum seekers who seriously disrupt security or the running of a centre can be taken to a special federal centre. Stricter rules apply there.
40931.m: There are special federal centres for disruptive asylum seekers.

40932.q: What do children of school age receive during their stay in a federal asylum centre?
40932.e: Children in the asylum procedure also have a right to primary school lessons. These are often provided directly in the centres.
40932.m: Children in asylum centres also have a right to school.

a: People who flee within their own country
People who flee across the sea
People who return to their country
40933.e: Internally displaced people have had to leave their homes but have stayed in their own state. The reasons are often war, violence or natural disasters.
40933.m: Internally displaced people have fled within their own country.

40934.q: What is a common reason for people becoming internally displaced?
40934.e: Internally displaced people have to leave their homes because of danger, such as war, violence or natural disasters. In English they are called IDPs.
40934.m: Internally displaced people usually flee war or disasters.

40935.q: Which UN organisation helps refugees and often also internally displaced people?
40935.e: The UNHCR is the UN refugee agency, based in Geneva. Since 1998 there have also been UN guiding principles on protecting internally displaced people.
40935.m: The UNHCR helps people who have fled.

40936.q: Which organisation adopted the Kampala Convention in 2009, the first binding treaty to protect internally displaced people?
40936.e: The Kampala Convention was adopted in Uganda. It requires African states to protect internally displaced people.
40936.m: The Kampala Convention protects internally displaced people in Africa.

40937.q: Why do internally displaced people not count as refugees under the Geneva Convention?
a: They have not crossed a state border
They only flee for a short time
40937.e: The convention only applies to people outside their home country. Internally displaced people stay in their own state and so are not refugees in legal terms.
40937.m: Anyone who stays in their own country is not a refugee in legal terms.

40938.q: Are there more internally displaced people or more refugees abroad worldwide?
a: There are no figures on this
40938.e: According to the UNHCR, most people flee within their own country. The number of internally displaced people is much higher than the number of refugees abroad.
40938.m: Most displaced people stay in their own country.

40939.q: In which city is the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) based?
40939.e: The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre belongs to the Norwegian Refugee Council and is based in Geneva. Every year it collects worldwide figures on internal displacement.
40939.m: The IDMC in Geneva counts internally displaced people worldwide.

40940.q: According to the IDMC, which country had the most internally displaced people at the end of 2024?
40940.e: Because of the war that broke out in 2023, over 11 million people in Sudan were displaced within their own country (as of the end of 2024). That is one of the highest figures ever measured for a single country.
40940.m: The war in Sudan has displaced millions of people within their own country.

40941.q: Under international law, do people who flee only because of climate change count as refugees?
a: No, environmental reasons do not count as a reason for flight there
Yes, if they come across the sea
40941.e: The Geneva Refugee Convention only protects against persecution, for example because of religion or political opinion. Droughts, storms or rising seas are not included.
40941.m: “Climate refugee” is not a term of international law.

a: People leave their homes because of the effects of climate change
40942.e: Droughts, floods or a rising sea level can force people to move away. This is called climate migration.
40942.m: Climate migration means moving away because of the effects of climate change.

40943.q: Which of these events can force people to move away because of climate change?
40943.e: When it does not rain for a long time, fields and pastures dry up. Many people then find no food and no work and move away.
40943.m: Droughts can force people to move away.

40944.q: Why does drinking water become scarce on flat islands when the sea rises?
a: Salt water gets into the groundwater
It never rains there any more
40944.e: When the sea level rises, seawater gets into the soil and wells. You cannot drink salty water, and plants grow badly in it.
40944.m: The rising sea makes drinking water salty on flat islands.

40945.q: In which ocean is the island state of Tuvalu, which is seriously threatened by rising sea levels?
40945.e: Tuvalu is made up of flat atolls in the Pacific. Its highest point is only a few metres above the sea. In 2023 Australia offered the people there a new home.
40945.m: Tuvalu is a flat island state in the Pacific.

40946.q: According to the World Bank’s Groundswell report (2021), how many people could migrate within their own country because of climate change by 2050?
40946.e: In its report, the World Bank expects up to 216 million internal migrants by 2050. With effective climate protection the number could be much smaller.
40946.m: By 2050 climate change could force many millions of people to move.

40947.q: Where do most people go who leave their homes because of environmental changes?
40947.e: Most environment-related moves are short, for example from the countryside to the city. Only a few people cross borders.
40947.m: Climate migration mostly happens within people’s own country.

40948.q: How can people who lose their homes because of climate change be helped?
a: By offering them protection and a new home
By banning them from entering everywhere
By forbidding them to move away
Not at all, it is impossible
40948.e: Some countries offer threatened people a right to stay. Climate protection is just as important, so that fewer people have to move away.
40948.m: People displaced by the climate need protection and a new home.

40949.q: What does free movement of persons between Switzerland and the EU allow?
a: Living and working in the other country more easily
Travelling to the USA without a passport
40949.e: Thanks to free movement of persons, people from the EU with a job contract can live in Switzerland more easily, and vice versa. It has applied since 2002.
40949.m: Free movement of persons makes living and working in the other country easier.

40950.q: What was the status called under which foreign workers until 2002 could work in Switzerland for only a few months a year and without their families?
40950.e: Seasonal workers worked, for example, in construction or tourism and then had to leave again. They were not allowed to bring their families.
40950.m: Seasonal worker status separated many workers from their families.

40951.q: From which country did especially many workers come to Switzerland in the 1950s and 1960s?
40951.e: Many Italians worked in Switzerland in construction, in factories and in hotels and restaurants. They helped to build Switzerland.
40951.m: In the past, especially many workers came from Italy.

40952.q: What did the mass immigration initiative, accepted in 2014, demand?
a: That women be given the vote
40952.e: The initiative demanded that Switzerland control immigration on its own. Voters narrowly accepted it with about 50.3 per cent.
40952.m: The mass immigration initiative wanted to limit immigration.

40953.q: Which permit do people receive who live abroad and work in Switzerland?
40953.e: The G stands for cross-border commuter (in German “Grenzgänger”). These people cross the border regularly to work, usually daily or weekly.
40953.m: Cross-border commuters hold the G permit.

40954.q: Why do many migrant workers send money to their country of origin?
a: Because they are not allowed to spend it in Switzerland
40954.e: Many people work abroad to provide for their family at home. For some countries this money is an important source of income.
40954.m: Many migrants support their families at home with their wages.

40955.q: What is it called when well-trained specialists leave their country of origin?
40955.e: When doctors or engineers emigrate, for example, their country of origin loses them. The term describes “brains” draining away.
40955.m: In a brain drain, a country loses its skilled workers.

40956.q: In which year did the civil war in Syria begin?
40956.e: During the Arab Spring in 2011, many people protested against the government. This developed into a long war with millions of displaced people.
40956.m: The war in Syria began in 2011.

40957.q: Which country has taken in the most refugees from Syria?
40957.e: For many years Turkey hosted over three million Syrians. This made it the largest host country in the world for a long time.
40957.m: Most Syrian refugees found refuge in Turkey.

a: A huge refugee camp for people from Syria
A river on the border with Syria
A mountain range in southern Jordan
40958.e: Zaatari camp was opened in northern Jordan in 2012. It became one of the largest refugee camps in the world.
40958.m: Zaatari in Jordan is a huge camp for people from Syria.

40959.q: Which neighbouring country of Syria took in especially many refugees compared with its own population?
40959.e: In little Lebanon there was at times about one refugee for every four to five inhabitants. No other country took in so many people per head.
40959.m: Lebanon carried an especially heavy burden per inhabitant.

40960.q: Which sea did many refugees cross from Turkey to Greece in 2015?
40960.e: Many people crossed the Aegean in small boats to Greek islands. In 2016 the EU and Turkey made an agreement to slow down this movement.
40960.m: In 2015 many refugees came to Greece across the Aegean.

40961.q: Which German Chancellor said “We can do this” (“Wir schaffen das”) in 2015 about taking in many refugees?
40961.e: Angela Merkel said the sentence in August 2015, when especially many people from Syria were coming to Germany. It became a much-discussed quotation.
40961.m: The sentence “We can do this” comes from Angela Merkel.

40962.q: Which Syrian ruler was overthrown in December 2024?
40962.e: After more than 13 years of war, rebels captured Damascus, and Assad fled to Russia. After that, many refugees faced the question of whether to return.
40962.m: The Assad regime in Syria ended in December 2024.

40963.q: Along which route did many refugees travel from Greece to central Europe in 2015?
40963.e: The Balkan route led through North Macedonia, Serbia and other countries to Austria and Germany. In 2016 it was largely closed.
40963.m: In 2015 many refugees travelled to central Europe along the Balkan route.

40964.q: In which year did the Federal Council activate protection status S for the first time?
40964.e: After the Russian attack on Ukraine, the Federal Council activated the status on 11 March 2022. It had never been used before.
40964.m: Protection status S was activated for the first time in 2022.

40965.q: In German, what does the letter S in protection status S stand for?
40965.e: The status applies to people in need of protection who flee because of a serious general danger such as war. They receive an S permit.
40965.m: Protection status S stands for people in need of protection.

40966.q: For people from which country was protection status S activated in 2022?
40966.e: After the Russian attack, many people fled Ukraine. For them the Federal Council activated protection status S, which has been in the Asylum Act since 1998.
40966.m: Protection status S was activated for refugees from Ukraine.

40967.q: What is the most important difference between protection status S and the normal asylum procedure?
a: No detailed asylum procedure is needed
40967.e: With status S, each individual case is not examined in detail. This means many people can receive protection in a short time.
40967.m: Status S gives quick protection without a long procedure.

40968.q: What goal is protection status S basically aimed at?
a: Returning home after the war ends
40968.e: The status is aimed at return. It applies as long as the danger in the country of origin lasts and can be lifted by the Federal Council.
40968.m: Protection status S is meant as temporary protection.

40969.q: From when may people from Ukraine with protection status S work in Switzerland?
40969.e: In 2022 the Federal Council decided that people with status S may take a job without a waiting period. However, the employer must report the job or have it approved.
40969.m: People with status S may work in Switzerland straight away.

40970.q: Which permit do people with protection status S receive in Switzerland?
40970.e: People in need of protection receive an S permit. It shows that they are receiving temporary protection in Switzerland.
40970.m: People with protection status S receive an S permit.

40971.q: What is the similar EU protection instrument called that was activated for people from Ukraine in 2022?
40971.e: The EU Temporary Protection Directive dates from 2001. It was used for the first time in March 2022.
40971.m: The EU gave Ukrainians temporary protection.

a: Moving refugees from a first host country to a third country
Refugees returning to their home country
40972.e: With resettlement, especially vulnerable refugees are taken from a first host country to another state. There they receive lasting protection.
40972.m: Resettlement brings refugees safely to a new host country.

40974.q: Which organisation proposes refugees for resettlement programmes?
40974.e: The UN refugee agency selects people who especially need protection and proposes them to host states. These then decide whether to take them in.
40974.m: The UNHCR selects refugees for resettlement.

40975.q: Besides resettlement, which is one of the UNHCR’s three lasting solutions for refugees?
40975.e: The UNHCR names three lasting solutions: voluntary return, integration in the host country and resettlement. The aim is for refugees to be able to live safely again.
40975.m: Voluntary return is a lasting solution for refugees.

40976.q: From which country did Switzerland take in thousands of refugees in 1956 after a popular uprising was crushed?
40976.e: After Soviet troops invaded, many Hungarians fled. Switzerland took in over 10,000 of them.
40976.m: Switzerland took in many refugees from Hungary in 1956.

40977.q: Which people from Asia found a new home in Switzerland from the 1960s?
40977.e: After the Dalai Lama fled in 1959, Tibetan refugees came to Switzerland. Today one of the largest Tibetan communities outside Asia lives here.
40977.m: A large Tibetan community lives in Switzerland.

40978.q: What were the Vietnamese refugees called who fled across the sea at the end of the 1970s?
40978.e: After the Vietnam War, many people fled in small boats. Switzerland also took in several thousand of them.
40978.m: The boat people fled Vietnam in small boats.

40979.q: What advantage does resettlement have for refugees?
a: They immediately get lots of money
They never have to learn a language
They can freely choose their country
40979.e: People do not have to make a dangerous journey with smugglers. They are brought to the host country in an organised way and with permission.
40979.m: Resettlement replaces a dangerous escape with a safe journey.

40980.q: Who decides in Switzerland how many refugees are taken in through resettlement?
40980.e: The Federal Council sets the admission quotas, usually for two years. The SEM then puts them into practice together with the cantons.
40980.m: The Federal Council decides Switzerland’s resettlement quotas.

40981.q: Which small Italian island is often the first place of arrival on the central Mediterranean route?
40981.e: Lampedusa is closer to Africa than to the Italian mainland. That is why many boats from North Africa arrive there.
40981.m: Lampedusa is close to Africa and is often the boats’ first destination.

40982.q: From which North African country do especially many boats set off on the central Mediterranean route?
40982.e: Since Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, there has been a lot of insecurity in Libya, which people smugglers exploit. Besides Libya, Tunisia is also an important departure point.
40982.m: Libya is an important starting point of the central Mediterranean route.

40983.q: Into which country does the western Mediterranean route lead from Morocco?
40983.e: The western route leads across the Strait of Gibraltar or to the Spanish exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla.
40983.m: The western Mediterranean route leads to Spain.

40984.q: Into which EU country does the eastern Mediterranean route lead from Turkey?
40984.e: Many people cross in boats from the Turkish coast to Greek islands in the Aegean. In places the distance is only a few kilometres.
40984.m: The eastern Mediterranean route leads from Turkey to Greece.

40985.q: Which country carried out the sea rescue operation “Mare Nostrum” after a serious boat disaster off Lampedusa in 2013?
40985.e: After the disaster in October 2013, in which more than 360 people died, the Italian navy started the operation. In one year it rescued a great many people in distress at sea.
40985.m: With “Mare Nostrum”, Italy rescued many people from the Mediterranean.

40986.q: What is the job of Frontex?
40986.e: Frontex is the European Border and Coast Guard Agency. It supports the Schengen states in protecting the external borders. Its headquarters are in Warsaw.
40986.m: Frontex helps protect Europe’s external borders.

40987.q: How did Swiss voters decide in May 2022 on a higher contribution to Frontex?
a: The majority of cantons was missing
40987.e: Around 71 per cent voted in favour of increasing the Swiss contribution. As a Schengen member, Switzerland takes part in Frontex.
40987.m: With the people’s approval, Switzerland takes part in Frontex.

40988.q: Which of the Mediterranean routes is considered the deadliest?
40988.e: The crossing from Libya or Tunisia to Italy is long, and the boats are often overcrowded. According to the International Organization for Migration, most people have died there.
40988.m: The central Mediterranean route is especially dangerous.

40989.q: On which Greek island did the overcrowded Moria camp burn down in September 2020?
40989.e: At that time more than 12,000 people lived crammed together in the Moria camp. After the fire they lost their shelter.
40989.m: The Moria camp on Lesbos burned down in 2020.

40990.q: Who jointly agreed on Switzerland’s Integration Agenda?
a: The federal government and the cantons
The municipalities entirely on their own
40990.e: Since 2019, the federal government and the cantons have been pursuing shared goals for integrating refugees and provisionally admitted people through the Integration Agenda.
40990.m: The federal government and the cantons pursue shared integration goals.

40991.q: What is the federal integration lump sum used for, for example?
40991.e: The federal government pays the cantons 18,000 francs per refugee. The money goes into things like language courses and education.
40991.m: The integration lump sum pays for language courses, for example.

40992.q: According to the Integration Agenda, what should refugees be able to do three years after arriving?
a: Communicate in everyday life in a national language
Speak all four national languages fluently
40992.e: The aim is basic knowledge of a national language, level A1. That way they can communicate in everyday life.
40992.m: After three years, refugees should have basic knowledge of a national language.

40993.q: How many years must you usually have lived in Switzerland to apply for ordinary naturalisation?
40993.e: Since 2018 you need ten years of residence and a C settlement permit. Years between your 8th and 18th birthdays count double.
40993.m: For ordinary naturalisation you need ten years of residence.

40994.q: What is the one-year programme called that specifically prepares refugees for an apprenticeship?
40994.e: The integration pre-apprenticeship has existed since 2018. It combines practical work in a company with language and school lessons.
40994.m: The integration pre-apprenticeship opens the way to an apprenticeship for refugees.

40995.q: Who mainly carries out integration support locally in Switzerland?
40995.e: The cantons run cantonal integration programmes for this. The federal government and the cantons fund them together.
40995.m: Integration happens mainly in the cantons and municipalities.

40996.q: Which principle describes Switzerland’s integration policy?
40996.e: The state supports immigrants, for example with courses, but also expects them to make an effort themselves. Both sides share responsibility.
40996.m: Integration means support and your own effort.

40997.q: What is the federal act called that regulates the residence and integration of foreign nationals in Switzerland?
40997.e: Since 2019 the former Foreign Nationals Act has been called the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, abbreviated AIG in German. The new name shows how important integration is.
40997.m: The AIG regulates residence and integration in Switzerland.

40998.q: Where was the 2030 Agenda adopted in September 2015?
a: At UN headquarters in New York
At the Palais des Nations in Geneva
At the EU headquarters in Brussels
At World Bank headquarters in Washington
40998.e: The 2030 Agenda was adopted on 25 September 2015 at a summit at the headquarters of the United Nations in New York. It has applied since 1 January 2016.
40998.m: The 2030 Agenda was agreed in New York in 2015.

40999.q: By which year should the goals of the 2030 Agenda be reached?
40999.e: As the name says, the goals should be reached by the year 2030. The period began in 2016.
40999.m: The 2030 Agenda has its target year in its name.

41000.q: What is the topic of the first of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals?
41000.e: Goal 1 is “No poverty”: poverty in all its forms should be ended everywhere. Goal 2 is about hunger.
41000.m: The first Sustainable Development Goal aims to end poverty.

41001.q: What is an important difference between the 2030 Agenda and the earlier Millennium Goals?
a: The 2030 Agenda applies to all countries, including rich ones
The 2030 Agenda applies only to Africa
The 2030 Agenda has no goals with numbers
The 2030 Agenda applies only to Europe
41001.e: The Millennium Goals were aimed mainly at developing countries. The 2030 Agenda commits all states, including Switzerland.
41001.m: The 2030 Agenda also applies to Switzerland.

41002.q: How many main goals for sustainable development does the 2030 Agenda have?
41002.e: The 2030 Agenda has 17 goals, for example no poverty, zero hunger and climate action. Each goal has its own colour and number.

41003.q: What do the “5 Ps” of the 2030 Agenda stand for?
41003.e: The five core messages are People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership. They group the goals into five areas.
41003.m: The 5 Ps stand for People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership.

41004.q: Which guiding principle of the 2030 Agenda is called “Leave no one behind”?
41004.e: The 2030 Agenda wants even the poorest and most disadvantaged people to benefit from development. That is why its guiding principle is “leave no one behind”.
41004.m: The 2030 Agenda wants to leave no one behind.

41005.q: What does “sustainable” mean in the sense of the 2030 Agenda?
a: Acting so that future generations can also live well
41005.e: Sustainable means using the Earth and its resources so that children and grandchildren can still live well. That is the idea behind the 2030 Agenda.
41005.m: Acting sustainably means thinking about the future.

41006.q: Which of these topics is a goal of the 2030 Agenda?
41006.e: Goal 13 of the 2030 Agenda calls for action against climate change. Other goals concern poverty, hunger and education, for example.
41006.m: Climate action is a goal of the 2030 Agenda.

41007.q: How many Millennium Development Goals were there?
41007.e: The Millennium Development Goals consisted of eight goals. In 2015 they were replaced by the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

41008.q: By which year were the Millennium Development Goals meant to be reached?
41008.e: The goals were set in the year 2000 and were meant to be reached by 2015. 1990 was usually used as the comparison year.

41009.q: What did the first Millennium Goal call for regarding extreme poverty?
a: Halving the share of extremely poor people
Doubling the share of poor people
41009.e: Goal 1 aimed to halve the share of people living on less than about one dollar a day between 1990 and 2015. Hunger was also to be halved.
41009.m: The first Millennium Goal aimed to halve extreme poverty.

41010.q: Which Millennium Goal was about school?
a: English as the language of school
41010.e: Goal 2 called for all girls and boys to be able to complete primary school by 2015.
41010.m: One Millennium Goal aimed to give all children primary schooling.

41011.q: What did the Millennium Development Goals want to achieve for young children?
a: That fewer children under five die
That all children get a mobile phone
That children no longer go to school
41011.e: Goal 4 called for reducing the death rate of children under five by two thirds by 2015. It fell by about half.
41011.m: The Millennium Goals aimed to reduce child mortality.

41012.q: How many states signed the UN Millennium Declaration in September 2000?
41012.e: The Millennium Declaration was adopted on 9 September 2000 by 189 UN member states. The eight Millennium Goals were derived from it.
41012.m: Almost all the world’s states supported the Millennium Declaration.

41013.q: How did extreme poverty in the world develop between 1990 and 2015?
41013.e: According to the UN, the number of extremely poor people fell from about 1.9 billion to about 836 million. A large part of the progress came from China and India.
41013.m: Extreme poverty fell sharply from 1990 to 2015.

41014.q: Which Millennium Goal was aimed mainly at the rich countries?
a: Goal 8: a global partnership for development
41014.e: Goal 8 asked rich countries for, among other things, more aid, fairer trade rules and debt relief. The other goals concerned mainly developing countries.
41014.m: The eighth Millennium Goal held the rich countries responsible.

41015.q: Which organisation sets the international poverty line for extreme poverty?
41015.e: The World Bank calculates the international poverty line. Anyone with less money available per day is considered extremely poor.
41015.m: The World Bank sets the line for extreme poverty.

41016.q: How high has the World Bank’s international poverty line been since 2025?
41016.e: In 2025 the World Bank raised the line to 3 US dollars per day; before that it was 2.15 dollars. The amount is adjusted for purchasing power, meaning it is converted to the prices in each country.
41016.m: Anyone with less than about 3 dollars a day is extremely poor.

41017.q: In which world region do most people in extreme poverty live today?
41017.e: Around seven out of ten extremely poor people live in sub-Saharan Africa (as of 2025). In the past, most lived in East and South Asia.
41017.m: Today extreme poverty is most widespread in sub-Saharan Africa.

41018.q: Roughly how many people lived in extreme poverty in 2025, according to estimates?
41018.e: Using the new poverty line of 3 dollars, about 830 million people live in extreme poverty. That is roughly one in ten people in the world.
41018.m: About one in ten people lives in extreme poverty.

41019.q: What does “adjusted for purchasing power” mean for the poverty line?
a: It takes into account how much you can buy with the money in each country
All prices are converted into francs
Only money in the bank is counted
41019.e: A dollar is often worth more in a poor country than in Switzerland, because many things are cheaper. Adjusting for purchasing power evens out these differences.
41019.m: Adjusted for purchasing power means the prices in the country are taken into account.

41020.q: What is the difference between absolute and relative poverty?
a: Absolute poverty threatens survival; relative poverty is measured against prosperity in your own country
Absolute poverty exists only in Switzerland
41020.e: You are absolutely poor if you lack the basics such as food or shelter. You are relatively poor if you have much less than most people in your country.
41020.m: Relative poverty compares with the standard of living in your own country.

41021.q: Roughly how many people in Switzerland were considered poor in 2022, according to the Federal Statistical Office?
41021.e: According to the FSO, the poverty rate in 2022 was about 8 per cent, which is about 700,000 people. The poverty line in Switzerland is based on the guidelines of SKOS, the Swiss conference for social welfare.
41021.m: There is poverty in Switzerland too.

41022.q: Roughly what share of the world’s population lived in extreme poverty in 1990?
41022.e: In 1990 more than 40 per cent of people lived in extreme poverty. By 2025 the share had fallen to about 10 per cent.
41022.m: The share of extremely poor people has fallen sharply since 1990.

41023.q: According to the World Bank, which of these countries has especially many extremely poor people (as of 2025)?
41023.e: A great many people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo live in extreme poverty. The country is rich in raw materials but suffers from long conflicts.
41023.m: Especially many extremely poor people live in the DR Congo.

41024.q: Who is the Max Havelaar label named after?
a: The main character of a Dutch novel
41024.e: Max Havelaar is the main character of a novel from 1860. The book shows how coffee farmers on the island of Java were exploited.
41024.m: Max Havelaar is a character from a novel who stands for fair treatment of farmers.

41025.q: What does the Max Havelaar label on a product stand for?
a: Fair trade with farmers in poorer countries
41025.e: Products with the label come from fair trade. The farmers and workers receive fair prices and better working conditions.
41025.m: The Max Havelaar label stands for fair trade.

41026.q: Which product was the first to be sold in Switzerland with the Max Havelaar label?
41026.e: In 1992 coffee was the first product with the label to reach the shops. Bananas, sugar, flowers and many other products followed later.
41026.m: Coffee was Switzerland’s first Max Havelaar product.

41027.q: Who founded the Max Havelaar Foundation Switzerland?
41027.e: It was founded by Bread for All, Caritas, Fastenopfer, HEKS, Helvetas and Swissaid. The aid organisations wanted to bring fairly traded products into ordinary shops.
41027.m: Aid organisations founded the Max Havelaar Foundation.

41028.q: What is the Fairtrade minimum price?
a: A price paid to farmers even when world market prices are low
The lowest price in the supermarket
41028.e: The minimum price is meant to cover production costs even when world market prices fall sharply. That gives producers a more reliable income.
41028.m: The minimum price protects farmers from prices that are too low.

41029.q: What is the Fairtrade premium used for?
a: Community projects such as schools or wells
41029.e: On top of the price, the cooperatives receive a premium. The farmers and workers decide together how to use it, for example for schools, health posts or better farming methods.
41029.m: The Fairtrade premium goes into shared projects.

41030.q: Which fairly traded product had a market share of over 50 per cent in Switzerland in 2014?
41030.e: In 2014 more than every second banana sold in Switzerland carried the Max Havelaar label. For coffee the share was about 10 per cent.
41030.m: More than every second banana in Switzerland is fairly traded.

41031.q: Roughly how much did people in Switzerland spend per person on Fairtrade products in 2021?
41031.e: According to the Max Havelaar Foundation, it was about 107 francs per person in 2021. That puts Switzerland among the world leaders in fair consumption.
41031.m: People in Switzerland buy especially many Fairtrade products per person.

41032.q: What does a world shop sell?
a: Fairly traded goods from all over the world
41032.e: World shops sell fairly traded goods such as coffee, chocolate or handicrafts. They are often run by volunteers.
41032.m: World shops sell fairly traded goods.

41033.q: What kind of organisation is Helvetas?
a: A Swiss aid organisation for development cooperation
41033.e: Helvetas was founded in Zurich in 1955. The organisation supports people in poorer countries so that they can improve their lives themselves.
41033.m: Helvetas is a Swiss aid organisation.

a: In poorer countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America
41034.e: Helvetas supports people in poorer countries, for example with access to water, education and work. When it was founded, it was called the Swiss Aid Organisation for Non-European Areas.
41034.m: Helvetas helps people in poorer countries.

a: It merged with another aid organisation
41035.e: In 2011 Helvetas and Intercooperation merged. Since then the organisation has been called Helvetas Swiss Intercooperation.

41036.q: What is Helvetas particularly known for in Nepal?
41036.e: In Nepal, Helvetas has been helping to build thousands of suspension bridges for decades. They save people in the mountains long and dangerous detours to schools and markets.
41036.m: Helvetas builds suspension bridges in Nepal.

41037.q: In roughly how many countries is Helvetas active?
41037.e: Helvetas works in about 30 countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe. It is supported by about 100,000 members and donors.

41038.q: Which principle is especially important to Helvetas?
41038.e: Helvetas wants to enable people to improve their living conditions themselves. That is why local experts and communities are closely involved.
41038.m: Helvetas relies on helping people to help themselves.

41039.q: What does Helvetas sell in its Fairshop?
a: Fairly made products from partner countries
41039.e: In the Fairshop, Helvetas sells, for example, fairly produced clothes, food and handicrafts. In this way it supports fair trade.
41039.m: Helvetas sells fairly made goods in the Fairshop.

41040.q: Which church does the aid organisation Caritas belong to?
41040.e: Caritas is the aid organisation of the Catholic Church. Caritas Switzerland was founded in 1901.
41040.m: Caritas is a Catholic aid organisation.

41041.q: In which city does Caritas Switzerland have its headquarters?
41041.e: The headquarters of Caritas Switzerland are in Lucerne. There are also 16 independent regional Caritas organisations.
41041.m: Caritas Switzerland is based in Lucerne.

41042.q: What does the Latin word “caritas” mean?
41042.e: In Latin, “caritas” means love for your neighbour or charity. The name shows that the organisation wants to support people in need.
41042.m: Caritas means love for your neighbour.

a: A shop with cheap food for people with little money
A flea market only for churches
41043.e: In Caritas markets, people affected by poverty can buy food and everyday products at low prices with a shopping card.
41043.m: Caritas markets help people with little money to do their shopping.

41044.q: What is the Caritas KulturLegi for?
a: It gives people with little money discounts on culture, sport and education
It is a pass for cyclists
41044.e: With the KulturLegi, people on low incomes get reductions, for example for museums, courses or sports clubs. This way they too can take part in social life.
41044.m: The KulturLegi makes culture cheaper for people with little money.

41045.q: Which worldwide network does Caritas Switzerland belong to?
41045.e: Caritas Switzerland is a member of Caritas Internationalis, a network in more than 160 countries. It also belongs to Caritas Europa.

41046.q: Where does Caritas Switzerland help people affected by poverty?
a: In Switzerland and in about 20 countries abroad
Only in the city of Lucerne
41046.e: Caritas supports people affected by poverty in Switzerland and provides emergency aid and development cooperation in about 20 countries.
41046.m: Caritas helps at home and abroad.

41048.q: What was Swissaid called when it was founded in 1948?
41048.e: Swissaid was founded in 1948 as Swiss Aid for Europe and first helped in war-torn Europe. Later it was renamed Swiss Foreign Aid and finally Swissaid.
41048.m: Swissaid began in 1948 as aid for Europe.

a: A Swiss aid organisation for development cooperation
An office of the Swiss army
41049.e: Swissaid is a foundation that supports people in poorer countries. It has been called Swissaid since 1969.
41049.m: Swissaid is a Swiss aid organisation.

41050.q: Which kind of farming does Swissaid especially promote?
a: Large monocultures with lots of poison
41050.e: Swissaid supports small farming families with agroecology, meaning farming methods that work with nature. This should help them feed themselves better.

41051.q: On which continent does Swissaid work, among others?
41051.e: Swissaid is active in nine countries, for example in Tanzania, Chad and Niger in Africa, but also in Latin America and Asia.
41051.m: Swissaid helps in Africa, among other places.

41052.q: In which country did Swissaid start one of its first projects outside Europe around 1960?
41052.e: In 1960 Swissaid started its first projects in India, and shortly afterwards also in Chad. India is still one of its project countries today.
41052.m: Swissaid has been active in India for a long time.

41053.q: What is Swissaid’s political and religious position?
a: It belongs to the Catholic Church
It belongs to the federal government
41053.e: Swissaid is a foundation that is tied neither to a party nor to a church. Part of its budget comes from the SDC.
41053.m: Swissaid is independent of parties and churches.

41054.q: Which topic does Swissaid often take up in its research on the commodities trade?
a: The trade in wood from Switzerland
41054.e: Swissaid investigates where the gold processed in Switzerland comes from. In some countries gold is mined under poor conditions.
41054.m: Swissaid asks critical questions about where gold comes from.

41055.q: What is the Glückskette called in French?
41055.e: The Glückskette (Swiss Solidarity) was founded in French-speaking Switzerland, where it is called Chaîne du Bonheur. In Italian it is called Catena della Solidarietà.
41055.m: In French, the Glückskette is called Chaîne du Bonheur.

41056.q: In which part of Switzerland was the Glückskette (Swiss Solidarity) founded in 1946?
41056.e: The Glückskette was founded in Lausanne in 1946 as a programme on Radio Sottens. One of its founders was the entertainer Jack Rollan.
41056.m: The Glückskette was founded in French-speaking Switzerland.

41057.q: How much money did the Glückskette (Swiss Solidarity) collect for the people of Ukraine in 2022?
41057.e: About 130 million francs were collected for the victims of the war in Ukraine. That is one of the biggest appeals in its history.
41057.m: In 2022 Switzerland donated a great deal of money for Ukraine through the Glückskette.

41058.q: For which event in Switzerland did the Glückskette (Swiss Solidarity) collect about 74 million francs in 2000?
a: Severe storms in Valais and Ticino
A forest fire in the Jura
41058.e: In October 2000, severe storms caused great damage in Valais and Ticino, for example in Gondo. The Glückskette collected about 74 million francs for this.
41058.m: In 2000 the Glückskette collected a lot of money for storm victims in Valais and Ticino.

41059.q: What legal form has the Glückskette (Swiss Solidarity) had since 1983?
41059.e: Since 1983 the Glückskette has been a foundation. Since then it has collected more than a billion francs in total.

41060.q: For which earthquake did the Glückskette (Swiss Solidarity) collect about 64 million francs in 2010?
41060.e: After the severe earthquake in Haiti in January 2010, the population donated about 64 million francs.
41060.m: After the earthquake in Haiti, the Glückskette helped.

a: A small loan for people without access to normal banks
A loan for very small countries
A loan only for big companies
41061.e: Microcredits are small loans, often only a few hundred dollars. They help poor people to start a small business.
41061.m: A microcredit is a small loan for poor people.

41062.q: Who receives most of the loans from the Grameen Bank?
41062.e: Around 97 per cent of the Grameen Bank’s borrowers are women (as of 2007). Women are considered especially reliable and often invest in the family.

41063.q: What does “Grameen” mean in the name of the bank from Bangladesh?
41063.e: “Grameen” comes from Bengali and means something like “village” or “rural”. The bank is aimed at poor people in the countryside.
41063.m: The Grameen Bank is a bank for the villages.

41064.q: How do many microcredits work so that the money is paid back?
a: Borrowers form small groups that support each other
You must give a house as security
41064.e: The borrowers join together in small solidarity groups. Only when the first ones repay regularly do other members get a loan.
41064.m: With microcredits, members of a group help each other.

41065.q: What do people often use a microcredit for?
a: To go on an expensive holiday
41065.e: With a microcredit, people buy, for example, a sewing machine, chickens or goods for a market stall. That way they can earn money themselves.
41065.m: Microcredits help people start a small business.

41066.q: What is a common criticism of microcredits?
a: High interest rates can lead to over-indebtedness
They only go to rich people
They must not be paid back
41066.e: The interest is often over 20 per cent a year. Some borrowers take out new loans to pay off old ones and fall into a debt trap.

41067.q: Which country does Muhammad Yunus come from?
41067.e: Muhammad Yunus was born in 1940 in the Chittagong area, which today belongs to Bangladesh. He founded the Grameen Bank there.

41068.q: Which prize did Muhammad Yunus receive in 2006?
41068.e: Yunus and the Grameen Bank jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006. They were honoured for their work for development from below.
41068.m: Yunus received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

41069.q: Which post did Muhammad Yunus take up in Bangladesh in August 2024?
41069.e: After protests and the resignation of the prime minister, Yunus became head of an interim government on 8 August 2024. After the elections in February 2026 he handed over the post.
41069.m: From 2024, Yunus led Bangladesh’s interim government.

41070.q: What does Muhammad Yunus call companies that solve social problems instead of handing out profits?
41070.e: In a social business, the profit is put back into the company. The aim is to solve social or environmental problems.
41070.m: A social business wants to help instead of paying out profits.

41071.q: What was Muhammad Yunus’s job before he founded the Grameen Bank?
41071.e: Yunus did his doctorate in economics in the USA. After Bangladesh became independent, he headed the economics department at the University of Chittagong.
41071.m: Muhammad Yunus was an economics professor.

41072.q: Between which values does the HDI lie?
41072.e: Each part is converted to a scale from 0 to 1. The closer the value is to 1, the higher the development.
41072.m: An HDI close to 1 means very high development.

41073.q: Where does Switzerland rank in the Human Development Index (HDI)?
a: Right at the top, among the best countries
It is not rated at all
41073.e: Switzerland has been among the world leaders in the HDI for years. In the 2025 report it is in 3rd place behind Iceland and Norway.
41073.m: Switzerland is among the world leaders in the HDI.

41074.q: On which continent are most of the countries with the lowest HDI?
41074.e: Many countries south of the Sahara have a low HDI. In the 2025 report South Sudan is in last place.
41074.m: The countries with the lowest HDI are mostly in Africa.

41075.q: What do some experts criticise about the HDI?
a: It does not take environmental effects into account
41075.e: A country can have a very high HDI and still put a heavy strain on the environment. That is why there has also been a planetary-pressures-adjusted HDI since 2020.
41075.m: The HDI does not show how environmentally friendly a country is.

41076.q: Which figure measures the area of health in the HDI?
41076.e: For health, the HDI uses the average life expectancy at birth. It shows how long and how healthily people live in a country.
41076.m: In the HDI, life expectancy stands for health.

41077.q: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Index (HDI)?
41077.e: The UN Development Programme (UNDP) has published the HDI since 1990. It compares how well people live in different countries.
41077.m: The HDI comes from the UN.

41078.q: How is the area of education measured in the HDI?
a: By the average and expected years of schooling
By the number of school buildings
41078.e: Since 2010 the HDI has counted how many years adults have spent at school on average and how many years a child is expected to go to school.
41078.m: In the HDI, what counts is how long people go to school.

41079.q: Which figure measures the standard of living in the HDI?
a: The number of cars per family
The number of days of holiday
41079.e: For the standard of living, the HDI uses gross national income per inhabitant, adjusted for purchasing power.
41079.m: In the HDI, income per person shows the standard of living.

41080.q: How many countries are included in the ranking of the 2025 HDI report?
41080.e: The 2025 report compares 193 countries and territories. It is based on data from 2023.
41080.m: The HDI ranking compares almost all the countries in the world.

a: Creditors give up all or part of the repayment
A country takes on new debt
41081.e: With debt relief, the lenders give up part of what they are owed. The country can use the money saved for schools or hospitals, for example.
41081.m: With debt relief, debts no longer have to be repaid in full.

41082.q: Which countries mainly receive debt relief?
a: Poor countries with very high debts
Rich countries with a lot of money
41082.e: Heavily indebted poor countries often cannot repay their debts. The IMF and the World Bank have set up their own programmes for this.
41082.m: Debt relief mainly helps poor, heavily indebted countries.

41083.q: Which international bank lends money to poorer countries for their development?
41083.e: The World Bank gives loans to poorer countries, for example for roads, schools or water. Together with the IMF it has also cancelled debts.
41083.m: The World Bank lends money to poorer countries.

a: Someone who has lent money and should get it back
41084.e: The creditor lends money, the debtor must pay it back. With debt relief, the creditor gives up part of the money.

41085.q: Where does the campaign “Jubilee 2000” get its name from?
a: From the jubilee year in the Bible, in which debts were cancelled
From a tax-free year in Switzerland
41085.e: The Old Testament describes a jubilee year in which debts are cancelled. At the turn of the millennium, the campaign called for debt relief for poor countries.
41085.m: The Jubilee campaign refers to an idea from the Bible.

41086.q: What is the group of creditor states called that negotiates debt rescheduling and meets in France?
41086.e: In the Paris Club, creditor states have been negotiating payment relief with debtor countries since 1956. Switzerland is also a member.
41086.m: In the Paris Club, states negotiate about debts.

41087.q: What can a country use the money for that it no longer has to repay thanks to debt relief?
41087.e: Countries receiving debt relief had to promise to use the money saved to fight poverty, for example for education and health.
41087.m: Money saved on debts should benefit the population.

41088.q: Which country in the Horn of Africa was one of the last to reach the completion point of the HIPC Initiative?
41088.e: Somalia went through the HIPC Initiative only in recent years and was able to get rid of a large part of its foreign debt.
41088.m: Somalia also received major debt relief.

41089.q: In which four priority regions is Swiss development cooperation active?
a: Sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa and the Middle East, Asia, Eastern Europe
North America, Western Europe, Australia, Japan
Scandinavia, the Alps, the Caribbean, Antarctica
41089.e: Since the 2021 to 2024 strategy, Switzerland has concentrated on these four regions. The 2025 to 2028 strategy keeps them.
41089.m: Switzerland helps mainly in Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

41090.q: What is the federal unit called that sends Swiss experts on humanitarian missions to crisis and disaster areas?
41090.e: The Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit (SHA) is part of the SDC. Its experts help after disasters, for example with water supply, construction or medicine.
41090.m: The SHA sends Swiss experts to disaster areas.

41091.q: How much money is set aside for Ukraine in the 2025 to 2028 strategy?
41091.e: Of the strategy’s total amount, 1.5 billion francs are reserved for Ukraine. With this, Switzerland supports the reconstruction of the country.
41091.m: Switzerland supports Ukraine’s reconstruction with 1.5 billion francs.

41092.q: What is the abbreviation of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation?
41092.e: The SDC belongs to the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA). It helps people in poorer countries and provides humanitarian aid.
41092.m: The SDC is responsible for Switzerland’s development cooperation.

41093.q: According to the UN target, what percentage of their gross national income should rich countries spend on development aid?
41093.e: For decades the UN has recommended that rich countries spend 0.7 per cent of their gross national income on official development aid. Only a few countries reach this target.
41093.m: The UN target for development aid is 0.7 per cent.

41094.q: Does Switzerland reach the UN target of spending 0.7 per cent of its income on development aid?
a: Yes, it is far above it
41094.e: In 2022 Switzerland spent about 0.56 per cent, which is less than the UN target. Only a few countries reach 0.7 per cent.
41094.m: Switzerland’s development aid is below the UN target.

41095.q: Which federal office is responsible for economic development cooperation alongside the SDC?
a: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs SECO
The Federal Office of Public Health FOPH
The Federal Office for the Environment FOEN
The Federal Office of Culture FOC
41095.e: SECO belongs to the economics department and promotes trade, jobs and good infrastructure in partner countries, for example.
41095.m: Besides the SDC, SECO also helps in poorer countries.

41096.q: Which of these countries in the Himalayas has long been a priority country of Swiss development cooperation?
41096.e: Switzerland has worked with Nepal since the 1950s. It is one of the oldest partner countries of Swiss development cooperation.
41096.m: Nepal is an old partner country of Switzerland.

41097.q: What does Switzerland do in development cooperation?
a: It helps poorer countries so that people there are better off
It sells weapons to other countries
It builds roads only in Switzerland
It hands out money to Swiss companies
41097.e: Through development cooperation, Switzerland supports poorer countries, for example with education, health or clean water. Parliament approves a large sum for this every four years.
41097.m: Through development cooperation, Switzerland helps poorer countries.

41098.q: In which year did the big UN Earth Summit take place in Rio de Janeiro?
41098.e: The UN Conference on Environment and Development took place in Rio de Janeiro from 3 to 14 June 1992. It is often simply called the Earth Summit.
41098.m: The Rio Earth Summit took place in 1992.

41099.q: What is the action programme for the 21st century called that was agreed at the Rio Earth Summit?
41099.e: Agenda 21 is an action programme for environmentally friendly development in the 21st century. Municipalities and cantons have also developed their own “Local Agenda 21s”.
41099.m: Agenda 21 is the action programme of the Rio Earth Summit.

41100.q: Which two major environmental treaties were opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit?
a: Framework Convention on Climate Change and Convention on Biological Diversity
Geneva Conventions and Convention on the Law of the Sea
41100.e: In Rio, the Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity were signed. Both are still considered the basis of global environmental policy today.
41100.m: The Climate Change Convention and the Biodiversity Convention came out of Rio.

41101.q: Which guiding idea was at the centre of the Rio Earth Summit?
41101.e: Sustainable development means that people today meet their needs without taking away the basis of life from future generations. Rio linked environmental protection and development.
41101.m: Sustainable development also thinks about the people of tomorrow.

41102.q: How old was the Canadian Severn Suzuki when she gave a famous speech to the delegates in Rio in 1992?
41102.e: Twelve-year-old Severn Suzuki called on the adults to protect the environment for her generation. Her speech later became famous around the world.
41102.m: As early as 1992, a twelve-year-old girl spoke for young people at the Earth Summit.

41103.q: What is the follow-up conference called that took place in Rio de Janeiro again in 2012?
41103.e: Twenty years after the first summit, the states met again in Rio in June 2012. That is why the conference was named Rio+20.
41103.m: Rio+20 took place twenty years after the first Earth Summit.

41104.q: Against which environmental problem did Rio set in motion another agreement, signed in 1994?
41104.e: The Earth Summit laid the foundation for the Convention to Combat Desertification. It was signed in Paris in 1994.
41104.m: The fight against desertification also goes back to the Earth Summit.

41105.q: In which country is Rio de Janeiro, where the Earth Summit took place in 1992?
41105.e: Rio de Janeiro is a big city in Brazil. In 1992 representatives of almost every country in the world met there for the Earth Summit.
41105.m: The 1992 Earth Summit took place in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.

41106.q: What is the English abbreviation for the world climate council?
41106.e: IPCC stands for “Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change”. In German it is often called the Weltklimarat.
41106.m: The world climate council is abbreviated IPCC in English.

41107.q: In which Swiss city does the IPCC have its secretariat?
41107.e: The IPCC secretariat is in Geneva, at the headquarters of the World Meteorological Organization. Geneva is an important location for international organisations.
41107.m: The IPCC has its secretariat in Geneva.

41108.q: Which prize did the IPCC receive in 2007 together with Al Gore?
41108.e: The IPCC and former US Vice President Al Gore were honoured in 2007 for their work to inform people about climate change. They received the Nobel Peace Prize.
41108.m: The IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.

41109.q: Who does the IPCC mainly write its big reports for?
41109.e: The IPCC brings together what is known about climate change. Governments use its reports to make decisions about climate protection.
41109.m: The IPCC’s reports help politicians make climate decisions.

41110.q: What does the IPCC mainly do?
41110.e: The IPCC does not carry out its own research. Thousands of experts voluntarily assess the published studies and summarise them for politicians.
41110.m: The IPCC summarises the knowledge from many studies.

41111.q: The Bern climate researcher Thomas Stocker worked with the IPCC. What does he study to research the climate of long ago?
41111.e: Tiny air bubbles are trapped in the ice of Antarctica. They show what the climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.
41111.m: Ice cores reveal what the climate used to be like.

41112.q: What did the IPCC’s special report on 1.5 degrees of warming show?
a: Even half a degree more warming causes much more damage
The Earth will soon get colder
Only the Arctic is affected by climate change
41112.e: The report showed that 2 degrees of warming causes much more damage than 1.5 degrees, for example more heatwaves and more dying corals.
41112.m: Every tenth of a degree of warming counts.

41113.q: Who works on the IPCC’s reports?
a: Experts from all over the world
41113.e: Thousands of researchers from many countries read the new studies and summarise them. Governments help check the summaries.
41113.m: Experts from all over the world work for the IPCC.

41114.q: Which substances, once found in spray cans and fridges, does the Montreal Protocol mainly regulate?
41114.e: Chlorofluorocarbons, CFCs for short, destroy the ozone in the atmosphere. The Montreal Protocol banned their production step by step.
41114.m: CFCs harm the ozone layer and were therefore banned.

41115.q: Which radiation from the sun does the ozone layer protect us from?
41115.e: Ozone filters out a large part of the ultraviolet radiation. Too much UV radiation causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer.
41115.m: The ozone layer protects us from dangerous UV radiation.

41116.q: Over which continent was the ozone hole discovered in the 1980s?
41116.e: In 1985 British researchers reported a strong thinning of the ozone layer over the South Pole. The ozone hole appears there every year in the southern hemisphere’s spring.
41116.m: The ozone hole was discovered over Antarctica.

41117.q: Which record did the Montreal Protocol set in 2009?
a: First UN treaty ratified by all member states
First treaty with a penalty for countries
41117.e: When East Timor joined on 16 September 2009, all UN member states had ratified the protocol. No UN treaty had ever managed that before.
41117.m: All UN states have ratified the Montreal Protocol.

41118.q: What has happened to the ozone hole since the Montreal Protocol?
a: The ozone layer has disappeared completely
There never was an ozone hole
41118.e: Since CFCs were banned, the ozone layer has been slowly recovering. Experts expect it to have fully recovered by about 2066.
41118.m: Thanks to the Montreal Protocol, the ozone layer is recovering.

41119.q: Why are some substitutes for CFCs still a problem?
a: They heat up the climate a lot
They make holes in the ground
41119.e: Some substitutes do not harm the ozone but are strong greenhouse gases. That is why the Montreal Protocol was extended in 2016 and now also restricts these substances.
41119.m: Today the Montreal Protocol also protects the climate.

41120.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is most of the ozone found?
41120.e: About 90 per cent of the ozone is in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground. This ozone layer works like a filter.
41120.m: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere.

41121.q: In which village in the Grisons has the ozone layer been measured since 1926, longer than anywhere else in the world?
41121.e: The researcher Paul Götz began the ozone measurements in Arosa. Today MeteoSwiss continues the longest ozone measurement series in the world.
41121.m: The world’s longest ozone measurement series comes from Arosa.

41122.q: What did Paul Crutzen, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1995?
41122.e: The three researchers explained how chemical substances destroy the ozone in the atmosphere. Their work was an important basis for the Montreal Protocol.
41122.m: Three chemists received the Nobel Prize for ozone research.

41123.q: How many states agreed on the climate agreement in Paris in 2015?
41123.e: At the world climate conference in Paris, almost all the states in the world agreed on the agreement. That was a great success for climate protection.
41123.m: Almost all the world’s states support the Paris Agreement.

41124.q: To what value should global warming be limited if possible, according to the Paris Agreement?
41124.e: The agreement aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees. The states also want to try to limit it to 1.5 degrees.
41124.m: Paris aims to limit warming to 1.5 degrees.

41125.q: With which period is warming compared for the 1.5-degree target?
41125.e: It is measured against the average before industrialisation, usually 1850 to 1900. Since then the burning of coal, oil and gas has increased greatly.
41125.m: Warming is compared with the time before industrialisation.

41126.q: What are the climate plans called that every country must submit under the Paris Agreement?
41126.e: Each country decides for itself how much it wants to cut its emissions. These plans are called nationally determined contributions, or NDCs.
41126.m: Each country sets its own climate contribution.

41127.q: How often should countries renew their climate plans under the Paris Agreement?
41127.e: Every five years the states should present new and, if possible, more ambitious targets. This is called the ambition mechanism.
41127.m: The climate plans are renewed every five years.

41128.q: What must countries do under the Paris Climate Agreement?
41128.e: Greenhouse gases such as CO2 warm the Earth. That is why all countries should emit less of them.
41128.m: The Paris Agreement calls for fewer greenhouse gases.

41129.q: Which country left the Paris Agreement twice under President Donald Trump?
41129.e: The USA left the agreement in 2020, rejoined in 2021 under Joe Biden and announced in January 2025 that it would leave again. It is one of the biggest emitters of greenhouse gases.
41129.m: The USA has left the Paris Agreement twice.

41130.q: By how much does Switzerland want to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 1990?
41130.e: Under the Paris Agreement, Switzerland has pledged to halve its emissions by 2030. Part of this may be achieved through projects abroad.
41130.m: Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030.

41131.q: Which gas does the formula CO2 stand for?
41131.e: CO2 consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. It is produced mainly by burning coal, oil and gas.
41131.m: CO2 is the chemical formula of carbon dioxide.

41132.q: What does Switzerland’s CO2 Act aim to achieve?
41132.e: The CO2 Act has been in force since 2000. It sets targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
41132.m: The CO2 Act is meant to cut CO2 emissions.

41133.q: On which products is the CO2 levy charged in Switzerland?
a: On heating oil and natural gas
41133.e: The CO2 levy applies to fossil fuels used for heating or process heat. Motor fuels such as petrol are exempt.
41133.m: The CO2 levy makes heating oil and natural gas more expensive.

41134.q: What does the CO2 levy do to heating oil?
a: Heating oil is only sold in summer
41134.e: Since 2022 the levy has been 120 francs per tonne of CO2. For a litre of heating oil, that comes to about 30 centimes.
41134.m: The CO2 levy makes heating oil more expensive.

41135.q: How does the population get a large part of the CO2 levy back?
a: Through a voucher for the train
41135.e: About two thirds of the revenue is paid back, with every person receiving the same amount through their health insurance. So people who cause little CO2 benefit.
41135.m: The CO2 levy flows back to the population through health insurance.

41136.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the revised CO2 Act on 13 June 2021?
41136.e: The revision was rejected with about 51.6 per cent voting no. Parliament then drew up a new proposal without new levies.
41136.m: The revised CO2 Act narrowly failed at the ballot box in 2021.

41137.q: What would the 2021 CO2 Act have introduced, among other things?
a: A ban on all petrol cars
41137.e: Depending on class and distance, the plane ticket levy would have been between 30 and 120 francs. Because of the no vote, it was not introduced.
41137.m: The 2021 CO2 Act would have brought a plane ticket levy.

41138.q: Which programme is paid for with part of the CO2 levy?
41138.e: Up to a third of the levy goes into the Buildings Programme. It supports, for example, better insulation and renewable heating systems.
41138.m: The Buildings Programme helps make houses more climate-friendly.

41139.q: Why has the CO2 levy been raised several times since it was introduced?
a: Because the climate targets were missed
Because the health insurers needed more money
41139.e: The levy was introduced in 2008 at 12 francs per tonne. Because the targets were missed, it rose step by step.
41139.m: The CO2 levy rose because the climate targets were missed.

41140.q: Which country does the climate activist Greta Thunberg come from?
41140.e: Greta Thunberg was born in Stockholm in 2003. Her protest made her famous worldwide.

41141.q: In which year did Greta Thunberg begin her school strike for the climate?
41141.e: In August 2018 the then 15-year-old sat in the street with a sign for the first time instead of going to school. Soon young people all over the world joined in.
41141.m: Greta Thunberg’s climate strike began in 2018.

41142.q: In front of which building did Greta Thunberg sit during her school strike?
41142.e: She protested in front of the Riksdag in Stockholm, Sweden’s parliament. In this way she wanted to push politicians to do more for the climate.
41142.m: Greta Thunberg went on strike in front of the Swedish parliament.

41143.q: What is the worldwide youth movement called that grew out of Greta Thunberg’s school strikes?
41143.e: Because the strikes took place on Fridays, the movement called itself Fridays for Future. In Switzerland it became the Klimastreik (Climate Strike).
41143.m: Fridays for Future grew out of the school strikes.

41144.q: How did Greta Thunberg travel across the Atlantic to the UN climate summit in New York in 2019?
41144.e: She crossed the Atlantic on the racing yacht “Malizia II”. She wanted to show that you can travel without a plane.
41144.m: Greta Thunberg sailed across the Atlantic in 2019.

41145.q: Which words made Greta Thunberg’s speech at the 2019 UN climate summit famous?
41145.e: With “How dare you!”, she accused the heads of state of letting young people down. The words went around the world.
41145.m: Greta Thunberg called out “How dare you!” to the heads of state.

41146.q: Which magazine named Greta Thunberg Person of the Year in 2019?
41146.e: The US magazine “Time” named her Person of the Year in 2019. At 16 she was the youngest person ever to receive this title.
41146.m: Greta Thunberg was “Time” Person of the Year in 2019.

41147.q: At which event in Switzerland did Greta Thunberg say “Our house is on fire” in 2019?
a: At the World Economic Forum in Davos
At the film festival in Locarno
41147.e: In January 2019 she spoke to business leaders at the World Economic Forum in Davos. She called for them to act as if their own house were in flames.
41147.m: In Davos, Greta Thunberg warned that our house is on fire.

41148.q: In which year did Swiss voters accept the Climate Protection Act?
41148.e: On 18 June 2023 the voters said yes to the federal act on climate protection targets. A referendum had been launched against it beforehand.
41148.m: The Climate Protection Act was accepted by the people in 2023.

41149.q: Who decided on the Climate Protection Act in Switzerland in 2023?
41149.e: A referendum was launched against the act. That is why the people voted on 18 June 2023 and said yes with about 59 per cent.
41149.m: The voters said yes to the Climate Protection Act in 2023.

41150.q: Which party launched the referendum against the Climate Protection Act?
41150.e: The SVP feared higher costs and electricity shortages. That is why it collected signatures for a popular vote.
41150.m: The SVP launched the referendum against the Climate Protection Act.

41151.q: By which year should Switzerland reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions, according to the Climate Protection Act?
41151.e: The act sets the target of net zero by 2050. There are also interim targets and guide values for buildings, transport and industry.
41151.m: Switzerland is meant to become climate-neutral by 2050.

41152.q: What does the target “net zero” mean in climate protection?
a: Emitting no more greenhouse gases than are removed
Not driving a car at all
41152.e: Remaining emissions that can hardly be avoided must be balanced out by storage in forests, soils or technology. The bottom line is then zero.
41152.m: Net zero means that emissions and removal of greenhouse gases are the same size.

41153.q: The Climate Protection Act was created as a counter-proposal to which popular initiative?
41153.e: The Glacier Initiative wanted to ban fossil fuels in the long term. Parliament set the Climate Protection Act against it, and the initiative was then withdrawn.
41153.m: The Climate Protection Act is the counter-proposal to the Glacier Initiative.

41154.q: What does the Climate Protection Act provide a total of 2 billion francs for over ten years?
a: Replacing old oil, gas and electric heating systems
41154.e: Homeowners receive contributions if they replace fossil-fuel or electric heating systems with climate-friendly ones. 200 million francs a year are available for this.
41154.m: The Climate Protection Act supports the replacement of old heating systems.

41155.q: Which measure in your own house helps climate protection in the way the Climate Protection Act supports?
a: Replacing an oil heating system with a heat pump
Leaving the windows open in winter
Installing a second oil heating system
41155.e: Oil heating systems burn heating oil and emit a lot of CO2. A heat pump uses heat from the air or the ground and is much more climate-friendly.
41155.m: Heat pumps instead of oil heating protect the climate.

41156.q: What does the word biodiversity mean?
41156.e: Biodiversity covers the variety of species, habitats and genes. The more varied nature is, the more resilient it is.
41156.m: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth.

41157.q: Besides protecting diversity and using it sustainably, what is the third goal of the Convention on Biological Diversity?
a: Fair sharing of the benefits from genetic resources
Building new zoos in every country
41157.e: If, for example, a medicine is developed from a plant, the country it comes from should also benefit. That is the third goal of the convention.
41157.m: The Convention on Biological Diversity wants to share nature’s benefits fairly.

41158.q: How many states take part in the Convention on Biological Diversity?
a: Almost all the states in the world
41158.e: Almost all the states in the world are parties. The convention’s secretariat is in Montreal in Canada.
41158.m: Almost all states take part in the Convention on Biological Diversity.

41159.q: What percentage of land and sea areas should be protected by 2030, according to the 2022 global biodiversity agreement?
41159.e: The Kunming-Montreal agreement was adopted in December 2022. Its best-known target is called “30 by 30”.
41159.m: By 2030, 30 per cent of the Earth should be protected.

41160.q: Which big state has never joined the Convention on Biological Diversity?
41160.e: The USA did sign the convention but never ratified it. Almost all the other states in the world are parties.
41160.m: The USA is not a member of the Convention on Biological Diversity.

a: Living things whose genetic material has been changed in a laboratory
41161.e: In genetically modified organisms, the genetic material has been deliberately changed. The Cartagena Protocol regulates how to handle them safely.
41161.m: In genetically modified organisms, the genetic material has been changed.

41162.q: What does the International Day for Biological Diversity draw attention to?
a: The variety of animals, plants and habitats
41162.e: The UN has declared 22 May the Day for Biological Diversity. It is meant to show how important the variety of nature is.
41162.m: The Day for Biological Diversity is about the variety of nature.

41163.q: Why is it important to protect many different species?
a: So that zoos have more animals
So that there are fewer plants
Because rare species are worth more money
41163.e: The more varied nature is, the better it survives diseases, droughts or other changes. That is why the Convention on Biological Diversity protects diversity.

41164.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the Biodiversity Initiative in September 2024?
