41450.q: Which country still does not recognise Kosovo’s independence today (as of 2026)?
41450.e: Serbia still regards Kosovo as one of its provinces. Some other states, such as Spain or Russia, also do not recognise Kosovo.
41450.m: Serbia does not recognise Kosovo’s independence.

41451.q: What is the Swiss Army contingent called that has been deployed in Kosovo since 1999?
41451.e: Swisscoy is part of the international peacekeeping force KFOR. It is the Swiss Army’s largest mission abroad.
41451.m: Swisscoy helps keep the peace in Kosovo.

41452.e: In 2008 Switzerland was one of the first countries to recognise Kosovo as an independent state. Many people in Switzerland have roots in Kosovo.

41453.q: Which alliance bombed targets in Serbia in 1999 to end the Kosovo War?
41453.e: The air strikes lasted from March to June 1999. Afterwards Serbian troops withdrew from Kosovo.
41453.m: NATO intervened in the Kosovo War in 1999.

41454.q: Which currency is used in Kosovo?
41454.e: Kosovo introduced the euro without being a member of the eurozone. Before that the Deutschmark was used.
41454.m: In Kosovo you pay with the euro.

41455.q: Against which population group was the genocide in Rwanda mainly directed?
41455.e: Extremist Hutu murdered mainly Tutsi, but also moderate Hutu. Estimates range from 800,000 to a million dead.
41455.m: The genocide in Rwanda was directed mainly against the Tutsi.

41456.q: Which event set off the genocide in Rwanda on 6 April 1994?
a: The shooting down of the president’s plane
41456.e: President Juvénal Habyarimana’s plane was shot down as it approached Kigali to land. The killings began that same night.
41456.m: The shooting down of the president’s plane set off the genocide.

41457.q: Which medium particularly stirred up people to kill in Rwanda?
41457.e: The station RTLM spread hatred against the Tutsi and called for violence. It insultingly called the Tutsi “cockroaches”.
41457.m: A radio station called for genocide in Rwanda.

41458.q: Roughly how long did the genocide in Rwanda last in 1994?
41458.e: The genocide began in April 1994 and ended in July 1994. In these roughly 100 days, hundreds of thousands of people were killed.
41458.m: The genocide in Rwanda lasted about 100 days.

41459.q: What is the capital of Rwanda?
41459.e: Kigali is in the centre of the country. A large memorial there commemorates the victims of the genocide.
41459.m: The capital of Rwanda is Kigali.

41460.q: What is Rwanda often called because of its landscape?
41460.e: Rwanda is very hilly and lies mostly more than 1,000 metres high. In French the nickname is “pays des mille collines”.
41460.m: Rwanda is the land of a thousand hills.

41461.q: What happened to many of those responsible after the genocide in Rwanda?
41461.e: The UN set up a special criminal tribunal for Rwanda. In addition, village courts in Rwanda itself judged many perpetrators.
41461.m: Many of those responsible for the genocide in Rwanda were put on trial.

41462.q: Which war did the Panmunjom armistice end?
41462.e: The war had begun in 1950 when North Korea invaded South Korea. Troops of the UN and China intervened.
41462.m: The Panmunjom armistice stopped the Korean War.

41463.q: In which year was the Panmunjom armistice signed?
41463.e: The agreement was signed on 27 July 1953. Since then the guns at the front have largely been silent.
41463.m: The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice.

41464.q: Why are North and South Korea legally still at war?
41464.e: A peace treaty was never signed. The 1953 armistice still applies today.
41464.m: There is only an armistice between North and South Korea.

41465.q: What is the border strip called that has separated North and South Korea since 1953?
41465.e: The strip is about 4 kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long. It is one of the most heavily guarded border areas in the world.
41465.m: The Demilitarised Zone separates North and South Korea.

41466.q: Which two neutral states have had officers on the supervisory commission in Korea since 1953?
41466.e: The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission checks that the armistice is kept. Originally Poland and Czechoslovakia were also members.
41466.m: Swiss officers have been monitoring the armistice in Korea since 1953.

41467.q: Which country did not sign the Panmunjom armistice?
41467.e: It was signed by the US-led UN Command, North Korea and China. South Korea’s president wanted to keep fighting and refused.
41467.m: South Korea did not sign the 1953 armistice.

41468.q: Who met in the border village of Panmunjom in April 2018?
a: The leaders of North and South Korea
The Pope and the US president
The coaches of two football teams
The kings of Sweden and Norway
41468.e: South Korean President Moon Jae-in and North Korea’s ruler Kim Jong-un met right at the border. Kim briefly stepped onto South Korean soil.
41468.m: In 2018 the leaders of both Koreas met in Panmunjom.

41469.q: From which country did Cyprus become independent in 1960?
41469.e: Cyprus had been under British administration since 1878 and later became a crown colony. After independence, the United Kingdom kept two military bases.
41469.m: Cyprus became independent from the United Kingdom in 1960.

41470.q: Which country occupied the north of Cyprus in 1974?
41470.e: It was triggered by a coup by Greek nationalist officers who wanted to unite Cyprus with Greece. The troops have remained in the north to this day.
41470.m: Turkey occupied the north of Cyprus in 1974.

41471.q: How many states recognise the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (as of 2026)?
41471.e: The north declared itself a separate state in 1983. Internationally the area is still considered part of the Republic of Cyprus.
41471.m: Only Turkey recognises Northern Cyprus as a state.

41472.q: Which capital is divided by the Cyprus conflict?
41472.e: The UN buffer zone runs right through the city. Since 2003 there have been crossing points between the two parts.

41473.q: Who monitors the buffer zone between the north and south of Cyprus?
41473.e: The UN mission UNFICYP has been on the island since 1964 and is one of the UN’s oldest peacekeeping missions. The buffer zone has existed since 1974 and is also called the Green Line.
41473.m: UN peacekeepers guard the buffer zone on Cyprus.

41474.q: Which two large ethnic groups live on Cyprus?
41474.e: Mainly Greek Cypriots live in the south, mainly Turkish Cypriots in the north. The island has been divided since 1974.
41474.m: Greek and Turkish Cypriots live on Cyprus.

41475.q: Since when has Cyprus been a member of the European Union?
41475.e: Cyprus joined on 1 May 2004, together with nine other countries. In the north, however, EU law is suspended.
41475.m: Cyprus has been in the EU since 2004.

41476.q: Why do peace talks, for example about Cyprus, often take place in Switzerland?
a: Because Switzerland is neutral and offers good offices
Because it never rains in Switzerland
41476.e: Switzerland is neutral and often invites parties to a conflict for talks. In 2017, for example, there were negotiations about Cyprus in Crans-Montana.
41476.m: Neutral Switzerland often hosts peace talks.

41477.q: With whom did the government of Colombia conclude a peace agreement in 2016?
a: With a rebel group in its own country
41477.e: In Colombia the rebel group FARC had been fighting the state since the 1960s. In 2016 the government and the FARC made peace, and the fighters laid down their weapons.
41477.m: Colombia made peace with the rebel group FARC in 2016.

41478.q: Which famous prize did the president of Colombia receive in 2016 for the peace with the FARC?
41478.e: President Juan Manuel Santos received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016. He was honoured for his efforts to end the long civil war in Colombia.
41478.m: Colombia’s president received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016.

41479.q: Colombia and the FARC negotiated for years in Havana. In which country is Havana?
41479.e: Havana is the capital of Cuba, an island in the Caribbean. The peace talks took place there from 2012 to 2016.
41479.m: The peace talks for Colombia took place in Havana in Cuba.

41480.q: What was the result of the referendum on the first peace agreement in Colombia in October 2016?
41480.e: About 50.2 per cent voted against the agreement. It was then revised and approved by parliament in November.
41480.m: The Colombian people narrowly rejected the first peace agreement.

41481.q: What did the FARC become after the peace agreement?
41481.e: The former fighters founded a party and received guaranteed seats in parliament for a few years. Today the party is called Comunes.
41481.m: After the peace, the FARC became a party.

41482.q: What was the pen made from that was used to sign the peace agreement in Colombia in 2016?
41482.e: The pen was made from a cartridge case and bore the words “Bullets wrote our past, education our future”. It was meant to show the path from violence to peace.
41482.m: The peace agreement was symbolically signed with a pen made from a bullet.

41483.q: Roughly how long did the armed conflict between the Colombian state and the FARC last?
41483.e: The FARC was founded in 1964. By 2016 the conflict had cost more than 200,000 lives and displaced millions of people.
41483.m: The conflict with the FARC lasted more than half a century.

41484.q: Was there peace everywhere in Colombia after the 2016 agreement with the FARC?
a: No, other armed groups kept fighting
Yes, all fighting stopped at once
Yes, Colombia even abolished its army
No, the FARC immediately started a new war
41484.e: The FARC laid down its weapons and became a party. But other groups such as the ELN did not take part in the agreement and kept fighting.
41484.m: After 2016, other groups such as the ELN kept fighting in Colombia.

41485.q: Which two countries have been arguing over the Kashmir region since 1947?
41485.e: Since the partition of British India in 1947, India and Pakistan have both claimed Kashmir. They have fought several wars over it.
41485.m: India and Pakistan have been arguing over Kashmir since 1947.

41486.q: Which event of 1947 is at the beginning of the Kashmir conflict?
41486.e: When British rule ended, India and Pakistan were created. The princely states had to join one of the two.
41486.m: The Kashmir conflict began with the partition of British India in 1947.

41487.q: In which mountain range is the Kashmir region?
41487.e: Kashmir lies in the north of India and Pakistan in the Himalayas and the Karakoram. There are very high mountains and large glaciers there.
41487.m: Kashmir lies high in the Himalayas.

41488.q: Which religion do most people in Kashmir follow?
41488.e: Most people living in Kashmir are Muslims. Pakistan is a mainly Muslim country, India mainly Hindu. This is also one reason for the dispute.
41488.m: Most people in Kashmir are Muslims.

41489.q: Which third country also controls part of the Kashmir region?
41489.e: China administers, among others, the area of Aksai Chin in the east. India also claims this area.
41489.m: Besides India and Pakistan, China also controls part of Kashmir.

41490.q: What is Kashmir, which India and Pakistan are arguing over?
a: A mountain region in South Asia
An island in the Indian Ocean
A port city by the sea
41490.e: Kashmir is a mountain region in the north of India and Pakistan. A small part is also controlled by China.
41490.m: Kashmir is a mountain region in South Asia.

41491.q: Which animal does the fine cashmere wool, named after the region, come from?
41491.e: The cashmere goat has very fine, soft hairs under its coat. Expensive cashmere wool is made from them.
41491.m: Cashmere wool comes from the cashmere goat.

41492.q: Why is the Kashmir conflict considered especially dangerous?
a: It affects the whole of Europe
It is fought only at sea
It is the newest conflict in the world
41492.e: India and Pakistan have both tested nuclear weapons, Pakistan most recently in 1998. So every escalation causes worry around the world.
41492.m: In the Kashmir conflict, two nuclear powers face each other.

41493.q: What is considered the highest battlefield in the world in the Kashmir conflict?
a: A glacier high in the mountains
41493.e: On the Siachen Glacier, Indian and Pakistani soldiers face each other at over 5,000 metres. More soldiers have died there from cold and avalanches than from fighting.
41493.m: The highest battlefield in the world is a glacier in Kashmir.

41495.q: What is the person called who heads an embassy?
41495.e: The ambassador is the highest representative of a country in the host country. He or she heads the embassy.
41495.m: An ambassador heads their country’s embassy.

41496.q: What must the host country do before a new ambassador may start work?
a: It must give them a house
It must have them elected by the people
41496.e: An ambassador may only work if the host country agrees. This approval is called accreditation.
41496.m: An ambassador needs the host country’s approval.

41497.q: What does a consulate help Swiss people abroad with, for example?
a: When they have lost their passport
41497.e: A consulate looks after its own citizens abroad. For example, it issues new identity documents or helps in emergencies.
41497.m: A consulate helps its own citizens abroad.

a: A person who represents their country abroad
A person with a school diploma
41498.e: Diplomats look after relations between countries. They negotiate, provide information and represent their country’s interests.

41499.q: What special protection do ambassadors have in the host country?
a: They may vote in elections there
41499.e: Diplomats enjoy immunity. The host country may not arrest them, but it can expel them.
41499.m: Diplomats are protected from arrest in the host country.

41500.q: In which Swiss city do most foreign embassies have their seat?
41500.e: Embassies are usually in the capital, where the government sits. In Switzerland that is Bern.
41500.m: The embassies in Switzerland are in Bern.

41501.q: Who sends a nuncio as ambassador to other countries?
41501.e: The Pope heads the Holy See, which has ambassadors like a state. They are called nuncios, and one works in Bern.
41501.m: The Pope’s ambassador is called a nuncio.

41502.q: What is a country’s mission in the capital of another country called?
41502.e: Diplomats work in an embassy. They represent their country and also help their own citizens abroad. The rules for this are in the Vienna Convention.
41502.m: An embassy represents a country abroad.

41503.q: What does it mean when a host country declares a diplomat “persona non grata”?
a: They are unwelcome and must leave
They are made a guest of honour
41503.e: Under Article 9 of the Convention, a host country can declare a diplomat unwelcome at any time and without giving reasons. The sending state must then recall them.
41503.m: A persona non grata is an unwelcome diplomat who must leave the country.

41504.q: What may the authorities of the host country not do without the consent of the head of mission?
a: List the embassy in the phone book
41504.e: The premises of an embassy are inviolable (Article 22). Police and other authorities may only enter them with the ambassador’s permission and must also protect them.
41504.m: An embassy’s premises are off limits to the host country’s authorities.

41505.q: May customs open an embassy’s official consignment?
41505.e: Official consignments of embassies, the so-called diplomatic bag, are protected. The host country’s authorities may neither open nor hold them back.
41505.m: An embassy’s official post must not be opened.

41506.q: What does a diplomat’s immunity mean?
a: They are exempt from the host country’s jurisdiction
They may take part in elections in the host country
They must do military service in the host country
They get a free flat in the host country
41506.e: Diplomats may not be arrested in the host country and usually cannot be put on trial. This lets them do their work without pressure from the host country.
41506.m: Thanks to immunity, a diplomat cannot be put on trial in the host country.

41507.q: Despite their immunity, must diplomats respect the laws of the host country?
a: Only if they were born there
41507.e: Article 41 obliges diplomats to respect the laws of the host country. Immunity only protects them from prosecution by the host country; it does not allow them to break the law.
41507.m: Diplomats too must keep to the laws of the host country.

41508.q: Must diplomats pay the usual taxes on their salary in the host country?
a: No, they are largely exempt from taxes
Only if they stay longer than a year
41508.e: According to Article 34 of the Convention, diplomats are exempt from most taxes of the host country. But they still pay indirect taxes included in the price of goods.
41508.m: In principle, diplomats pay no income tax in the host country.

41509.q: Which heads of mission belong to the highest class according to the Convention?
41509.e: The Convention divides heads of mission into three classes. Ambassadors belong to the first class, followed by envoys and chargés d’affaires.
41509.m: Ambassadors are in the highest class of diplomats.

41510.q: Who receives a foreign head of state on a state visit in Switzerland?
41510.e: Switzerland has no single head of state; the Federal Council performs this role together. That is why the whole Federal Council receives the state guest, led by the President of the Confederation.
41510.m: On a state visit, the whole Federal Council welcomes the guest.

41511.q: On which square in Bern does the ceremonial welcome often take place during state visits?
41511.e: The Bundesplatz is right in front of the Federal Palace. State guests are often received there with military honours.
41511.m: In Bern, state guests are often received on the Bundesplatz in front of the Federal Palace.

41512.q: What is the group of soldiers called that ceremonially welcomes a state guest on arrival?
41512.e: An army guard of honour stands ready at the welcome, and the guest inspects it with the host. This is part of the military honours of a state visit.
41512.m: A guard of honour gives the state guest military honours.

41513.q: What is meant by “protocol” in diplomacy?
a: The rules for how official events are run
A list of all embassies worldwide
41513.e: Protocol sets out who greets whom and how, who sits where and in which order things happen. At the FDFA a separate department deals with protocol.
41513.m: Diplomatic protocol governs the running and order of rank at official events.

41514.q: What is the formal dinner called that the host gives in honour of a state guest?
41514.e: The state banquet is a highlight of a state visit. The host and the guest usually each give a speech at the table.
41514.m: At a state banquet, a state guest is entertained festively.

41515.q: What is the order called that decides who comes before whom at official events?
41515.e: The order of precedence decides, for example, who is greeted first or who sits next to the host. It helps to avoid arguments about the guests’ honour.
41515.m: The order of precedence decides who goes first at official events.

41516.q: Which kind of visit by a head of state has the most ceremonial protocol?
41516.e: The state visit is the highest form of an official visit, with military honours and a banquet. On a working visit, by contrast, talks come first and the programme is simpler.
41516.m: A state visit is the most ceremonial form of visit between states.

41517.q: What is NOT one of the three classic features of a state?
41517.e: According to the three-element theory, a state needs a territory, a people and effective state authority. Its own currency is not necessary; Liechtenstein, for example, uses the Swiss franc.
41517.m: A state consists of territory, a people and state authority.

41518.q: What does it mean when a country “recognises” a new country?
a: It officially accepts it as a state
It closes the border with it
41518.e: By recognising it, a state says that it treats the new country as an equal state. Then the two can, for example, exchange ambassadors.
41518.m: Recognising means officially accepting a country as a state.

41519.q: What is the forcible incorporation of foreign territory into your own state called?
41519.e: An annexation breaks the ban on the use of force in the UN Charter. That is why most states do not recognise such changes of territory.
41519.m: Territory taken by annexation is usually not recognised internationally.

41520.q: Why is it important for a new country to be recognised by other states?
a: So that it can conclude treaties with them
So that it may have a flag
So that it may choose a capital
41520.e: Without recognition it is difficult to trade, open embassies or become a member of the UN.
41520.m: Recognised states can conclude treaties with other states.

41521.q: Which territory has its own government but is officially recognised as a state by only a few countries?
41521.e: The People’s Republic of China regards Taiwan as part of its territory. That is why only a few states officially recognise Taiwan, though many have unofficial relations.
41521.m: Despite its own government, Taiwan is officially recognised by only a few states.

41522.q: Which country in Europe is not recognised by all states?
41522.e: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008. Switzerland recognised Kosovo, but Serbia and some other states do not.
41522.m: Kosovo is not recognised by all states.

41523.q: Which country came into being in 1993 when Czechoslovakia peacefully split into two states?
41523.e: On 1 January 1993 Czechoslovakia was divided into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Both states were recognised immediately.
41523.m: In 1993 Czechoslovakia became the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

41524.q: What does it mean when a state is sovereign?
a: It is ruled by a king
It is a member of the European Union
It has its own army with nuclear weapons
41524.e: Sovereignty means that a state has the highest authority internally and is independent of other states externally. No other state may give it orders.
41524.m: A sovereign state decides its own affairs.

41525.q: What is part of a state’s sovereignty?
a: It must adopt its neighbour’s laws
41525.e: A sovereign state decides for itself which laws apply in it. The term sovereignty was shaped by the French thinker Jean Bodin in the 16th century.
41525.m: A sovereign state makes its own laws.

41526.q: With which peace settlement of 1648 was the Swiss Confederation’s independence from the Holy Roman Empire recognised?
41526.e: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years’ War. It is also seen as the beginning of an order of equal sovereign states in Europe.
41526.m: Since the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, the Swiss Confederation has also been legally independent of the Empire.

41527.q: According to the Federal Constitution, the cantons are sovereign. What limits their sovereignty?
41527.e: Article 3 of the Federal Constitution says that the cantons are sovereign except where their sovereignty is limited by the Federal Constitution. Everything not assigned to the Confederation is regulated by the cantons themselves.
41527.m: The cantons are sovereign unless the Federal Constitution says otherwise.

41528.q: What is the principle called that states must not interfere in the internal affairs of other states?
41528.e: The principle of non-intervention follows directly from the sovereignty of states. It is set out in the UN Charter.
41528.m: No state should interfere in the internal affairs of another.

41529.q: How many votes does each member state have in the UN General Assembly?
a: As many as it has millions of inhabitants
Depending on the size of its contribution
41529.e: The UN is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all member states. That is why little Switzerland has as much voting power in the General Assembly as a big country.
41529.m: In the UN General Assembly, every state has exactly one vote.

41530.q: What is the idea called that all state power comes from the people?
41530.e: With popular sovereignty, the people are the highest holder of state power. In Switzerland this can be seen especially in referendums and initiatives.
41530.m: Popular sovereignty means that power in the state comes from the people.

41531.q: What is a state’s authority over all people and things on its territory called?
41531.e: Territorial sovereignty means that the laws of a state apply on its own territory. Personal jurisdiction, by contrast, concerns the state’s own citizens, even abroad.
41531.m: Through territorial sovereignty, the laws of a state apply on its territory.

41533.q: A nautical mile measures 1,852 metres. Roughly how many kilometres are 12 nautical miles?
41533.e: You calculate 12 times 1,852 metres, which makes 22,224 metres. Rounded, that is about 22 kilometres.
41533.m: A nautical mile is almost twice as long as a kilometre.

41534.q: What right do foreign ships have in a state’s territorial sea?
a: The right to fish freely there
The right to extract raw materials
The right to hold military exercises
41534.e: Foreign ships may pass through the territorial sea as long as they do not disturb the peace and security of the coastal state. They may not fish or extract raw materials there.
41534.m: Ships may pass peacefully through foreign territorial seas.

41535.q: Is a harbour on the sea part of the country’s territory?
a: No, the sea belongs to everyone
Only the seabed, not the water
Only when a ship is anchored there
41535.e: Harbours and bays count as internal waters. They belong entirely to the state, just like the land.
41535.m: Harbours and bays belong entirely to the state’s territory.

41536.q: According to which old rule was the territorial sea often only about three nautical miles wide in the past?
41536.e: In the past, the sea counted as state territory as far as a cannon could fire from the shore. That was about three nautical miles.
41536.m: In the past, the range of a cannon decided the width of the territorial sea.

41537.q: What is the open sea far out, which belongs to no state, called?
41537.e: No state has sovereignty on the high seas. All countries may, for example, sail ships there.
41537.m: The high seas belong to no state.

41538.q: Over what does a state exercise its sovereignty in its territorial sea?
a: Over the water, the seabed and the airspace
Only over the surface of the water
41538.e: The sovereignty of the coastal state extends to the water, the seabed and the subsoil. The airspace above the territorial sea is also included.
41538.m: The territorial sea includes the seabed and the airspace above it.

41539.q: What may a coastal state do in its territorial sea that foreign ships may not?
41539.e: In the territorial sea, fish and mineral resources belong to the coastal state. Foreign ships may only pass through peacefully.
41539.m: In the territorial sea, only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials.

41540.q: What does the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea regulate?
a: The rights and duties of states at sea
The prices of fish in shops
The building of harbours in Switzerland
41540.e: The Convention on the Law of the Sea was signed in 1982. It sets out, for example, which sea areas belong to a coastal state and which are open to all.
41540.m: The Convention on the Law of the Sea regulates who owns which parts of the sea.

41541.q: According to the Convention on the Law of the Sea, what are the high seas?
a: The open sea, which belongs to no state
The sea right in front of a beach
The sea around the North Pole only
41541.e: The high seas begin outside the zones of the coastal states. All states may sail and fish there. The convention was signed in Montego Bay in Jamaica.
41541.m: The high seas belong to no state and are open to all.

41542.q: What may only the coastal state do in its exclusive economic zone?
a: Fish and extract raw materials such as oil
Ban all foreign ships from passing through
Charge foreign ships an entrance fee
41542.e: The exclusive economic zone reaches up to 200 nautical miles from the coast. Only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials there, but foreign ships may pass through freely.
41542.m: In its economic zone, only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials.

41543.q: What is the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea responsible for?
a: Disputes between states about the law of the sea
Rowing boat accidents on Swiss lakes
41543.e: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea was created by the Convention on the Law of the Sea. It decides disputes about the law of the sea and is based in Hamburg.
41543.m: The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea decides disputes about the law of the sea.

41544.q: What does the convention call the mineral resources on the seabed outside national zones?
a: The property of the nearest state
The possession of whoever comes first
The property of the veto powers
41544.e: The deep seabed of the high seas belongs to no single state. An international authority is meant to regulate its use for the benefit of all people.
41544.m: The treasures of the deep seabed are considered the common heritage of mankind.

41545.q: Which right does the Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantee to landlocked states such as Switzerland?
a: Access to the sea and use of the high seas
Its own territorial sea on the Mediterranean
A share of other states’ fishing
41545.e: States without a coast have the right to reach the sea through neighbouring states. Their ships may use the high seas just like the ships of coastal states.
41545.m: Countries without a coast may also use the sea and the high seas.

41546.q: Which city is the home port of ocean-going ships sailing under the Swiss flag?
41546.e: Although Switzerland has no coast, ocean-going ships sail under the Swiss flag. Their home port is Basel on the Rhine, via which you can reach the North Sea.
41546.m: Swiss ocean-going ships have Basel as their home port.

41547.q: What may foreign ships do in a coastal state’s economic zone?
a: Nothing at all, they may not enter
41547.e: The economic zone does not belong entirely to the coastal state. Only the fish and raw materials belong to it, but foreign ships may pass through freely.
41547.m: Ships may sail freely through a foreign economic zone.

41548.q: In which city does the Permanent Court of Arbitration have its seat?
41548.e: The Permanent Court of Arbitration has worked in the Dutch seat of government since 1902. Other international courts are also based there.
41548.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration sits in The Hague.

41549.q: Which conference decided in 1899 to found the Permanent Court of Arbitration?
41549.e: At the First Hague Peace Conference, a convention for the peaceful settlement of international disputes was concluded. The Permanent Court of Arbitration grew out of it.
41549.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration was created after the First Hague Peace Conference of 1899.

41550.q: What is the building called where the Permanent Court of Arbitration and the International Court of Justice work?
41550.e: The Peace Palace opened in 1913 and was built with money from the industrialist Andrew Carnegie. It is seen as a symbol of peace through law.
41550.m: The Peace Palace is home to the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

41551.q: Who decides a dispute at the Permanent Court of Arbitration?
41551.e: The Permanent Court of Arbitration is not a court with permanent judges. It keeps a list of experts from which the parties to a dispute choose their arbitrators for each case.
41551.m: At the Permanent Court of Arbitration, the parties choose their own arbitrators.

41552.q: Which sea was the well-known 2016 arbitration case Philippines versus China about?
41552.e: The Philippines challenged China’s territorial claims in the South China Sea. In 2016 the arbitral tribunal largely ruled in favour of the Philippines, but China does not recognise the decision.
41552.m: In 2016 an arbitration case decided about the South China Sea.

41553.q: What is the Permanent Court of Arbitration for?
a: It helps states settle disputes peacefully
It organises sports tournaments between countries
It hands out aid in war zones
41553.e: At the Permanent Court of Arbitration, states can have a dispute decided by arbitrators instead of going to war. About 130 states, including Switzerland, are parties to it.
41553.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration helps settle disputes between states peacefully.

41554.q: Is the Permanent Court of Arbitration older or younger than the UN?
a: Younger, it was created only around 2000
The same age, both were created in 1945
It was founded together with the EU
41554.e: The Permanent Court of Arbitration was agreed in 1899 and has worked since 1902. The UN was created only in 1945.
41554.m: The Permanent Court of Arbitration is older than the UN.

41555.q: What is meant by extradition in international law?
a: Handing over a wanted person to another state
41555.e: In an extradition, a state hands over a suspected or convicted person to another state. There the person is to be put on trial or serve their sentence.
41555.m: In an extradition, a wanted person is handed over to another state.

41556.q: May Swiss citizens be extradited to another state against their will?
a: Yes, but only to EU states
Yes, if the Federal Council agrees
41556.e: Article 25 of the Federal Constitution allows Swiss citizens to be extradited only with their consent. Instead, Switzerland can put them on trial itself.
41556.m: Switzerland extradites its own citizens only with their consent.

41557.q: What is the principle called that an act must be a crime in both states for extradition to happen?
41557.e: Switzerland usually extradites only if the act would also be a crime under Swiss law. That way nobody is prosecuted for something that is allowed here.
41557.m: Extradition happens only if the act is a crime in both states.

41558.q: According to the Federal Constitution, to which state may nobody be extradited?
a: To a state where they face torture
To a state without a coast
To a neighbouring state of Switzerland
41558.e: Article 25 of the Federal Constitution forbids extraditing people to a state where they face torture or other cruel treatment. This applies to everyone, not just Swiss citizens.
41558.m: Nobody may be extradited to a state where torture threatens.

41559.q: What does Switzerland demand before extraditing someone to a state with the death penalty?
a: An assurance that the death penalty will not be carried out
41559.e: Switzerland rejects the death penalty. It extradites only if the other state gives a binding assurance that the person will not be executed.
41559.m: Without a guarantee against the death penalty, Switzerland extradites nobody.

41560.q: Which federal office is responsible for extraditions in Switzerland?
41560.e: The Federal Office of Justice handles extradition requests from other states and makes such requests itself. It belongs to the Federal Department of Justice and Police.
41560.m: In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Justice deals with extraditions.

41561.q: Which Interpol notice is used to look for a person for arrest and extradition?
41561.e: With a Red Notice, a state asks police worldwide to provisionally arrest a wanted person. It can then request their extradition.
41561.m: The Interpol Red Notice seeks people for arrest and extradition.

41562.q: For which kind of offence is extradition usually not granted?
41562.e: Political offences are traditionally excluded from extradition. This is so that political opponents cannot be persecuted with the help of criminal law.
41562.m: Extradition is usually not granted for purely political offences.

41563.q: What colour is the cover of the Swiss passport?
41563.e: The Swiss passport is red and bears the white Swiss cross. Red is also the colour of the diplomatic and service passports.
41563.m: The Swiss passport is red with a Swiss cross.

41564.q: Which special passport do ambassadors receive for their work abroad?
41564.e: Ambassadors are diplomats. They travel with their own passport that shows their role.
41564.m: Diplomats travel with a special diplomatic passport.

41565.q: How long is a Swiss passport valid for children and young people under 18?
41565.e: Children’s appearance changes quickly. That is why their passport is valid for only five years, so that the photo stays up to date.
41565.m: Children’s passports are valid for a shorter time because children change quickly.

41566.q: For people aged 12 and over, what is stored on the chip of the Swiss passport in addition to the photo?
41566.e: Since 2010 the Swiss passport has had a chip. The photo and, from the age of 12, the fingerprints are stored on it.
41566.m: The chip in the passport stores the photo and fingerprints.

41567.q: What is shown on the visa pages of the new 2022 Swiss passport?
a: The members of the Federal Council
41567.e: The new passport was introduced on 31 October 2022. Each visa page is dedicated to a canton and shows its coat of arms and a typical motif.
41567.m: The 26 cantons are shown in the new Swiss passport.

41568.q: What is a visa, which sometimes goes into your passport?
a: Permission to enter a particular country
A receipt for the plane ticket
41568.e: Some countries require a visa. It shows that you may enter the country and stay there for a certain time.
41568.m: A visa allows you to enter a particular country.

41569.q: What is the area of letters and symbols at the bottom of a passport’s data page called, which machines can read?
41569.e: The machine-readable zone contains the name, passport number and date of birth in a fixed form. Border controls can quickly capture it with a reader.
41569.m: The machine-readable zone in the passport can be captured by readers.

41570.q: Which document is enough for Swiss people travelling to the countries of the Schengen area?
41570.e: For travel to Schengen states, a valid identity card is enough. For many countries outside Europe, on the other hand, you need a passport.
41570.m: You can travel to Schengen countries with the Swiss identity card.

41571.q: What is a visa called that you only get on arrival at the airport or border?
41571.e: Some countries issue travellers with a visa directly on entry. This is called a “visa on arrival”.
41571.m: For some countries, you get the visa only on arrival.

41572.q: What is a Schengen visa meant for?
a: Short trips into the Schengen area
41572.e: With a Schengen visa, people from certain countries may travel to the Schengen area for a short time, for example as tourists. Anyone who wants to stay longer needs a different permit.
41572.m: A Schengen visa is valid for short trips.

41574.q: Where do you normally apply for a visa for a foreign country?
a: At the destination country’s travel agency
41574.e: Visas are issued by the missions of the destination country, that is by embassies or consulates. Some countries also offer electronic visas today.
41574.m: You apply for a visa at the embassy or consulate of the destination country.

41575.q: In which country is the village of Schengen, after which the Schengen area is named?
41575.e: Schengen is a small wine village on the Moselle where three countries meet. The first agreement on removing border controls was signed there in 1985.
41575.m: The Schengen area is named after a village in Luxembourg.

41576.q: What does the Latin word “visum”, from which “visa” comes, mean?
41576.e: “Visum” is a form of the Latin verb “videre”, which means “to see”. In the past, an authority used this note to confirm that it had checked a document.
41576.m: The word visa comes from the Latin word for seen.

41577.q: What is the electronic travel authorisation called that you need for a visa-free trip to the USA?
41577.e: Anyone from Switzerland who wants to travel to the USA without a visa must first apply online for an ESTA authorisation. It is valid for short trips as a tourist or on business.
41577.m: For visa-free travel to the USA you need an ESTA authorisation.

41578.q: Who should a Swiss woman contact if she has lost her passport abroad?
a: The lost property office in Bern
The embassy of the neighbouring country
41578.e: Swiss missions abroad help Swiss citizens in emergencies. This includes help when identity documents are lost or stolen.
41578.m: Abroad, the Swiss embassy or consulate helps in emergencies.

41579.q: Which document can a Swiss mission issue if your passport has been stolen abroad?
41579.e: With a provisional passport you can continue your journey or return home. It is issued only for a short time.
41579.m: After losing a passport, the embassy can issue a provisional passport.

41580.q: According to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, what right does a person arrested abroad have?
a: Contact with the consulate of their home country
A trial in their home country
A journey home at state expense
41580.e: Under Article 36, the authorities must inform an arrested foreigner that they can have their consulate notified. Consular officials may then visit them.
41580.m: Anyone arrested abroad may contact their consulate.

41581.q: Which federal department is responsible for Swiss embassies and consulates?
41581.e: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) looks after relations with other countries. This includes the embassies and consulates.
41581.m: The FDFA is responsible for Switzerland’s missions abroad.

41583.q: Does the Swiss embassy pay a fine that a Swiss tourist has received abroad?
a: No, the tourist must pay it
Yes, but only for young people
41583.e: Abroad, the principle of personal responsibility applies. The embassy helps in emergencies but does not pay fines, bail or lawyers’ fees.
41583.m: You have to pay fines abroad yourself.

41584.q: What is the FDFA’s information on the security situation in other countries called?
41584.e: In its travel advice, the FDFA informs about dangers such as unrest, crime or natural hazards. You should read it before every trip.
41584.m: Before a trip, it is worth checking the FDFA’s travel advice.

41585.q: Which mission abroad mainly looks after citizens’ passports and emergencies, not politics?
41585.e: Consulates carry out administrative tasks for their own citizens, for example identity documents or help in emergencies. Political relations, by contrast, are handled by the embassy.
41585.m: A consulate helps its own citizens abroad with practical matters.

41586.q: In which city did Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev meet for the first time in 1985?
41586.e: In November 1985 the US president and the Soviet party leader met in Geneva. The meeting is seen as the beginning of a thaw in the Cold War.
41586.m: Reagan and Gorbachev first met in Geneva in 1985.

41587.q: Which event happened in autumn 1989, shortly before the summit between Bush and Gorbachev in Malta?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The start of the Second World War
41587.e: The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. A few weeks later Bush and Gorbachev met in Malta. The summit is seen as a sign of the end of the Cold War.
41587.m: The Malta summit of 1989 stands for the end of the Cold War.

41589.q: What is the person called who prepares a summit for a head of state or government?
41589.e: Just as a mountain guide in the Himalayas prepares the way to the summit, the sherpa negotiates the texts and topics in advance. That way the leaders can decide quickly at the meeting.
41589.m: A sherpa prepares a summit for their leader.

41591.q: Which British prime minister coined the term “summit” for meetings of the powerful in 1950?
41591.e: In a speech in 1950 he spoke of a “parley at the summit” between the great powers. Since then meetings of heads of state and government have been called summits.
41591.m: Winston Churchill brought the word summit into politics.

41592.q: On which peninsula did the leaders of the USA, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union meet at Yalta in February 1945?
41592.e: The Yalta Conference took place on the Black Sea. There the three victorious powers discussed the order of Europe after the Second World War.
41592.m: The Yalta Conference took place in Crimea in 1945.

41594.q: What is a state of emergency?
a: A situation in which the government gets special powers
A particularly nice holiday across the country
A rule for behaviour in exams
A law on shop opening hours
41594.e: In a state of emergency the government gets special powers because of a crisis. Basic rights can be temporarily restricted.
41594.m: In a state of emergency the government gets special powers because of a crisis.

41595.q: Why do dictators like to misuse a state of emergency?
a: Because it lets them suspend basic rights
41595.e: In a state of emergency the government can restrict basic rights such as freedom of assembly. Dictators often extend it to persecute opponents more easily.
41595.m: A permanent state of emergency is a warning sign of dictatorship.

41596.q: After which event did France declare a state of emergency in November 2015?
a: After winning the football World Cup
41596.e: After the attacks of 13 November 2015 in Paris, France was in a state of emergency for around two years. During this time the police could search homes more easily.
41596.m: After the 2015 attacks France was in a state of emergency for around two years.

41597.q: After which event did Turkey declare a state of emergency in July 2016?
41597.e: After the failed coup attempt in July 2016, Turkey was in a state of emergency for two years. During this time tens of thousands of people were arrested or dismissed.
41597.m: Turkey was in a state of emergency for two years after the 2016 coup attempt.

41598.q: How long should a state of emergency really last?
a: Only as long as the crisis
41598.e: A state of emergency is only meant for emergencies. If it lasts very long, like around 30 years in Egypt, that is a warning sign.
41598.m: A state of emergency should only apply during the crisis.

41599.q: When, for example, can a state declare a state of emergency?
a: At the start of the summer holidays
41599.e: War, terrorism, epidemics or major natural disasters can justify a state of emergency. Then the state must be able to act quickly.
41599.m: A state of emergency is meant for severe crises.

41600.q: Why did the Federal Council declare the “extraordinary situation” in March 2020?
41600.e: Because of the coronavirus the Federal Council could order measures such as closing schools directly. The extraordinary situation lasted until June 2020.
41600.m: In the coronavirus crisis the Federal Council got special powers.

41601.q: Which basic right may never be restricted under the European Convention on Human Rights, even in an emergency?
41601.e: Article 15 of the ECHR allows some rights to be set aside in an emergency. But the ban on torture is one of the rights that always applies.
41601.m: The ban on torture applies even in the worst emergency.

41602.q: Which country declared martial law for a few hours in December 2024, until parliament lifted it?
41602.e: President Yoon Suk-yeol imposed martial law on 3 December 2024. Parliament voted against it that same night, and he had to withdraw it.
41602.m: In South Korea parliament stopped martial law in 2024 after a few hours.

41603.q: What could the President of the Weimar Republic do in emergencies?
41603.e: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution gave him this power. From 1930 Germany was governed almost entirely by emergency decrees.
41603.m: Emergency decrees made the Weimar Republic open to abuse.

41604.q: What happened after the Reichstag fire in February 1933?
a: There were free new elections without the NSDAP
The Reichstag was rebuilt straight away
41604.e: The day after the fire Hindenburg signed the Reichstag Fire Decree. Among other things it abolished freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.
41604.m: After the Reichstag fire in 1933 basic rights in Germany were abolished.

41605.q: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow Hitler’s government to do?
41605.e: With the Enabling Act the government could pass laws itself, even against the constitution. In this way the Reichstag gave up its own power.
41605.m: With the Enabling Act the German parliament stripped itself of power in 1933.

41606.q: Why did many students in Germany protest against the emergency laws in 1968?
a: They feared abuse as in the Weimar period
41606.e: The emergency laws were passed in May 1968. Many people remembered how emergency powers had been abused before 1933.
41606.m: The German emergency laws of 1968 sparked big protests.

41607.q: What did the Swiss Federal Council receive in 1939 at the start of the Second World War?
41607.e: Parliament gave the Federal Council extraordinary full powers. This is known as the full powers regime. It could then regulate many things without parliament and the people.
41607.m: In the Second World War the Federal Council governed with special full powers.

41608.q: Which situation did the Federal Council declare under the Epidemics Act in March 2020 because of the coronavirus?
41608.e: On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation. This allowed it to order measures such as school closures across Switzerland.
41608.m: In March 2020 the extraordinary situation applied in Switzerland.

41609.q: How do emergency powers in a democracy differ from emergency powers in a dictatorship?
a: They are only used in secret
41609.e: In democracies emergency powers are limited in time, and parliament and the courts can review them. Dictatorships, by contrast, often use emergency powers permanently and without checks.
41609.m: Democratic emergency powers are time-limited and checked.

41610.q: During which event did the Federal Council use emergency powers in March 2023?
a: The takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS
The building of the Gotthard Base Tunnel
41610.e: To prevent Credit Suisse from collapsing, the Federal Council issued emergency decrees in March 2023. This allowed UBS to take over the bank quickly.
41610.m: The rescue of Credit Suisse in 2023 was done with emergency powers.

41611.q: How many candidates are usually on offer per constituency in elections in North Korea?
41611.e: In North Korea there is normally only one candidate per constituency on the ballot paper. Anyone who wants to vote against must cross out the name, which hardly anyone dares to do.
41611.m: In North Korea there is no real choice in elections.

41612.q: How could people usually vote in elections in East Germany?
a: Not at all; there were never elections
41612.e: In East Germany there was a single list of the National Front. Voters could only approve it, because the share of seats was already fixed.
41612.m: In East Germany there was only a single list to vote for.
